title: Primariness and the Primary Factorisation PropertyThanks: IM CAS (RVO 67985840).
author: Antonio Acuaviva & Tomasz Kania
abstract: We study the relation between primariness of Banach spaces and the stronger operator-theoretic notions of the primary factorisation property (PFP) and the uniform primary factorisation property (UPFP). We revisit several classical primariness arguments and isolate the additional information needed to factor the identity through arbitrary operators. In the separable setting, this recovers quantitative factorisation versions of the Casazza–Kottman–Lin method for spaces with symmetric bases and treats the exceptional cases of \(\ell_{1}\) and \(\ell_{\infty}\). We then develop support-reduction and free-selection tools for uncountable direct sums, allowing one to transfer primariness and the PFP/UPFP from countable building blocks to non-separable \(\ell_{p}\)-, \(c_{0}\)- and more general symmetric sums. As applications, we obtain, among others, the primariness of \(C[0,1]^{*}\) under the negation of the Continuum Hypothesis and UPFP results for uncountable sums of ordinal \(C(\alpha)\)-spaces. Finally, using the finite-block representation of \(\mathcal{B}(\ell_{p})\), we prove a uniform primary factorisation theorem for the Banach space \(\mathcal{B}(\ell_{p})\), \(1<p<\infty\), and end with open problems concerning the gap between primariness and factorisation.
html:
1.

Introduction

−

A Banach space \(E\) is primary if for every bounded projection \(P\colon E\to E\) one has

\(PE\simeq E\qquad\text{or}\qquad(\mathrm{Id}_{E}-P)E\simeq E.\)

Equivalently, whenever \(E\) is written as a topological direct sum \(E=Y\oplus Z\), one of the two summands must already be isomorphic to \(E\). In this sense, primary spaces are building blocks for Banach-space decompositions; the systematic study of primary spaces was to an extend triggered by Lindenstrauss’ note , They belong to the same circle of ideas as prime spaces, indecomposable spaces and spaces with few operators, and they form one of the central structural classes in Banach-space theory.

Classical proofs of primariness usually proceed in two steps. First, one establishes a dichotomy for projections: given a projection \(P\) on \(E\), either \(PE\) or \((\mathrm{Id}_{E}-P)E\) contains a complemented copy of \(E\). Second, one invokes Pełczyński’s decomposition method to upgrade this complemented-copy dichotomy to an isomorphism statement. This strategy underlies many of the classical primariness results for sequence spaces, function spaces and iterated constructions.

In this paper we focus on a stronger operator-theoretic property. We say that \(E\) has the primary factorisation property (PFP) if for every bounded operator \(T\colon E\to E\), the identity operator factors either through \(T\) or through \(\mathrm{Id}_{E}-T\). If this can be done with a uniform bound on the factorisation constants, then \(E\) has the uniform primary factorisation property (UPFP). Thus the PFP replaces the projection dichotomy by a dichotomy for all bounded operators. Whenever \(E\) is stable under an \(\ell_{p}\)- or \(c_{0}\)-sum, the PFP implies primariness via Pełczyński’s decomposition method; however, the factorisation viewpoint is strictly stronger and is often the more natural one for the operator algebra \(\mathcal{B}(E)\). In particular, it is closely related to the problem of identifying the unique maximal ideal of \(\mathcal{B}(E)\).

Our first aim is to revisit a number of classical primariness arguments and extract from them the stronger conclusion of PFP or UPFP. The guiding principle is that many classical proofs already contain an operator dichotomy strong enough to produce factorisations, but this is often left implicit. A second aim is to make this mechanism systematic in the non-separable setting, where uncountable symmetry and free-selection arguments allow one to sharpen the classical perturbative constructions.

The paper has three main themes. In Section 3 we analyse Banach spaces with symmetric bases and refine the classical arguments of Casazza, Kottman and Lin. This yields quantitative factorisation results in the separable setting and, in particular, uniform versions of several classical primariness theorems. We also discuss variants involving \(\ell_{\infty}\) and iterated constructions.

In Section 4 we prove transfer principles for uncountable direct sums. Roughly speaking, once the relevant countable sum of a “small” Banach space \(X\) is known to be primary or to have the PFP/UPFP, one can often pass to uncountable \(\ell_{p}\)-, \(c_{0}\)- or more general symmetric sums of copies of \(X\). The key input is a support-reduction mechanism showing that operators into such large sums are controlled on a countable set of coordinates, combined with free-selection arguments that force exact vanishing of the off-diagonal interaction. These results lead to new examples of primary spaces and spaces with the UPFP, including uncountable sums of ordinal \(C(\alpha)\)-spaces.

In the final substantive section, we discuss further classes of primary spaces and the extent to which their known proofs yield the PFP or UPFP. Some cases fit naturally into the general framework developed earlier, while others require additional ideas. We also include a catalogue of examples and a final section of open problems, with particular emphasis on the gap between primariness and the factorisation properties.

A recurring point of the paper is that primariness and factorisation should be carefully distinguished. For instance, the classical theorem of Casazza–Kottman–Lin gives, in great generality, a range dichotomy for complemented copies, but a range dichotomy does not by itself yield a factorisation of the identity. One of the purposes of the present work is precisely to isolate those situations in which the stronger factorisation conclusion can in fact, be obtained.

2.

Preliminaries

−
2.1.

Basic notation and primariness

−

Throughout the paper, all Banach spaces are over the scalar field \(\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}\), and all operators are assumed to be bounded and linear. For Banach spaces \(E\) and \(F\) we write \(\mathcal{B}(E,F)\) for the Banach space of all bounded operators from \(E\) to \(F\), and \(\mathcal{B}(E)=\mathcal{B}(E,E)\). If \(Y\subseteq E\) is a closed subspace, we write \(Y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\hookrightarrow}}E\) to indicate that \(Y\) is complemented in \(E\). We denote by \(\operatorname{ran}T\) and \(\ker T\) the range and kernel of an operator \(T\).

Let \(E,F\) be Banach spaces and \(C\geqslant 1\). We write \(E\simeq_{C}F\) if there exists an isomorphism \(T\colon E\to F\) with \(\lVert T\rVert\,\lVert T^{-1}\rVert\leqslant C\). We set

\(d_{BM}(E,F)=\inf\{\lVert T\rVert\,\|T^{-1}\|:\ T\colon E\to F\text{ is an isomorphism}\}.\)

Thus \(d_{BM}(E,F)\leq C\) if and only if, for every ε > 0, there is an isomorphism of distortion at most C + ε.

Correction in this reading edition

The printed equivalence at the endpoint need not follow from an infimum. The approximate bound displayed here is the equivalence proved in Lean.

Let \(C\colon[1,\infty)\to[1,\infty)\) be an increasing function. A Banach space \(E\) is \(C\)-primary if for every bounded projection \(P\colon E\to E\) one has

\(PE\simeq_{C(\max\{1,\lVert P\rVert\})}E\qquad\text{or}\qquad(\mathrm{Id}_{E}-P)E\simeq_{C(\max\{1,\lVert P\rVert\})}E.\)

We call \(E\) uniformly primary if it is \(C\)-primary for some such function \(C\).

Correction in this reading edition

The control function is defined on [1, ∞). Evaluating it at max(1, ‖P‖) includes the zero projection; this is the thesis convention.

To show that a Banach space \(E\) is primary, it suffices to prove that for every projection \(P\colon E\to E\), either \(PE\simeq E\) or \((\mathrm{Id}_{E}-P)E\simeq E\). In practice, this is typically achieved in two steps. First, one proves a dichotomy for projections: for every projection \(P\colon E\to E\), either \(PE\) or \((\mathrm{Id}_{E}-P)E\) contains a complemented subspace isomorphic to \(E\). Second, one applies Pełczyński’s decomposition method to deduce that \(E\) is isomorphic to either \(PE\) or \((\mathrm{Id}_{E}-P)E\); we recall this method now.

(Pełczyński decomposition method ).

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces such that \(X\) is isomorphic to a complemented subspace of \(Y\) and \(Y\) is isomorphic to a complemented subspace of \(X\). Suppose further that

  1. (a)

    \(X\simeq X\oplus X\) and \(Y\simeq Y\oplus Y\), or

  2. (b)

    \(X\simeq c_{0}(X)\) or \(X\simeq\ell_{p}(X)\) for some \(1\leqslant p\leqslant\infty\).

Then \(X\simeq Y\).

The argument in Theorem 2.3 is qualitative. It is natural to ask whether one can obtain a quantitative version, controlling the Banach–Mazur distance between \(X\) and \(Y\) in terms of the corresponding complementability constants. We return to this question in Section 7.

In general, it is difficult to control the structure of \(PE\) (and that of \((\mathrm{Id}_{E}-P)E\)) and hence to guarantee condition (a). However, in many cases, condition (b) holds automatically for the space \(E\), and thus primariness reduces to establishing the dichotomy for projections. In passing, we observe that by , one may replace the \(\ell_{p}\)- or \(c_{0}\)-sum in (b) by a direct sum with respect to any Banach space with a symmetric basis.

Finally, we note that the two steps above are, in general, independent: one may establish a dichotomy for projections while still being unable to deduce primariness, as is the case for certain Banach spaces with a symmetric basis; see .

2.2.

Primary factorisation property

−

As discussed above, proofs of primariness typically proceed by establishing a dichotomy for projections. In many cases, one can obtain a stronger property, namely a dichotomy that holds for all bounded operators on the space.

Recall that if \(S,T\colon E\to E\) are bounded operators, we say that \(S\) factors through \(T\) if there exist bounded operators \(U,V\colon E\to E\) such that \(S=UTV\).

Let \(E\) be a Banach space.

  1. (a)

    We say that \(E\) has the primary factorisation property (PFP) if for every bounded operator \(T\colon E\to E\), the identity \(\mathrm{Id}_{E}\) factors either through \(T\) or through \(\mathrm{Id}_{E}-T\).

  2. (b)

    Let \(C\geqslant 1\). We say that \(E\) has the \(C\)-primary factorisation property (\(C\)-PFP) if for every bounded operator \(T\colon E\to E\) there exist bounded operators \(U,V\colon E\to E\) such that either

    \(UTV=\mathrm{Id}_{E}\quad\text{ or }\quad U(\mathrm{Id}_{E}-T)V=\mathrm{Id}_{E}\)

    and \(\lVert U\rVert\,\lVert V\rVert\leqslant C.\)

  3. (c)

    Let \(C\geqslant 1\). We say that \(E\) has the \(C^{+}\)-primary factorisation property (\(C^{+}\)-PFP) if it has the \((C+\varepsilon)\)-PFP for every \(\varepsilon>0\).

  4. (d)

    We say that \(E\) has the uniform primary factorisation property (UPFP) if there exists \(C\geqslant 1\) such that \(E\) has the \(C\)-PFP.

Naturally, although the constant may change, the UPFP is invariant under isomorphisms, as the following proposition shows.

Let \(E,F\) be Banach spaces and let \(S\colon E\to F\) be an isomorphism. If \(F\) has the \(C\)-PFP, then \(E\) has the \(C\,\lVert S\rVert^{2}\lVert S^{-1}\rVert^{2}\)-PFP.

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(T\in\mathcal{B}(E)\) and set \(\widetilde{T}=STS^{-1}\in\mathcal{B}(F)\). By the \(C\)-PFP in \(F\), there exist operators \(\widetilde{U},\widetilde{V}\in\mathcal{B}(F)\) such that either

\(\widetilde{U}\,\widetilde{T}\,\widetilde{V}=\mathrm{Id}_{F}\quad\text{or}\quad\widetilde{U}(\mathrm{Id}_{F}-\widetilde{T})\widetilde{V}=\mathrm{Id}_{F},\)

and \(\lVert\widetilde{U}\rVert\lVert\widetilde{V}\rVert\leqslant C\).

Set \(U=S^{-1}\widetilde{U}S\) and \(V=S^{-1}\widetilde{V}S\). Then \(UTV=\mathrm{Id}_{E}\) (or \(U(\mathrm{Id}_{E}-T)V=\mathrm{Id}_{E}\)), and

\(\lVert U\rVert\lVert V\rVert\leqslant(\lVert S\rVert\lVert S^{-1}\rVert)^{2}\,\lVert\widetilde{U}\rVert\lVert\widetilde{V}\rVert\leqslant C\,\lVert S\rVert^{2}\lVert S^{-1}\rVert^{2}.\qed\)

Note that the PFP is strictly stronger than the requirement that projection ranges contain complemented copies of the space. Nevertheless, it is often the more natural hypothesis in applications. Closely related factorisation dichotomies have appeared implicitly in the literature for some time. For example, in , spaces with PFP are treated under the name of ‘nice’ spaces for the purposes of that paper. The terminology of the primary factorisation property is now used explicitly in recent work on factorisation and maximal ideals; see, for instance, .

A closely related predecessor is due to Casazza–Kottman–Lin : if \(X\) has a symmetric basis and \(E\) contains a complemented copy of \(X\), then for every bounded operator \(T\colon E\to E\), either \(T(E)\) or \((\mathrm{Id}_{E}-T)(E)\) contains a complemented subspace isomorphic to \(X\). This is most naturally stated as a range dichotomy, not as a factorisation theorem: the presence of a complemented copy of \(X\) inside \(\operatorname{ran}T\) does not, in general, produce a bounded right inverse for \(T\). Nevertheless, the diagonal part of their argument contains the additional information needed for factorisation.

Although the PFP is, a priori, stronger than primariness, it appears to be at least as prevalent. The same is true for the UPFP, which, through a careful analysis of classical proofs of primariness, can often be obtained. Indeed, while primariness alone does not impose any uniform operator-theoretic dichotomy, many such proofs implicitly establish the PFP, and in several cases even its uniform version.

As observed in the factorisation literature, Pełczyński’s decomposition method (Theorem 2.3) shows that the PFP implies primariness whenever the space is \(\ell_{p}\)-stable. However, verifying this structural assumption is not always straightforward, and a space can have the PFP without primariness being known. For instance, while \(\ell_{\infty}/c_{0}\) is known to have the UPFP (see Proposition 5.1), its primariness is only known under the additional assumption of \(\mathrm{CH}\).

Finally, the PFP is closely related to the problem of the existence of a unique maximal ideal in \(\mathcal{B}(E)\). Indeed, Dosev and Johnson introduced the set

\(\mathcal{M}_{E}=\{T\in\mathcal{B}(E):\mathrm{Id}_{E}\text{ does not factor through }T\}\subseteq\mathcal{B}(E),\)

as a natural candidate for such an ideal. For a deeper discussion of this problem, and in particular for the treatment of the cases \(L_{p}\), \(1\leqslant p<\infty\), we refer the reader to .

We have the following observation.

Assume that E is nonzero.

Let \(E\) be a Banach space and set

\(\mathcal{M}_{E}=\{T\in\mathcal{B}(E):\ \mathrm{Id}_{E}\text{ does not factor through }T\}.\)

Then \(E\) has the PFP if and only if \(\mathcal{M}_{E}\) is a maximal ideal of \(\mathcal{B}(E)\). In this case \(\mathcal{M}_{E}\) is the unique maximal ideal of \(\mathcal{B}(E)\).

Correction in this reading edition

The nonzero hypothesis is necessary. For the zero space the set of nonfactorising operators is empty, so the printed equivalence fails.

Proof.Fold proof

Assume first that \(E\) has the PFP. Plainly \(\mathrm{Id}_{E}\notin\mathcal{M}_{E}\), and \(\mathcal{M}_{E}\) is stable under left and right multiplication by arbitrary operators: if \(\mathrm{Id}_{E}\) factors through \(ATB\), then it factors through \(T\).

We next check additivity. Suppose that \(S,T\in\mathcal{M}_{E}\) and that \(S+T\notin\mathcal{M}_{E}\). Then there are \(A,B\in\mathcal{B}(E)\) such that

\(A(S+T)B=\mathrm{Id}_{E}.\)

Apply the PFP to the operator \(ASB\). Since

\(\mathrm{Id}_{E}-ASB=ATB,\)

the identity factors either through \(ASB\) or through \(ATB\), and therefore through \(S\) or through \(T\), a contradiction. Thus \(\mathcal{M}_{E}\) is a proper two-sided ideal. It is closed: if \(T_{n}\to T\) and \(\mathrm{Id}_{E}=ATB\), then \(AT_{n}B\to\mathrm{Id}_{E}\), so for all large \(n\) the operator \(AT_{n}B\) is invertible and \(\mathrm{Id}_{E}\) factors through \(T_{n}\).

Finally, every proper ideal \(\mathcal{J}\) of \(\mathcal{B}(E)\) is contained in \(\mathcal{M}_{E}\); indeed, if \(T\in\mathcal{J}\) and \(\mathrm{Id}_{E}\) factors through \(T\), then \(\mathrm{Id}_{E}\in\mathcal{J}\). Hence \(\mathcal{M}_{E}\) is the largest proper ideal, and therefore the unique maximal ideal.

Conversely, suppose that \(\mathcal{M}_{E}\) is a maximal ideal. If the PFP failed, then there would be \(T\in\mathcal{B}(E)\) such that both \(T\) and \(\mathrm{Id}_{E}-T\) belong to \(\mathcal{M}_{E}\). Since \(\mathcal{M}_{E}\) is an ideal, it is a linear subspace, and hence

\(\mathrm{Id}_{E}=T+(\mathrm{Id}_{E}-T)\in\mathcal{M}_{E},\)

contradicting properness. Thus \(E\) has the PFP. ∎

The preceding proposition identifies the PFP with the assertion that the specific set \(\mathcal{M}_{E}\) is a maximal ideal. It should not be read as saying that the mere existence of a unique maximal ideal in \(\mathcal{B}(E)\) automatically implies the PFP: in examples where a unique maximal ideal is known by other means, one must still verify that it coincides with \(\mathcal{M}_{E}\).

2.3.

A catalogue of primary spaces

−

We have not attempted full completeness, and some examples, refinements, or later quantitative improvements may be missing. For readability, we group together closely related classes of examples, even when the original results were obtained at different times. We have also included a few entries that are especially relevant to the present paper, namely those concerning mixed sums, operator spaces and factorisation-based methods.

Recent work on strategically reproducible bases, stopping-time spaces and Haar-system Hardy spaces shows that the factorisation viewpoint extends well beyond the classical symmetric-basis setting; see, for example, .

The table is deliberately representative rather than exhaustive. We have kept a broadly chronological order, while grouping together closely related classes when this improves readability. The last entries illustrate the point of view of the present paper: several classical primariness arguments can be sharpened to factorisation dichotomies, while the uncountable transfer principles below produce new non-separable examples once the relevant support-reduction hypotheses are available.

The present paper adds two kinds of entries to the classical list. First, several classical primariness arguments are upgraded to PFP or UPFP statements. Second, the uncountable transfer results below produce non-separable analogues such as \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma,C(\alpha))\) and more general \(E(\Gamma,X)\)-sums under support-reduction hypotheses.

3.

Symmetric-like bases and the UPFP

−

As we mentioned, the standard methods for proving primariness of a space rely on two main steps: proving a factorisation of the identity for (projection) operators and then applying the Pełczyński decomposition method. In this section, we will discuss the first problem in the particular case of Banach spaces with a (sub-)symmetric basis.

We begin by fixing some notation. Let \(X\) be a Banach space with a normalised basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) and biorthogonal functionals \((e_{n}^{*})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\). We say that the basis is symmetric if it is equivalent to each of its permutations and sign-changes; after replacing the norm by an equivalent one, we may and shall assume that the basis is equipped with a symmetric norm. In particular, the basis is \(1\)-unconditional.

The aim of this section is twofold. First, we revisit the classical separable arguments of Casazza, Kottman and Lin and recast them in a form that yields factorisations of the identity through arbitrary operators, rather than only complemented copies inside operator ranges. Second, we record a number of natural extensions of these ideas, including constructions involving \(\ell_{1}\) and \(\ell_{\infty}\).

As will become apparent later, the case when the basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) is equivalent to the unit basis of \(\ell_{1}\) behaves rather differently from all other cases. Therefore, from now on and unless explicitly stated otherwise, we assume that the basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) is not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\).

3.1.

Banach spaces \(X\) with (sub-)symmetric basis

−

We begin with what is arguably the simpler class of spaces known to possess the PFP factorisation property: Banach spaces with a symmetric basis. The key ingredients for the proof go back to the work of Casazza and Lin .

Roughly speaking, the argument shows that for a given operator \(T\colon X\to X\), either \(T\) or \(\mathrm{Id}_{X}-T\) acts (almost) as a diagonal operator on some subsequence \((e_{n_{k}})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) of the basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), with the diagonal entries uniformly bounded away from zero. The proof relies on a gliding-hump argument together with two key observations: first, under the action of \(T\) each basis element \(e_{n}\) can, up to a small error, affect only finitely many other elements; and second, each \(e_{n}\) can, again up to a small error, be affected by only finitely many others. We will formalise this shortly. Throughout this section, we fix a Banach space \(X\) with a symmetric norm and symmetric basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\).

We will need the following result of Casazza, Kottman, and Lin . For completeness, we provide a proof.

Let \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a normalised unconditional basis of a Banach space \(X\). Then no subsequence of \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) spans a subspace isomorphic to \(\ell_{1}\) if and only if \(\lim_{m\to\infty}e_{n}^{*}(Te_{m})=0\) for any operator \(T\colon X\to X\) and any \(n\in\mathbb{N}\).

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(K\) be the unconditional constant of \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\).

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Assume that

\(\lim_{m\to\infty}e_{n}^{*}(Te_{m})=0\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal{B}(X)\text{ and every }n\in\mathbb{N}.\)

Fix \(f\in X^{*}\) and \(n_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\), and consider the rank–one operator

\(T_{f}\colon X\to X,\qquad T_{f}(x)=f(x)\,e_{n_{0}}.\)

Then, for every \(m\in\mathbb{N}\),

\(e_{n_{0}}^{*}(T_{f}e_{m})=e_{n_{0}}^{*}\bigl(f(e_{m})e_{n_{0}}\bigr)=f(e_{m}).\)

Hence \(f(e_{m})\to 0\) for every \(f\in X^{*}\), i.e. \((e_{m})_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\) is weakly null. If a subsequence \((e_{m_{k}})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) spanned a subspace isomorphic to \(\ell_{1}\), then the corresponding isomorphism \(S\colon[e_{m_{k}}:k\in\mathbb{N}]\to\ell_{1}\) would send the weakly null sequence \((e_{m_{k}})\) to a weakly null sequence in \(\ell_{1}\), hence (by the Schur property of \(\ell_{1}\)) to a norm–null sequence. Since \(S\) is an isomorphism and \((e_{m_{k}})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) is normalised, this is impossible. Therefore, no subsequence of \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) spans a copy of \(\ell_{1}\).

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Assume now that no subsequence of \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) spans a subspace isomorphic to \(\ell_{1}\). Suppose, towards a contradiction, that there exist \(T\in\mathcal{B}(X)\) and \(n_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\limsup_{m\to\infty}\bigl|e_{n_{0}}^{*}(Te_{m})\bigr|>0.\)

Then there are \(\varepsilon>0\) and a strictly increasing sequence \((m_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) such that for all \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) we have \(\bigl|e_{n_{0}}^{*}(Te_{m_{k}})\bigr|\geqslant\varepsilon.\) Set \(f=T^{*}e_{n_{0}}^{*}\in X^{*}\). Passing to a subsequence and, in the complex case, to a sector of aperture strictly smaller than \(\pi/2\), we may find a unimodular scalar \(\lambda\) such that

\(\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\lambda f(e_{m_{k}})\bigr)\geqslant\varepsilon/2\qquad(k\in\mathbb{N}).\)

In the real case this is just the usual passage to a subsequence of constant sign. Replacing \(f\) by \(\lambda f\), we therefore have

\(\operatorname{Re}f(e_{m_{k}})\geqslant\varepsilon/2\qquad(k\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Let \((a_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) be finitely supported. By unconditionality,

\(\Bigl\|\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}}a_{k}e_{m_{k}}\Bigr\|\geqslant\frac{1}{K}\Bigl\|\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}}|a_{k}|e_{m_{k}}\Bigr\|.\)

Moreover,

\(\displaystyle\Bigl\|\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}}|a_{k}|e_{m_{k}}\Bigr\|\) \(\displaystyle\geqslant\frac{1}{\|f\|}\,\operatorname{Re}f\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}}|a_{k}|e_{m_{k}}\Bigr)\)
\(\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\|f\|}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}}|a_{k}|\operatorname{Re}f(e_{m_{k}})\geqslant\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|f\|}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}}|a_{k}|.\)

Combining these estimates gives

\(\Bigl\|\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}}a_{k}e_{m_{k}}\Bigr\|\geqslant\frac{\varepsilon}{2K\|f\|}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}}|a_{k}|.\)

On the other hand, since the basis is normalised,

\(\Bigl\|\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}}a_{k}e_{m_{k}}\Bigr\|\leqslant\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}}|a_{k}|.\)

Hence \((e_{m_{k}})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) is equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\), so its closed linear span is isomorphic to \(\ell_{1}\), contradicting the hypothesis. Therefore \(\lim_{m\to\infty}e_{n}^{*}(Te_{m})=0\) for all \(T\in\mathcal{B}(X)\) and all \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). ∎

We also require the following elementary observation.

Let \(X\) be a Banach space with a normalised \(1\)-unconditional basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), and let \(T\colon X\to X\) be bounded. Suppose there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that

\(|e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{n+m}}\qquad(m,n\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Then \(\lVert T\rVert\leqslant\varepsilon\).

Proof.Fold proof

For each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\),

\(\lVert Te_{n}\rVert=\Bigl\|\sum_{m\in\mathbb{N}}(e_{m}^{*}Te_{n})e_{m}\Bigr\|\leqslant\sum_{m\in\mathbb{N}}|e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}|<\sum_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{n+m}}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{n}}.\)

Now let \(x=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}a_{n}e_{n}\in B_{X}\). Since the basis is normalised and \(1\)-unconditional, we have \(\lVert e_{n}^{*}\rVert=1\) for every \(n\), and therefore \(|a_{n}|=|e_{n}^{*}(x)|\leqslant 1\). Hence

\(\lVert Tx\rVert=\Bigl\|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}a_{n}Te_{n}\Bigr\|\leqslant\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|a_{n}|\,\lVert Te_{n}\rVert<\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{n}}=\varepsilon.\)

This proves that \(\lVert T\rVert\leqslant\varepsilon\). ∎

Let \(X\) be a separable Banach space with a symmetric basis, not equivalent to the \(\ell_{1}\)-basis, and a symmetric norm. Then \(X\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP.

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(T\colon X\to X\) and fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(\delta>0\) small enough so that

\(\frac{2}{1-\delta}<2+\varepsilon.\)

For each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) we have

\(1=e_{n}^{*}(\mathrm{Id}_{X}-T)e_{n}+e_{n}^{*}Te_{n}.\)

Hence, there exists an infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that either \(|e_{n}^{*}Te_{n}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\) for all \(n\in M\), or \(|e_{n}^{*}(\mathrm{Id}_{X}-T)e_{n}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\) for all \(n\in M\). Replacing \(T\) by \(\mathrm{Id}_{X}-T\) if necessary, we may assume that \(|e_{n}^{*}Te_{n}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\) for all \(n\in M\). Enumerate \(M\) increasingly as \((n_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\).

For each fixed \(k\), since \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) is a normalised basis,

\(\lim_{j\to\infty}e_{n_{j}}^{*}Te_{n_{k}}=0,\)

and by Lemma 3.1, together with the assumption that the basis is not equivalent to the unit basis of \(\ell_{1}\),

\(\lim_{j\to\infty}e_{n_{k}}^{*}Te_{n_{j}}=0.\)

We now thin the sequence explicitly. Suppose \(n_{1},\ldots,n_{k-1}\) have been chosen. The two preceding limits allow us to choose \(n_{k}\in M\) larger than all previously chosen indices so that, for every \(1\leqslant j<k\),

\(|e_{n_{j}}^{*}Te_{n_{k}}|<\frac{\delta}{2^{j+k+1}}\quad\text{and}\quad|e_{n_{k}}^{*}Te_{n_{j}}|<\frac{\delta}{2^{j+k+1}}.\)

Since all diagonal entries on \(M\) have modulus at least \(1/2\), the resulting subsequence, still denoted \((n_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\), satisfies for all \(j\neq k\)

\(\left|\frac{e_{n_{j}}^{*}Te_{n_{k}}}{e_{n_{j}}^{*}Te_{n_{j}}}\right|<\frac{\delta}{2^{j+k}}.\)

Let \(Y=[e_{n_{k}}:k\in\mathbb{N}]\). Since \(X\) is equipped with a symmetric norm, \(Y\) is isometrically isomorphic to \(X\). Let \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) be the coordinate projection and \(\iota\colon Y\hookrightarrow X\) the canonical inclusion. Define the diagonal operator \(D\colon Y\to Y\) by

\(De_{n_{k}}=\frac{1}{e_{n_{k}}^{*}Te_{n_{k}}}e_{n_{k}}\qquad(k\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Since \(|e_{n_{k}}^{*}Te_{n_{k}}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\), we have \(\lVert D\rVert\leqslant 2\).

Set

\(A=D\pi T\iota\qquad\text{and}\qquad S=\mathrm{Id}_{Y}-A.\)

Then \(e_{n_{k}}^{*}Se_{n_{k}}=0\) for every \(k\), while for \(j\neq k\),

\(|e_{n_{j}}^{*}Se_{n_{k}}|=\left|\frac{e_{n_{j}}^{*}Te_{n_{k}}}{e_{n_{j}}^{*}Te_{n_{j}}}\right|<\frac{\delta}{2^{j+k}}.\)

By Lemma 3.2, \(\lVert S\rVert<\delta\). Therefore \(A=\mathrm{Id}_{Y}-S\) is invertible, and if we put \(R=A^{-1}\) then

\(\lVert R\rVert\leqslant\frac{1}{1-\delta}.\)

Hence

\(\mathrm{Id}_{Y}=RD\pi T\iota.\)

If \(J\colon X\to Y\) denotes the canonical isometric isomorphism induced by the subsequence \((e_{n_{k}})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\), then

\(\mathrm{Id}_{X}=J^{-1}RD\pi\,T\,\iota J.\)

Thus \(\mathrm{Id}_{X}\) factors through either \(T\) or \(\mathrm{Id}_{X}-T\), and the factorisation constant is bounded by

\(\lVert J^{-1}RD\pi\rVert\,\lVert\iota J\rVert\leqslant\frac{2}{1-\delta}<2+\varepsilon.\)

This proves that \(X\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP. ∎

The same argument applies to spaces with a subsymmetric basis after replacing the isometric subsequence identifications by the canonical isomorphisms supplied by subsymmetry and tracking the corresponding constants. The non-separable setting is treated separately in Section 4.

3.1.1.

Iterated constructions not involving \(\ell_{1}\)

−

For a Banach space \(X\) with an unconditional basis \(\mathcal{E}=(e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) and a Banach space \(Y\), we recall that we can define the \((X,\mathcal{E})\)-sum of \(Y\), as the space

\((X,\mathcal{E})(Y)=\{(y_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}Y:\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\lVert y_{n}\rVert e_{n}\in X\},\)

equipped with norm

\(\lVert(y_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\rVert=\lVert\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\lVert y_{n}\rVert e_{n}\rVert\)

Observe that the previous sum depends not only on \(X\) but also on the choice of unconditional basis \(\mathcal{E}=(e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\). In an abuse of notation, we will simply write \(X(Y)\), where the choice of basis of \(X\) will be implicitly assumed.

For each \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(\mathbb{N}^{k}\) be the set of sequences \(\{(i_{1},\dots,i_{k}):i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{k}\in\mathbb{N}\}\). Given two sequences \(I=(i_{1},\dots,i_{k})\in\mathbb{N}^{k}\) and \(J=(j_{1},\dots,j_{r})\in\mathbb{N}^{r}\) we define its concatenation \(I\smallfrown J=(i_{1},\dots,i_{k},j_{1},\dots,j_{r})\in\mathbb{N}^{k+r}\). For a sequence \(I=(i_{1},\dots,i_{k})\) we denote by \(|I|\) the length of the sequence, that is, \(|I|=k\).

Let \(X_{1},\dots,X_{N}\) be Banach spaces with symmetric basis \(\mathcal{E}_{j}=(e^{j}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), \(j=1,\dots,N\) and symmetric norms, and let \(Y=X_{1}(X_{2}(\dots(X_{N-1}(X_{N}))))\).

For each ordered \(I=(i_{1},\dots,i_{N})\in\mathbb{N}^{N}\) we can define \(e_{I}=(0,\dots,e_{J},0,\dots,0)\) where \(J=(i_{2},\dots,i_{N})\in\mathbb{N}^{N-1}\), \(e_{J}\in X_{2}(X_{3}(\dots(X_{N})))\) is defined recursively in the natural way and it is placed in the \(i_{1}\)th-coordinate. Let \(\Phi:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}^{N}\) be the Cantor ordering. It is clear that \(\mathcal{E}=(e_{\Phi(n)})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) is a \(1\)-unconditional basis for \(Y\).

We now show that a Banach space \(Y\) constructed as above always has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP. The proof is an iterative version of the argument used in Theorem 3.3; see also the ideas underlying . Before proceeding to the proof, some notation is in order.

Let \(Y=X_{1}(X_{2}(\dots(X_{N-1}(X_{N}))))\) and \(T\colon Y\to Y\) be an operator. We define the property of a sequence \(J\in\bigcup_{k=1}^{N}\mathbb{N}^{k}\) supporting \(T\) by backward induction on the length of \(J\):

  1. (1)

    Base Case (\(|J|=N\)): A sequence \(I\in\mathbb{N}^{N}\) supports \(T\) if \(|e_{I}^{*}Te_{I}|\geqslant 1/2\).

  2. (2)

    Inductive Step (\(|J|<N)\): A sequence \(J\in\mathbb{N}^{k}\) (for \(1\leqslant k<N\)) supports \(T\) if the set of extensions

    \(\{j\in\mathbb{N}:J\smallfrown(j)\text{ supports }T\}\)

    is infinite.

The following is immediate by backward induction, exploiting the fact that for any operator \(T\colon Y\to Y\) and any \(I\in\mathbb{N}^{N}\), then \(I\) supports either \(T\) or \(\mathrm{Id}_{Y}-T\).

Let \(Y=X_{1}(X_{2}(\cdots(X_{N-1}(X_{N}))))\) and let \(T\in\mathcal{B}(Y)\). Then one of the two operators \(T\) and \(\mathrm{Id}_{Y}-T\) is supported by infinitely many first-level nodes \((i_{1})\).

Proof.Fold proof

We prove by backward induction that every node \(J\in\bigcup_{k=1}^{N-1}\mathbb{N}^{k}\) supports at least one of \(T\) and \(\mathrm{Id}_{Y}-T\). At level \(N\), every terminal node \(I\in\mathbb{N}^{N}\) supports at least one of them, since

\(1=e_{I}^{*}Te_{I}+e_{I}^{*}(\mathrm{Id}_{Y}-T)e_{I}\)

and hence at least one of the two summands has modulus at least \(1/2\).

Assume the assertion has been proved at level \(k+1\). If a node \(J\in\mathbb{N}^{k}\) supported neither \(T\) nor \(\mathrm{Id}_{Y}-T\), then only finitely many immediate successors \(J\smallfrown(j)\) would support \(T\), and only finitely many would support \(\mathrm{Id}_{Y}-T\). This contradicts the induction hypothesis applied to all immediate successors. Thus, every node at level \(k\) supports at least one of the two operators. In particular, every first-level node supports at least one of the two alternatives. Since there are only two alternatives, one of them is supported by infinitely many first-level nodes. ∎

(CKL tree selection).

Let \(Y=X_{1}(X_{2}(\cdots(X_{N-1}(X_{N}))))\), where each \(X_{j}\) has a symmetric basis not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\). Let \(T\in\mathcal{B}(Y)\) and let \(\eta>0\). Suppose that infinitely many first-level nodes support \(T\). Then there is a subset \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{N}\), order-isomorphic to \(\mathbb{N}^{N}\) in the natural tree sense, such that

\(Z=[e_{I}:I\in\mathcal{A}]\)

is isometrically isomorphic to \(Y\), every \(I\in\mathcal{A}\) satisfies

\(|e_{I}^{*}Te_{I}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2},\)

and, after enumerating \(\mathcal{A}\) as \((I_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\),

\(|e_{I_{j}}^{*}Te_{I_{k}}|<\frac{\eta}{2^{j+k+1}}\qquad(j\neq k).\)
Proof.Fold proof

The supporting condition gives an infinitely splitting subtree of terminal nodes on which the diagonal estimate holds. The product basis \((e_{I})_{I\in\mathbb{N}^{N}}\) has no subsequence equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\): this follows by induction on \(N\), since an infinite sequence of terminal nodes either has infinitely many distinct first coordinates, in which case it is equivalent to a subsequence of the basis of \(X_{1}\), or else it has an infinite subsequence contained in a single first fibre.

Lemma 3.1 therefore gives \(e_{I}^{*}Te_{J}\longrightarrow 0\) whenever \(I\) is fixed and \(J\) tends to infinity inside any infinitely splitting branch-subtree. Since \((e_{I})\) is a Schauder basis, we also have \(e_{J}^{*}Te_{I}\longrightarrow 0\) for fixed \(I\) as \(J\) tends to infinity. Now enumerate the terminal nodes of the desired subtree as they are chosen. At the \(m\)th step only finitely many previously selected terminal nodes have to be protected, and the two displayed limits allow us to discard finitely many successors from finitely many nodes while keeping every remaining node infinitely splitting. Choosing the next terminal node from the remaining tree and iterating this thinning gives an infinitely splitting subtree whose terminal set can be enumerated as \((I_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) and satisfies

\(|e_{I_{j}}^{*}Te_{I_{k}}|<\frac{\eta}{2^{j+k+1}}\qquad(j\neq k).\)

The resulting subtree is order-isomorphic to \(\mathbb{N}^{N}\), so symmetry of the bases identifies its closed span isometrically with \(Y\). ∎

Let \(X_{1},\dots,X_{N}\) be Banach spaces with symmetric norms and symmetric bases \(\mathcal{E}_{j}\), none of which is equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\). Then the Banach space \(Y=X_{1}(X_{2}(\dots(X_{N-1}(X_{N}))))\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP.

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(T\in\mathcal{B}(Y)\) and fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(\delta>0\) such that

\(\frac{2}{1-\delta}<2+\varepsilon.\)

By Lemma 3.6, after replacing \(T\) by \(\mathrm{Id}_{Y}-T\) if necessary, infinitely many first-level nodes support \(T\).

Apply Lemma 3.7 with \(\eta=\delta\) and write the selected terminal nodes as \((I_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\). Let

\(Z=[e_{I_{k}}:k\in\mathbb{N}].\)

Then \(Z\) is isometrically isomorphic to \(Y\). Let \(\pi\colon Y\to Z\) be the coordinate projection and \(\iota\colon Z\hookrightarrow Y\) the inclusion. Define \(D\colon Z\to Z\) by

\(De_{I_{k}}=\frac{1}{e_{I_{k}}^{*}Te_{I_{k}}}e_{I_{k}}\qquad(k\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Then \(\|D\|\leqslant 2\). As in the proof of Theorem 3.3, the operator \(S=\mathrm{Id}_{Z}-D\pi T\iota\) satisfies \(\|S\|<\delta\). Hence \(D\pi T\iota\) is invertible; writing \(R=(D\pi T\iota)^{-1}\), we have

\(\mathrm{Id}_{Z}=RD\pi T\iota\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|RD\|\leqslant\frac{2}{1-\delta}<2+\varepsilon.\)

If \(J\colon Y\to Z\) is the canonical isometric isomorphism induced by the selected subtree, then

\(\mathrm{Id}_{Y}=J^{-1}RD\pi\,T\,\iota J.\)

Thus the identity on \(Y\) factors through either \(T\) or \(\mathrm{Id}_{Y}-T\) with constant smaller than \(2+\varepsilon\). ∎

3.2.

The \(\ell_{1}\)-case

−
3.2.1.

The space \(\ell_{1}\).

−

The fact that \(\ell_{1}\) is primary, and indeed prime, goes back to Pełczyński , whose argument exploits the complete homogeneity of the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\). To establish the UPFP for this space, we shall use a different method, which will also be useful for the iterated constructions.

Observe that the key difference with other Banach spaces with a symmetric basis is that Lemma 3.1 is no longer true. We see now how to solve this.

Let \(T\colon\ell_{1}\to\ell_{1}\) be an operator. Then for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists an infinite subset \(M=\{m_{k}:k\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that for all \(k<j\) we have \(|e_{m_{k}}^{*}Te_{m_{j}}|<\varepsilon.\)

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(\varepsilon>0\) be fixed. We will construct inductively a strictly increasing sequence \((m_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) and a decreasing sequence of infinite subsets \((M_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) of \(\mathbb{N}\) such that \(m_{k}\in M_{k-1}\), \(M_{k}\subseteq M_{k-1}\), \(m_{k}<n\) for every \(n\in M_{k}\), and

\(|e_{m_{k}}^{*}Te_{n}|<\varepsilon\quad\text{for all }n\in M_{k}.\)

Once this is done, if \(k<j\), then \(m_{j}\in M_{j-1}\subseteq M_{k}\), and hence \(|e_{m_{k}}^{*}Te_{m_{j}}|<\varepsilon,\) as required.

Set \(M_{0}=\mathbb{N}\). Suppose that \(M_{k-1}\) has already been chosen and is infinite. Choose \(N_{k}\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(N_{k}>m_{k-1}\) if \(k>1\), and such that

\(|M_{k-1}\cap\{1,\dots,N_{k}\}|>\lVert T\rVert/\varepsilon.\)

Set \(F_{k}=M_{k-1}\cap\{1,\dots,N_{k}\}\), so that \(F_{k}\) is finite and \(|F_{k}|>\lVert T\rVert/\varepsilon\). For each \(n\in M_{k-1}\) with \(n>N_{k}\), define

\(A_{k}(n)=\{m\in F_{k}:|e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}|\geqslant\varepsilon\}.\)

Since

\(\lVert T\rVert\geqslant\lVert Te_{n}\rVert\geqslant\sum_{m\in A_{k}(n)}|e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}|\geqslant|A_{k}(n)|\varepsilon,\)

we have \(|A_{k}(n)|\leqslant\lVert T\rVert/\varepsilon<|F_{k}|\). Hence, for each \(n\in M_{k-1}\) with \(n>N_{k}\), there exists \(m\in F_{k}\) such that \(m\notin A_{k}(n)\), that is, \(|e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}|<\varepsilon\).

Since \(F_{k}\) is finite and \(M_{k-1}\cap\{n\in\mathbb{N}:n>N_{k}\}\) is infinite, the pigeonhole principle yields some \(m_{k}\in F_{k}\) such that the set

\(M_{k}=\{n\in M_{k-1}:n>N_{k}\text{ and }|e_{m_{k}}^{*}Te_{n}|<\varepsilon\}\)

is infinite. This completes the induction. ∎

We also have the following analogue to Lemma 3.2.

Let \(T\colon\ell_{1}\to\ell_{1}\) be an operator. Suppose that there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for all \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) we have

\(\sum_{m\in\mathbb{N}}|e^{*}_{m}Te_{n}|<\varepsilon.\)

Then \(\lVert T\rVert\leqslant\varepsilon\).

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(x=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}x_{n}e_{n}\in B_{\ell_{1}}\). Then

\(\lVert Tx\rVert=\lVert\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}x_{n}Te_{n}\rVert\leqslant\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|x_{n}|\lVert Te_{n}\rVert\leqslant\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\lVert Te_{n}\rVert\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|x_{n}|\leqslant\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\lVert Te_{n}\rVert.\)

On the other hand, for each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) we have

\(\lVert Te_{n}\rVert=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{N}}|e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}|<\varepsilon.\)

Hence \(\lVert Tx\rVert<\varepsilon\) for every \(x\in B_{\ell_{1}}\), and therefore \(\lVert T\rVert\leqslant\varepsilon\). ∎

The space \(\ell_{1}\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP.

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(T\colon\ell_{1}\to\ell_{1}\) and fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(\delta>0\) small enough so that

\(\frac{2}{1-\delta}<2+\varepsilon.\)

As in the proof of Theorem 3.3, after replacing \(T\) by \(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{1}}-T\) if necessary, passing to an isometric copy and reindexing, we may assume that

\(|e_{n}^{*}Te_{n}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\qquad(n\in\mathbb{N}).\)

We now recursively choose a strictly increasing sequence \((m_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) and decreasing infinite sets

\(\mathbb{N}=M_{0}\supseteq M_{1}\supseteq M_{2}\supseteq\ldots\)

so that for every \(k\in\mathbb{N}\):

  1. (i)

    \(m_{k}\in M_{k-1}\);

  2. (ii)

    \(|e_{m_{k}}^{*}Te_{n}|<\delta/2^{k+2}\) for all \(n\in M_{k}\);

  3. (iii)

    \(\sum_{n\in M_{k}}|e_{n}^{*}Te_{m_{k}}|<\delta/2^{k+2}\).

Suppose that \(M_{k-1}\) has been chosen. By the argument used in Lemma 3.9, applied inside the infinite set \(M_{k-1}\) with threshold \(\delta/2^{k+2}\), we may choose \(m_{k}\in M_{k-1}\) and an infinite set \(A_{k}\subseteq M_{k-1}\) with \(m_{k}<n\) for all \(n\in A_{k}\) such that

\(|e_{m_{k}}^{*}Te_{n}|<\delta/2^{k+2}\qquad(n\in A_{k}).\)

Since \(Te_{m_{k}}\in\ell_{1}\), there exists an infinite subset \(M_{k}\subseteq A_{k}\) such that

\(\sum_{n\in M_{k}}|e_{n}^{*}Te_{m_{k}}|<\delta/2^{k+2}.\)

This completes the construction.

Set \(Y=[e_{m_{k}}:k\in\mathbb{N}]\). Then \(Y\) is isometric to \(\ell_{1}\). Let \(\pi\colon\ell_{1}\to Y\) be the coordinate projection and \(\iota\colon Y\hookrightarrow\ell_{1}\) the inclusion. Define the diagonal operator \(D\colon Y\to Y\) by

\(De_{m_{k}}=\frac{1}{e_{m_{k}}^{*}Te_{m_{k}}}e_{m_{k}}\qquad(k\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Since \(|e_{m_{k}}^{*}Te_{m_{k}}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\), we have \(\lVert D\rVert\leqslant 2\).

Set

\(A=D\pi T\iota\qquad\text{and}\qquad S=\mathrm{Id}_{Y}-A.\)

Then \(e_{m_{k}}^{*}Se_{m_{k}}=0\) for every \(k\). Moreover, for fixed \(j\),

\(\displaystyle\sum_{k\neq j}|e_{m_{k}}^{*}Se_{m_{j}}|\) \(\displaystyle\leqslant 2\sum_{k\neq j}|e_{m_{k}}^{*}Te_{m_{j}}|\)
\(\displaystyle=2\sum_{k<j}|e_{m_{k}}^{*}Te_{m_{j}}|+2\sum_{k>j}|e_{m_{k}}^{*}Te_{m_{j}}|\)
\(\displaystyle<2\sum_{k<j}\frac{\delta}{2^{k+2}}+2\sum_{n\in M_{j}}|e_{n}^{*}Te_{m_{j}}|\)
\(\displaystyle<\frac{\delta}{2}+\frac{\delta}{2^{j+1}}<\delta.\)

Hence, by Lemma 3.10, \(\lVert S\rVert\leqslant\delta\). Therefore \(A=\mathrm{Id}_{Y}-S\) is invertible, and if we write \(R=A^{-1}\) then

\(\lVert R\rVert\leqslant\frac{1}{1-\delta}.\)

Thus

\(\mathrm{Id}_{Y}=RD\pi T\iota.\)

If \(J\colon\ell_{1}\to Y\) is the canonical isometric isomorphism induced by the subsequence \((e_{m_{k}})\), then

\(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{1}}=J^{-1}RD\pi\,T\,\iota J.\)

Therefore \(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{1}}\) factors through either \(T\) or \(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{1}}-T\), and the factorisation constant is bounded by

\(\lVert J^{-1}RD\pi\rVert\,\lVert\iota J\rVert\leqslant\frac{2}{1-\delta}<2+\varepsilon.\)

This proves that \(\ell_{1}\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP. ∎

3.2.2.

Iterated constructions with \(\ell_{1}\)

−

We now consider iterated constructions involving \(\ell_{1}\). The result proved below is for \(X(\ell_{1})\); this is the case needed in the sequel. Throughout the section, \(X\) will denote a Banach space with a symmetric basis and endowed with a symmetric norm, and we assume that this basis is not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\).

Recall that \(e_{(i,j)}\) denotes the vector \((0,\dots,0,e_{j},0,\dots)\in X(\ell_{1})\) with \(e_{j}\) in the \(i\)th coordinate, and that \(e_{(i,j)}^{*}\) denotes the corresponding coordinate functional. When \(\mathbb{N}^{2}\) is endowed with the Cantor ordering, the family \((e_{(i,j)})_{(i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}}\) forms a \(1\)-unconditional basis for \(X(\ell_{1})\).

We can now state the first step of the proof, which provides the technical ingredients needed to construct vectors spanning an isometric copy of \(X(\ell_{1})\) with only small interference between them.

Let \(X\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis and symmetric norm whose basis is not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\), and let \(T\colon X(\ell_{1})\to X(\ell_{1})\) be an operator. Then the following hold:

  1. (a)

    For every \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), the set

    \(\{r\in\mathbb{N}:\exists s\in\mathbb{N}\text{ such that }|e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)}|\geqslant\varepsilon\}\)

    is finite.

  2. (b)

    For every \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), the set

    \(\{(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}:|e^{*}_{(r,s)}Te_{(i,j)}|\geqslant\varepsilon\}\)

    is finite.

  3. (c)

    For every \(r\in\mathbb{N}\), every infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), every \(\varepsilon>0\), every finite set \(\{i_{1},\dots,i_{K}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and every choice of infinite sets \(M_{1},\dots,M_{K}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), there exists \(s\in M\) such that

    \(\{m\in M_{k}:|e^{*}_{(r,s)}Te_{(i_{k},m)}|\leqslant\varepsilon\}\)

    is infinite for every \(k=1,\dots,K\).

Proof.Fold proof

We first prove (a). Fix \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). Suppose, towards a contradiction, that there are strictly increasing rows \((r_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) and indices \((s_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) such that

\(|e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r_{k},s_{k})}|\geqslant\varepsilon\qquad(k\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Passing to a subsequence and, in the complex case, to a sector, we may assume that there is a unimodular scalar \(\lambda\) such that

\(\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\lambda e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r_{k},s_{k})}\bigr)\geqslant\varepsilon/2\qquad(k\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Put \(f=\lambda e^{*}_{(i,j)}T\). For finitely supported scalar sequences \((a_{k})\), unconditionality gives

\(\displaystyle\Bigl\|\sum_{k}a_{k}e_{(r_{k},s_{k})}\Bigr\|_{X(\ell_{1})}\) \(\displaystyle\geqslant\Bigl\|\sum_{k}|a_{k}|e_{(r_{k},s_{k})}\Bigr\|_{X(\ell_{1})}\)
\(\displaystyle\geqslant\frac{1}{\|f\|}\operatorname{Re}f\Bigl(\sum_{k}|a_{k}|e_{(r_{k},s_{k})}\Bigr)\geqslant\frac{\varepsilon}{2\|f\|}\sum_{k}|a_{k}|.\)

The reverse estimate follows from the normalisation of the basis. Hence \((e_{(r_{k},s_{k})})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) is equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\). Since the rows \(r_{k}\) are distinct and the norm of \(\sum_{k}a_{k}e_{(r_{k},s_{k})}\) is exactly \(\|\sum_{k}|a_{k}|e_{r_{k}}\|_{X}\), this would make a subsequence of the basis of \(X\) equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\). By symmetry this is equivalent to saying that the whole basis of \(X\) is equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\), a contradiction.

We next prove (b). Since \((e_{(r,s)})_{(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}}\), with the Cantor ordering, is a Schauder basis for \(X(\ell_{1})\), the scalar coordinates of the vector \(Te_{(i,j)}\) tend to zero. Therefore, for each \(\varepsilon>0\), only finitely many pairs \((r,s)\) can satisfy \(|e^{*}_{(r,s)}Te_{(i,j)}|\geqslant\varepsilon\).

For (c), we argue by induction on \(K\). The case \(K=1\) is the same pigeonhole argument used in Lemma 3.9. Choose \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(N>\|T\|/\varepsilon\), and choose a finite subset \(F\subseteq M\) with \(|F|=N\). For each \(m\in M_{1}\), set

\(A(m)=\{s\in F:|e_{(r,s)}^{*}Te_{(i_{1},m)}|>\varepsilon\}.\)

Since the projection onto the \(r\)th \(\ell_{1}\)-fibre has norm one,

\(\|T\|\geqslant\|Te_{(i_{1},m)}\|\geqslant\sum_{s\in A(m)}|e_{(r,s)}^{*}Te_{(i_{1},m)}|>|A(m)|\varepsilon.\)

Thus \(|A(m)|<|F|\). For every \(m\in M_{1}\) there is therefore some \(s\in F\) such that \(|e_{(r,s)}^{*}Te_{(i_{1},m)}|\leqslant\varepsilon\). Since \(F\) is finite and \(M_{1}\) is infinite, one such \(s\) works for infinitely many \(m\in M_{1}\).

Suppose now that the assertion has been proved for \(K\), and consider rows \(i_{1},\dots,i_{K},i_{K+1}\) with infinite sets \(M_{1},\dots,M_{K},M_{K+1}\). Choose \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(N>\|T\|/\varepsilon\), and partition \(M\) into pairwise disjoint infinite subsets \(M^{(1)},\dots,M^{(N)}\). By the induction hypothesis, for each \(n=1,\dots,N\) there is \(s_{n}\in M^{(n)}\) such that

\(\{m\in M_{k}:|e_{(r,s_{n})}^{*}Te_{(i_{k},m)}|\leqslant\varepsilon\}\)

is infinite for every \(k=1,\dots,K\). Put \(F=\{s_{1},\dots,s_{N}\}\). For each \(m\in M_{K+1}\), define

\(A(m)=\{n\in\{1,\dots,N\}:|e_{(r,s_{n})}^{*}Te_{(i_{K+1},m)}|>\varepsilon\}.\)

As above, \(|A(m)|<N\) for every \(m\in M_{K+1}\). Hence, by the pigeonhole principle, there is \(n_{0}\in\{1,\dots,N\}\) such that

\(\{m\in M_{K+1}:|e_{(r,s_{n_{0}})}^{*}Te_{(i_{K+1},m)}|\leqslant\varepsilon\}\)

is infinite. The choice of \(s_{n_{0}}\) already gives the required infinite sets for \(k=1,\dots,K\), so \(s=s_{n_{0}}\) completes the induction. ∎

We now show that a suitable small-interference condition forces the resulting operator to have small norm.

Let \(S\colon X(\ell_{1})\to X(\ell_{1})\) be an operator. Suppose that, for every \(r,i\in\mathbb{N}\),

\(\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}|e^{*}_{(r,s)}Se_{(i,j)}|\leqslant\varepsilon 2^{-(r+i)}.\)

Then \(\lVert S\rVert\leqslant\varepsilon\).

Proof.Fold proof

For \(r,i\in\mathbb{N}\), let

\(S_{r,i}=Q_{r}SJ_{i}\colon\ell_{1}\to\ell_{1},\)

where \(J_{i}\colon\ell_{1}\to X(\ell_{1})\) denotes the canonical embedding of \(\ell_{1}\) into the \(i\)th coordinate and \(Q_{r}\colon X(\ell_{1})\to\ell_{1}\) denotes the \(r\)th coordinate projection. Then

\(\lVert S_{r,i}\rVert=\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}|e^{*}_{(r,s)}Se_{(i,j)}|\leqslant\varepsilon 2^{-(r+i)}.\)

Let \(x=(x_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\in B_{X(\ell_{1})}\), so that \(\lVert x_{i}\rVert\leqslant 1\) for all \(i\in\mathbb{N}\). For each \(r\in\mathbb{N}\) we have

\(\displaystyle\lVert Q_{r}Sx\rVert_{\ell_{1}}=\lVert Q_{r}S\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}J_{i}x_{i}\rVert\leqslant\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\lVert S_{r,i}\rVert\lVert x_{i}\rVert_{\ell_{1}}\) \(\displaystyle\leqslant\varepsilon\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}2^{-(r+i)}=\varepsilon 2^{-r}.\)

Hence

\(\lVert Sx\rVert_{X(\ell_{1})}=\left\|\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\lVert Q_{r}Sx\rVert_{\ell_{1}}e_{r}\right\|_{X}\leqslant\varepsilon\sum_{r\in\mathbb{N}}2^{-r}=\varepsilon,\)

so that \(\lVert S\rVert\leqslant\varepsilon\). This completes the proof. ∎

Lastly, we show that Lemma 3.12 allows us to pass to an isometric copy on which the interference is sufficiently small.

Let \(X\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis and symmetric norm whose basis is not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\), and let \(T\colon X(\ell_{1})\to X(\ell_{1})\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist a strictly increasing sequence \((n_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\) and infinite sets \(M_{i}=\{m_{i}^{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\), with \(m_{i}^{1}<m_{i}^{2}<\ldots\) for every \(i\), such that

\(|e^{*}_{(n_{r},m_{r}^{s})}Te_{(n_{i},m_{i}^{j})}|\leqslant\varepsilon 2^{-(r+i+s)}\qquad((r,s)\neq(i,j)).\)
Proof.Fold proof

Fix an enumeration \((\rho_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\) of \(\mathbb{N}^{2}\) such that \((k,1)\) appears before \((k,2)\), \((k,2)\) before \((k,3)\), and the rows are opened in the order \(1,2,\dots\). Write \(\rho_{t}=(k_{t},\ell_{t})\).

We construct the coordinates recursively. After stage \(n\) we have selected \(m_{i}^{j}\) for all pairs \((i,j)=\rho_{t}\) with \(t\leqslant n\), selected outer indices \(n_{i}\) for the active rows, and chosen infinite reservoirs \(R_{i}^{(n)}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) for the active rows. Let \(A_{n}\) be the set of active rows. We require:

  1. (i)

    for every selected pair \(\rho_{t}=(q,w)\), every active row \(i\in A_{n}\), and every \(m\in R_{i}^{(n)}\),

    \(|e^{*}_{(n_{q},m_{q}^{w})}Te_{(n_{i},m)}|\leqslant\varepsilon 2^{-(q+i+w)};\)
  2. (ii)

    for every two selected pairs \(\rho_{s}=(i,j)\) and \(\rho_{t}=(q,w)\) with \((q,w)\neq(i,j)\),

    \(|e^{*}_{(n_{q},m_{q}^{w})}Te_{(n_{i},m_{i}^{j})}|\leqslant\varepsilon 2^{-(q+i+w)};\)
  3. (iii)

    every element of \(R_{i}^{(n)}\) is larger than all coordinates already selected in row \(i\).

At stage \(0\) there is nothing to verify.

Suppose the construction has been completed up to stage \(n\), and let \(\rho_{n+1}=(k,\ell)\). If \(\ell=1\), row \(k\) has not yet been opened. Choose \(n_{k}\) as follows. If there are no previously selected pairs, take \(n_{k}=1\). Otherwise, for each previously selected pair \((q,w)\) put

\(B_{q,w}=\{r\in\mathbb{N}:\exists s\in\mathbb{N}\text{ such that }|e^{*}_{(n_{q},m_{q}^{w})}Te_{(r,s)}|>\varepsilon 2^{-(q+k+w)}\}.\)

By Lemma 3.12(a), each \(B_{q,w}\) is finite. Hence we may choose \(n_{k}\) larger than all previously chosen outer indices and outside the finite union of the sets \(B_{q,w}\). Then

(3.1) \(|e^{*}_{(n_{q},m_{q}^{w})}Te_{(n_{k},m)}|\leqslant\varepsilon 2^{-(q+k+w)}\)

for every previously selected pair \((q,w)\) and every \(m\in\mathbb{N}\). In this case set \(\widetilde{R}=\mathbb{N}\).

If \(\ell>1\), row \(k\) is already active. Set \(\widetilde{R}=R_{k}^{(n)}\). Then (i) gives (3.1) for every previously selected pair \((q,w)\) and every \(m\in\widetilde{R}\).

We next make sure that the new target coordinate is not significantly affected by any previously selected source coordinate. For every previously selected pair \((q,w)\) define

\(F_{q,w}=\{m\in\widetilde{R}:|e^{*}_{(n_{k},m)}Te_{(n_{q},m_{q}^{w})}|>\varepsilon 2^{-(k+q+\ell)}\}.\)

By Lemma 3.12(b), each \(F_{q,w}\) is finite. Thus

\(R=\widetilde{R}\setminus\bigcup_{\rho_{t}=(q,w),\,t\leqslant n}F_{q,w}\)

is infinite, and every \(m\in R\) satisfies

(3.2) \(|e^{*}_{(n_{k},m)}Te_{(n_{q},m_{q}^{w})}|\leqslant\varepsilon 2^{-(k+q+\ell)}\)

for every previously selected pair \((q,w)\).

Let \(A_{n+1}=A_{n}\cup\{k\}\). For \(i\in A_{n+1}\) define

\(H_{i}=\begin{cases}R,&i=k,\\ R_{i}^{(n)},&i\in A_{n}\setminus\{k\}.\end{cases}\)

Put

\(\eta=\min_{i\in A_{n+1}}\varepsilon 2^{-(k+i+\ell)}.\)

Apply Lemma 3.12(c) with source row \(n_{k}\), source reservoir \(R\), threshold \(\eta\), target rows \(\{n_{i}:i\in A_{n+1}\}\) and target reservoirs \((H_{i})_{i\in A_{n+1}}\). We obtain \(m_{k}^{\ell}\in R\) such that, for every \(i\in A_{n+1}\),

\(L_{i}=\{m\in H_{i}:|e^{*}_{(n_{k},m_{k}^{\ell})}Te_{(n_{i},m)}|\leqslant\eta\}\)

is infinite. Since \(\eta\leqslant\varepsilon 2^{-(k+i+\ell)}\), these sets preserve the reservoir estimate for the newly selected target.

For each \(i\in A_{n+1}\), let \(p_{i}\) be the largest coordinate already selected in row \(i\) after adding \(m_{k}^{\ell}\), and set

\(R_{i}^{(n+1)}=\{m\in L_{i}:m>p_{i}\}.\)

These reservoirs are infinite. The estimates above verify (i) and (ii) at stage \(n+1\): old estimates are inherited from the previous reservoirs; (3.1) handles old targets against the new source; (3.2) handles the new target against old sources; and the definition of the sets \(L_{i}\) handles the new target against future sources.

This completes the recursion. For each row \(i\), put \(M_{i}=\{m_{i}^{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\). The construction makes each \(M_{i}\) infinite and strictly increasing. Since every pair of distinct selected coordinates appears at some finite stage, (ii) gives

\(|e^{*}_{(n_{r},m_{r}^{s})}Te_{(n_{i},m_{i}^{j})}|\leqslant\varepsilon 2^{-(r+i+s)}\qquad((r,s)\neq(i,j)),\)

as required. ∎

Finally, we are ready to prove the UPFP for \(X(\ell_{1})\).

Let \(X\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis and symmetric norm whose basis is not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\). Then \(X(\ell_{1})\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP.

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(T\colon X(\ell_{1})\to X(\ell_{1})\) and fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(\delta>0\) small enough so that

\(\frac{2}{1-\delta}<2+\varepsilon.\)

For each row \(i\), colour an index \(j\) red if \(|e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(i,j)}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\) and blue otherwise. In the blue case, \(|e^{*}_{(i,j)}(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{1})}-T)e_{(i,j)}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\). In every row at least one colour occurs infinitely often, and therefore one colour occurs infinitely often in infinitely many rows. Passing to those rows and to the corresponding infinite subsets of their fibres gives a \(1\)-complemented isometric copy of \(X(\ell_{1})\). Replacing \(T\) by \(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{1})}-T\) if necessary, and reindexing, we may assume that

\(|e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(i,j)}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\qquad((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}).\)

Apply Lemma 3.14 with parameter \(\delta/2\), and pass to a further \(1\)-complemented isometric copy so that, after reindexing, we have

\(|e^{*}_{(r,s)}Te_{(i,j)}|\leqslant(\delta/2)2^{-(r+i+s)}\qquad((r,s)\neq(i,j)).\)

Define the diagonal operator \(D\colon X(\ell_{1})\to X(\ell_{1})\) by

\(D(e_{(i,j)})=\frac{1}{e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(i,j)}}\,e_{(i,j)}\qquad((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}).\)

Since

\(\left|\frac{1}{e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(i,j)}}\right|\leqslant 2\qquad((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}),\)

we have \(\lVert D\rVert\leqslant 2\). We claim that

\(\lVert\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{1})}-DT\rVert\leqslant\delta.\)

Indeed, let \(r,i,j\in\mathbb{N}\). For each \(s\in\mathbb{N}\), if \((r,s)\neq(i,j)\) then

\(e^{*}_{(r,s)}(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{1})}-DT)e_{(i,j)}=-\frac{e^{*}_{(r,s)}Te_{(i,j)}}{e^{*}_{(r,s)}Te_{(r,s)}}.\)

On the other hand,

\(e^{*}_{(i,j)}(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{1})}-DT)e_{(i,j)}=0.\)

Therefore

\(\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}|e^{*}_{(r,s)}(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{1})}-DT)e_{(i,j)}|\leqslant 2\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in\mathbb{N}\\ (r,s)\neq(i,j)\end{subarray}}|e^{*}_{(r,s)}Te_{(i,j)}|\leqslant\delta 2^{-(r+i)}.\)

Lemma 3.13 applied to \(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{1})}-DT\) gives \(\lVert\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{1})}-DT\rVert\leqslant\delta\).

Thus \(DT\) is invertible and \(\lVert(DT)^{-1}\rVert\leqslant 1/(1-\delta)\) and \((DT)^{-1}DT=\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{1})}\). Consequently, on the selected copy, \(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{1})}\) factors through the selected restriction of \(T\) with factorisation constant bounded by

\(\lVert(DT)^{-1}\rVert\lVert D\rVert\leqslant\frac{2}{1-\delta}<2+\varepsilon.\)

Composing with the canonical isometry onto the selected copy, its inclusion, and the norm-one coordinate projection gives the same bound for the original operator, or for \(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{1})}-T\) if that was the chosen colour. This proves that \(X(\ell_{1})\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP. ∎

As an immediate consequence, we obtain the following primarity result for \(c_{0}(\ell_{1})\) and \(\ell_{p}(\ell_{1})\), \(1<p<\infty\), in the spirit of the theorem of Casazza, Kottman, and Lin . We note that the \(\ell_{p}(\ell_{1})\) cases also follow from an earlier paper of Samuel , where the primarity of \(\ell_{r}(\ell_{s})\) is proved for \(1\leqslant r,s\leqslant\infty\), with the non-standard convention that \(\ell_{\infty}\) denotes \(c_{0}\). The corresponding \(c_{0}\)-case is not explicitly carried out there, although Samuel indicates that it is analogous. Since these consequences do not seem to have been explicitly recorded in the later literature, we include the details here.

The space \(c_{0}(\ell_{1})\) and the spaces \(\ell_{p}(\ell_{1})\), \(1<p<\infty\), are primary.

Proof.Fold proof

Apply Theorem 3.15 with \(X=c_{0}\) and with \(X=\ell_{p}\), \(1<p<\infty\). Since the canonical bases of \(c_{0}\) and \(\ell_{p}\) are symmetric, it follows that \(c_{0}(\ell_{1})\) and \(\ell_{p}(\ell_{1})\) have the \(2^{+}\)-PFP. Since they are \(c_{0}\)- and \(\ell_{p}\)-stable, respectively, Pełczyński’s decomposition method, Theorem 2.3, yields their primariness. ∎

3.3.

The \(\ell_{\infty}\)-case

−

We have seen that if a Banach space \(X\) has a symmetric basis, then for every operator \(T\colon X\to X\) one can pass to a subsequence of the original basis so that either \(T\) or \(\mathrm{Id}_{X}-T\) acts, up to an arbitrarily small perturbation, as a diagonal operator whose diagonal entries are uniformly bounded away from zero. This then allows us to factor the identity on \(X\).

An inspection of the proof reveals that, for this construction, we require two properties. First, for each fixed \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), we need

\(\lim_{k\to\infty}e_{k}^{*}Te_{n}=0,\)

meaning that each basis vector contributes, up to a small perturbation, to only finitely many coordinates. This followed easily from the fact that \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) was a basis. Second, we need that

\(\lim_{k\to\infty}e_{n}^{*}Te_{k}=0,\)

meaning that each coordinate is influenced, up to a small perturbation, by only finitely many basis vectors. This is essentially Lemma 3.1. Using these properties, a straightforward iterative argument yields the desired diagonal form. More concretely, one exploits the two conditions to construct a subsequence \((e_{n_{k}})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) so that, for every \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), we have that \(\sum_{r\not=k}|e^{*}_{n_{k}}Te_{n_{r}}|\) is arbitrarily small. In other words, the off-diagonal interactions between the images are negligible, which leads to the required diagonalisation.

In this section, we consider the case \(X=\ell_{\infty}\). Although this space does not possess a Schauder basis in the usual sense, one may still view the canonical unit vectors \(e_{n}=(0,\dots,0,1,0,\dots)\), with \(1\) in the \(n\)th coordinate, as playing the role of a basis. This can be formalised by identifying \(\ell_{\infty}\) with the dual of \(\ell_{1}\), in which case the canonical vectors \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) form a weak∗-Schauder basis. For our purposes, we simply emphasise that the unit vectors \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(\ell_{\infty}\) exhibit sufficient basis-like behaviour. Consequently, a suitable modification of the techniques discussed previously, combined with some ideas of Lindenstrauss , will enable us to establish the desired results.

3.3.1.

The space \(\ell_{\infty}\)

−

Let \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) denote the canonical unit vectors in \(\ell_{\infty}\), and let \(e_{n}^{*}\) be the coordinate functionals defined by \(e_{n}^{*}(x)=x(n)\) for \(x=(x(k))_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{\infty}\). As before, our goal is to argue that we can pass to a subsequence so that the cross-interaction between images of the unit vectors \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) is small. The following results are streamlined version tailored to our purposes; the underlying ideas go back to the original paper of Lindenstrauss, see . For a vector \(x\in\ell_{\infty}\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), define

\(M(x,\varepsilon)=\{m\in\mathbb{N}:|e_{m}^{*}x|>\varepsilon\}.\)

Let \((x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a sequence in \(\ell_{\infty}\) and suppose that there exists \(K>0\) such that, for every finite set \(F\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and every scalar family \((\lambda_{n})_{n\in F}\),

\(\lVert\sum_{n\in F}\lambda_{n}x_{n}\rVert\leqslant K\max_{n\in F}|\lambda_{n}|.\)

Then the following hold:

  1. (a)

    For every \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty}e^{*}_{m}x_{n}=0\).

  2. (b)

    For every \(\varepsilon>0\), every infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and every \(N_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\), there exists \(n\in M\) with \(n>N_{0}\) such that \(M\setminus M(x_{n},\varepsilon)\) is infinite.

Proof.Fold proof

We prove (a) by contradiction. If it fails, then there are \(m_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\), \(\delta>0\) and distinct indices \(n_{1},n_{2},\dots\) such that \(|e^{*}_{m_{0}}x_{n_{k}}|>\delta\) for all \(k\). Choose \(L\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(L\delta>K\) and choose unimodular scalars \(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{L}\) so that the numbers \(\lambda_{k}e^{*}_{m_{0}}x_{n_{k}}\) have the same argument. Then

\(K\geqslant\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{L}\lambda_{k}x_{n_{k}}\rVert\geqslant\left|e^{*}_{m_{0}}\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^{L}\lambda_{k}x_{n_{k}}\Bigr)\right|=\sum_{k=1}^{L}|e^{*}_{m_{0}}x_{n_{k}}|>L\delta,\)

a contradiction.

We prove (b). Assume it is false. Then there are \(\varepsilon>0\), an infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and \(N_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(M\setminus M(x_{n},\varepsilon)\) is finite for every \(n\in M\) with \(n>N_{0}\). Choose \(L\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(L\varepsilon>K\), and choose distinct \(n_{1},\dots,n_{L}\in M\) with \(n_{k}>N_{0}\). Since each \(M\setminus M(x_{n_{k}},\varepsilon)\) is finite, the intersection

\(M\cap\bigcap_{k=1}^{L}M(x_{n_{k}},\varepsilon)\)

is non-empty; choose \(m\) in it. Pick unimodular scalars \(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{L}\) aligning the numbers \(e_{m}^{*}x_{n_{k}}\). Then

\(K\geqslant\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{L}\lambda_{k}x_{n_{k}}\rVert\geqslant\left|e_{m}^{*}\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^{L}\lambda_{k}x_{n_{k}}\Bigr)\right|=\sum_{k=1}^{L}|e_{m}^{*}x_{n_{k}}|>L\varepsilon,\)

a contradiction. ∎

We will also need the following result.

Let \((x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\ell_{\infty}\) be a sequence of vectors and suppose that there exists \(K>0\) such that, for every finite set \(F\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and every scalar family \((\lambda_{n})_{n\in F}\),

(3.3) \(\lVert\sum_{n\in F}\lambda_{n}x_{n}\rVert\leqslant K\max_{n\in F}|\lambda_{n}|.\)

Then for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \((n_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) such that

\(\sum_{j\not=k}|e_{n_{k}}^{*}x_{n_{j}}|<\varepsilon\quad\text{ for all }k\in\mathbb{N}.\)
Proof.Fold proof

Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). We recursively choose a decreasing sequence of infinite sets

\(\mathbb{N}=A_{0}\supseteq A_{1}\supseteq A_{2}\supseteq\ldots,\)

and integers \(n_{k}\in A_{k-1}\) such that for every \(k\in\mathbb{N}\),

  1. (i)

    \(n_{k}\in A_{k-1}\);

  2. (ii)

    \(|e_{m}^{*}x_{n_{k}}|<\varepsilon/2^{k+1}\) for every \(m\in A_{k}\);

  3. (iii)

    \(\sum_{m\in A_{k}}|e_{n_{k}}^{*}x_{m}|<\varepsilon/2^{k+1}\).

We start with \(A_{0}=\mathbb{N}\). Assume that \(A_{k-1}\) has been chosen. Apply Lemma 3.17 (b) with \(M=A_{k-1}\), with \(N_{0}=0\) if \(k=1\) and \(N_{0}=n_{k-1}\) otherwise, and with parameter \(\varepsilon/2^{k+2}\). We obtain \(n_{k}\in A_{k-1}\) such that the set

\(B_{k}:=A_{k-1}\setminus M(x_{n_{k}},\varepsilon/2^{k+2})\)

is infinite. Therefore

\(|e_{m}^{*}x_{n_{k}}|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{k+1}}\qquad(m\in B_{k}).\)

By Lemma 3.17 (a), we have \(e_{n_{k}}^{*}x_{m}\to 0\) as \(m\to\infty\) along \(B_{k}\). Hence we may choose an infinite subset \(A_{k}=\{m_{r}^{(k)}:r\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq B_{k}\) such that

\(|e_{n_{k}}^{*}x_{m_{r}^{(k)}}|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{k+1+r}}\qquad(r\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Then (ii) and (iii) hold.

Now fix \(k\in\mathbb{N}\). If \(j<k\), then \(n_{k}\in A_{j}\), so by (ii) at stage \(j\),

\(|e_{n_{k}}^{*}x_{n_{j}}|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{j+1}}.\)

On the other hand, since \(n_{j}\in A_{k}\) for every \(j>k\), property (iii) at stage \(k\) gives

\(\sum_{j>k}|e_{n_{k}}^{*}x_{n_{j}}|\leqslant\sum_{m\in A_{k}}|e_{n_{k}}^{*}x_{m}|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{k+1}}.\)

Therefore,

\(\sum_{j\neq k}|e_{n_{k}}^{*}x_{n_{j}}|=\sum_{j<k}|e_{n_{k}}^{*}x_{n_{j}}|+\sum_{j>k}|e_{n_{k}}^{*}x_{n_{j}}|<\sum_{j<k}\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{j+1}}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{k+1}}<\varepsilon.\)

This proves the lemma. ∎

If \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) were a basis, then for every \(x=(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) we would have \(Tx=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}x_{n}\,Te_{n}\), so that the action of \(T\) would be completely determined by its behaviour on the vectors \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\). However, this representation is no longer available in \(\ell_{\infty}\), since \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) does not form a Schauder basis of the space. We now see how to recover this property by exploiting a clever observation of Lindenstrauss, as seen in .

For an element \(x\in\ell_{\infty}\), we define the support of \(x\) as \(\operatorname{supp}(x)=\{n\in\mathbb{N}:e_{n}^{*}(x)\not=0\}\). For an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), we write \(\ell_{\infty}(M)\) for the \(1\)-complemented subspace of \(\ell_{\infty}\) defined by \(\ell_{\infty}(M)=\{x\in\ell_{\infty}:\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq M\}\) and denote by \(P_{M}:\ell_{\infty}\to\ell_{\infty}\) the canonical projection onto it.

Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}\to\ell_{\infty}\) be an operator. Then there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that for all \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) and all \(x=(x(n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{\infty}(M)\) we have

\(e_{m}^{*}Tx=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}x(n)(e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}).\)
Proof.Fold proof

For each fixed \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(N\in\mathbb{N}\), choose unimodular scalars \(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{N}\) so that

\(\sum_{n=1}^{N}|e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}|=\Bigl|e_{m}^{*}T\Bigl(\sum_{n=1}^{N}\lambda_{n}e_{n}\Bigr)\Bigr|\leqslant\lVert T\rVert.\)

Hence

\(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}|\leqslant\lVert T\rVert.\)

Therefore, for every \(x=(x(n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{\infty}\), the series

\(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}x(n)\,e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}\)

is absolutely convergent, and we may define

\(\Lambda_{m}(x)=e_{m}^{*}Tx-\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}x(n)\,e_{m}^{*}Te_{n},\qquad\Theta(m,x)=|\Lambda_{m}(x)|.\)

Clearly,

\(\Theta(m,x)\leqslant 2\lVert T\rVert\lVert x\rVert_{\ell_{\infty}}\qquad(m\in\mathbb{N},\ x\in\ell_{\infty}).\)

If \(x\) is finitely supported, then by linearity

\(Tx=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}x(n)\,Te_{n},\)

so \(\Lambda_{m}(x)=0\). Consequently, for every \(N\in\mathbb{N}\),

\(\Lambda_{m}(x)=\Lambda_{m}\bigl(P_{[N,\infty)}x\bigr),\)

because \(x-P_{[N,\infty)}x\) is finitely supported. Thus \(\Theta(m,x)\) depends only on the tail of \(x\).

Moreover, given \(x,y\in\ell_{\infty}\), choose a unimodular scalar \(\lambda\in\mathbb{K}\) so that \(\Lambda_{m}(x)\) and \(\lambda\Lambda_{m}(y)\) have the same argument (or one of them is zero). Then

\(\Theta(m,x+\lambda y)=|\Lambda_{m}(x)+\lambda\Lambda_{m}(y)|=|\Lambda_{m}(x)|+|\Lambda_{m}(y)|=\Theta(m,x)+\Theta(m,y).\)

Now let \((M_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\) be an uncountable almost disjoint family of infinite subsets of \(\mathbb{N}\). For \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), define

\(\Gamma(m,\varepsilon)=\Bigl\{\gamma\in\Gamma:\exists x\in B_{\ell_{\infty}(M_{\gamma})}\text{ with }\Theta(m,x)>\varepsilon\Bigr\}.\)

We claim that \(\Gamma(m,\varepsilon)\) is finite.

Indeed, suppose that \(\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{k}\in\Gamma(m,\varepsilon)\) are distinct. Choose \(x_{j}\in B_{\ell_{\infty}(M_{\gamma_{j}})}\) with \(\Theta(m,x_{j})>\varepsilon\). Since the family is almost disjoint, there exists \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) such that the vectors \(P_{[N,\infty)}x_{1},\dots,P_{[N,\infty)}x_{k}\) have pairwise disjoint supports. Replacing each \(x_{j}\) by \(P_{[N,\infty)}x_{j}\), we preserve the inequality \(\Theta(m,x_{j})>\varepsilon\) and may therefore assume from the outset that the supports are pairwise disjoint.

Choose unimodular scalars \(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{k}\) inductively so that

\(\Theta\Bigl(m,\sum_{j=1}^{k}\lambda_{j}x_{j}\Bigr)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Theta(m,x_{j}).\)

Because the supports are disjoint and each \(\lVert x_{j}\rVert_{\infty}\leqslant 1\), the vector

\(x=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\lambda_{j}x_{j}\)

belongs to \(B_{\ell_{\infty}}\). Hence

\(2\lVert T\rVert\geqslant\Theta(m,x)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Theta(m,x_{j})>k\varepsilon.\)

Thus \(k<2\lVert T\rVert/\varepsilon\), proving that \(\Gamma(m,\varepsilon)\) is finite.

Finally, set

\(\widetilde{\Gamma}=\bigcup_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\bigcup_{r\in\mathbb{N}}\Gamma(m,1/r).\)

This is countable, while \(\Gamma\) is uncountable, so choose \(\gamma_{0}\in\Gamma\setminus\widetilde{\Gamma}\) and put \(M=M_{\gamma_{0}}\). Then for every \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) and every \(x\in\ell_{\infty}(M)\) we have \(\Theta(m,x)=0\), that is,

\(e_{m}^{*}Tx=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}x(n)\,e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}.\)

This is exactly the desired conclusion. ∎

The previous proposition shows that, after restricting to a suitable isometric copy of \(\ell_{\infty}\), the operator \(T\) can be represented as an infinite matrix. Equivalently, this restriction of \(T\) may be viewed as a weak∗–to–weak∗ continuous operator. As a consequence, we obtain the following corollary, which, to the best of our knowledge, has not been noted in the literature. In the following, we see \(P_{M}\) as landing inside of \(\ell_{\infty}(M)\) in the natural way.

Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}\to\ell_{\infty}\). Then there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that \(P_{M}T|_{\ell_{\infty}(M)}\colon\ell_{\infty}(M)\to\ell_{\infty}(M)\) is weak∗-to-weak∗ continuous, where \(\ell_{\infty}(M)\) is seen as the dual space of \(\ell_{1}(M)\).

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) be given by Proposition 3.19, and for \(m,n\in M\) set

\(a_{m,n}=e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}.\)

By the first part of the proof of Proposition 3.19, for each fixed \(m\in M\) we have

\(\sum_{n\in M}|a_{m,n}|\leqslant\lVert T\rVert.\)

Define \(S\colon\ell_{1}(M)\to\ell_{1}(M)\) by

\((Sa)(n)=\sum_{m\in M}a_{m}a_{m,n},\qquad a=(a_{m})_{m\in M}\in\ell_{1}(M),\ \ n\in M.\)

Then

\(\lVert Sa\rVert_{\ell_{1}(M)}\leqslant\sum_{n\in M}\sum_{m\in M}|a_{m}|\,|a_{m,n}|=\sum_{m\in M}|a_{m}|\sum_{n\in M}|a_{m,n}|\leqslant\lVert T\rVert\,\lVert a\rVert_{\ell_{1}(M)},\)

so \(S\in\mathcal{B}(\ell_{1}(M))\).

Now let \(x\in\ell_{\infty}(M)\) and \(a\in\ell_{1}(M)\). By Proposition 3.19,

\(\displaystyle\langle P_{M}Tx,a\rangle\) \(\displaystyle=\sum_{m\in M}a_{m}e_{m}^{*}Tx=\sum_{m\in M}a_{m}\sum_{n\in M}x(n)a_{m,n}\)
\(\displaystyle=\sum_{n\in M}x(n)\sum_{m\in M}a_{m}a_{m,n}=\sum_{n\in M}x(n)(Sa)(n)=\langle x,Sa\rangle.\)

Thus

\(P_{M}T|_{\ell_{\infty}(M)}=S^{*},\)

so that \(P_{M}T|_{\ell_{\infty}(M)}\) is weak∗-to-weak∗ continuous. ∎

In particular, one may simply invoke the fact that \(\ell_{1}\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP property to deduce the corresponding result for \(\ell_{\infty}\). Indeed, given an operator \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}\to\ell_{\infty}\), applying Corollary 3.20 and restricting to a suitable isometric copy of \(\ell_{\infty}\), we may assume that \(T\) is weak∗–to–weak∗ continuous. Consequently, there exists an operator \(S\colon\ell_{1}\to\ell_{1}\) such that \(T=S^{*}\). Since \(\ell_{1}\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP property, either \(S\) or \(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{1}}-S\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{1}\) with appropriate constant. Dualising, it follows that the same holds for either \(T\) or \(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{\infty}}-T\). It is conceivable that similar arguments apply to spaces of the form \(X(\ell_{\infty})\) and \(\ell_{\infty}(X)\) whenever \(X\) is a dual space; however, we do not pursue this direction here.

Nevertheless, since we wish to emphasise the method based on bases, we provide a different proof using the previous results. Observe that the argument is now essentially the same as that of Theorem 3.3.

The space \(\ell_{\infty}\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP.

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}\to\ell_{\infty}\) and fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(\delta>0\) small enough so that

\(\frac{2}{1-\delta}<2+\varepsilon.\)

By Proposition 3.19, after passing to an isometric \(1\)-complemented copy of \(\ell_{\infty}\) and reindexing, we may assume that

(3.4) \(e_{m}^{*}Tx=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}x(n)\,e_{m}^{*}Te_{n}\qquad(m\in\mathbb{N},\ x\in\ell_{\infty}).\)

For each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\),

\(1=e_{n}^{*}(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{\infty}}-T)e_{n}+e_{n}^{*}Te_{n}.\)

Hence, there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that either \(|e_{n}^{*}Te_{n}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\) for all \(n\in M\), or \(|e_{n}^{*}(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{\infty}}-T)e_{n}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\) for all \(n\in M\). Replacing \(T\) by \(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{\infty}}-T\) if necessary, and then reindexing, we may assume that

\(|e_{n}^{*}Te_{n}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\qquad(n\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Set \(x_{n}=Te_{n}\). Then for every finite set \(F\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and every scalar family \((\lambda_{n})_{n\in F}\),

\(\Bigl\|\sum_{n\in F}\lambda_{n}x_{n}\Bigr\|=\Bigl\|T\Bigl(\sum_{n\in F}\lambda_{n}e_{n}\Bigr)\Bigr\|\leqslant\lVert T\rVert\,\max_{n\in F}|\lambda_{n}|.\)

Therefore, by Lemma 3.18, after passing to a further subsequence and reindexing, we may assume that

\(\sum_{m\neq n}|e_{n}^{*}Te_{m}|<\frac{\delta}{2}\qquad(n\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Define the diagonal operator \(D\colon\ell_{\infty}\to\ell_{\infty}\) by

\(Dx=\Bigl(\frac{x(n)}{e_{n}^{*}Te_{n}}\Bigr)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}.\)

Since \(|e_{n}^{*}Te_{n}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\), we have \(\lVert D\rVert\leqslant 2\).

Let \(x\in B_{\ell_{\infty}}\) and \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Using (3.4),

\(\displaystyle e_{n}^{*}(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{\infty}}-DT)x\) \(\displaystyle=x(n)-\frac{1}{e_{n}^{*}Te_{n}}\sum_{m\in\mathbb{N}}x(m)e_{n}^{*}Te_{m}\)
\(\displaystyle=-\sum_{m\neq n}x(m)\,\frac{e_{n}^{*}Te_{m}}{e_{n}^{*}Te_{n}}.\)

Hence

\(|e_{n}^{*}(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{\infty}}-DT)x|\leqslant 2\sum_{m\neq n}|e_{n}^{*}Te_{m}|<\delta.\)

Taking the supremum over \(x\in B_{\ell_{\infty}}\) and \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), we obtain \(\lVert\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{\infty}}-DT\rVert<\delta.\) Thus \(DT\) is invertible; writing \(R=(DT)^{-1}\), we have

\(\lVert R\rVert\leqslant\frac{1}{1-\delta}\qquad\text{and}\qquad RDT=\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{\infty}}.\)

Therefore, on the selected copy, \(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{\infty}}\) factors through either \(T\) or \(\mathrm{Id}_{\ell_{\infty}}-T\), and the factorisation constant is bounded by

\(\lVert RD\rVert\leqslant\frac{2}{1-\delta}<2+\varepsilon.\)

Composing with the canonical isometry onto the selected copy, its inclusion, and the norm-one coordinate projection gives the same bound for the original operator. This proves that \(\ell_{\infty}\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP. ∎

3.3.2.

Iterated construction with \(\ell_{\infty}\)

−

We now argue that, in the same spirit as the iterated constructions available for spaces with a symmetric basis, an analogous procedure can be carried out for spaces of the form \(X(\ell_{\infty})\), where \(X\) is a Banach space with a symmetric basis and symmetric norm. Throughout this subsubsection we assume that the basis of \(X\) is not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\).

Before proceeding, we recall the relevant primariness results. The primariness of \(\ell_{p}(\ell_{\infty})\) for \(1\leqslant p<\infty\) was established by Casazza, Kottman and Lin , while the primariness of \(\ell_{\infty}(X)\), when \(X\) has a symmetric basis, was proved by Capon .

The idea is to replicate the reasoning in Subsection 3.1.1, but using the techniques developed in Subsection 3.3.1 to bypass the lack of a Schauder basis in the space. Thus, let \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be the canonical unit vectors in \(\ell_{\infty}\) and for each \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) we let \(e_{(i,j)}=(0,\dots,0,e_{j},0,\dots)\in X(\ell_{\infty})\) where the unit vector \(e_{j}\in\ell_{\infty}\) is placed in the \(i\)th-coordinate. Naturally, we denote by \(e_{(i,j)}^{*}\) the associated coordinate functional, so that \(e^{*}_{(i,j)}e_{(r,k)}=1\) if \((i,j)=(r,k)\) and \(0\) otherwise. For \(x\in X(\ell_{\infty})\) we define the support of \(x\) by \(\operatorname{supp}{(x)}=\{(i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}:e^{*}_{(i,j)}x\not=0\}\). For any \(L,M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), we let
