\(\displaystyle X(L)(\ell_{\infty}(M))\) \(\displaystyle=\{x\in X(\ell_{\infty}):\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq L\times M\}\)
\(\displaystyle=\{(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in X(\ell_{\infty}):x_{n}=0\text{ for }n\notin L\text{ and }x_{n}\in\ell_{\infty}(M)\text{ for }n\in L\}.\)

and observe that naturally \(X(L)(\ell_{\infty}(M))\) is \(1\)-complemented in \(X(\ell_{\infty})\).

As in the case of \(\ell_{\infty}\), we begin by showing that, after passing to a subsequence, the off-diagonal interactions can be made arbitrarily small. We first introduce a preliminary lemma. Throughout, for \((r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\), \(i\in\mathbb{N}\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), define

\(M((r,s),i,\varepsilon)=\{j\in\mathbb{N}:|e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)}|>\varepsilon\}.\)

The set \(M((r,s),i,\varepsilon)\) records the indices in the \(i\)-th row where the image of \(e_{(r,s)}\) under \(T\) has magnitude exceeding \(\varepsilon\).

Let \(X\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis and symmetric norm whose basis is not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\), and let \(T\colon X(\ell_{\infty})\to X(\ell_{\infty})\) be an operator. Then the following hold:

  1. (a)

    For every \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), the set

    \(\{(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}:|e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)}|>\varepsilon\}\)

    is finite.

  2. (b)

    For every \(r\in\mathbb{N}\), every infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), every \(\varepsilon>0\), every finite set \(\{i_{1},\dots,i_{K}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), every choice of infinite sets \(M_{1},\dots,M_{K}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), and every \(N_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\), there exists \(s\in M\) with \(s>N_{0}\) such that

    \(M_{k}\setminus M((r,s),i_{k},\varepsilon)\)

    is infinite for every \(k=1,\dots,K\).

  3. (c)

    For every \((r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) we have

    \(\lim_{i\to\infty}\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}|e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)}|=0.\)
Proof.Fold proof

We first prove (a). Fix \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). If there were infinitely many rows \(r\) for which some \(s\) satisfies \(|e_{(i,j)}^{*}Te_{(r,s)}|>\varepsilon\), then we could choose distinct rows \(r_{k}\) and indices \(s_{k}\) with this property. The vectors \((e_{(r_{k},s_{k})})_{k}\) are isometrically equivalent to a subsequence of the basis of \(X\), while the bounded functional \(e_{(i,j)}^{*}T\) is bounded below on them. The argument from Lemma 3.1 would then force that subsequence, and hence by symmetry the whole basis of \(X\), to be equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\), a contradiction.

Thus only finitely many outer rows can occur. For each such row \(r\), suppose that \(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}\) satisfy \(|e_{(i,j)}^{*}Te_{(r,s_{t})}|>\varepsilon\). Choose unimodular scalars \(\lambda_{t}\) so that

\(\lambda_{t}e_{(i,j)}^{*}Te_{(r,s_{t})}=|e_{(i,j)}^{*}Te_{(r,s_{t})}|.\)

The vector \(x=\sum_{t=1}^{m}\lambda_{t}e_{(r,s_{t})}\) lies in a single \(\ell_{\infty}\)-fibre and has norm one. Hence

\(\|T\|\geqslant|e_{(i,j)}^{*}Tx|=\sum_{t=1}^{m}|e_{(i,j)}^{*}Te_{(r,s_{t})}|>m\varepsilon.\)

Hence \(m\leqslant\|T\|/\varepsilon\), which proves (a).

We prove (b). Suppose the assertion fails. Then there are \(r\in\mathbb{N}\), an infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), \(\varepsilon>0\), rows \(i_{1},\ldots,i_{K}\), infinite sets \(M_{1},\ldots,M_{K}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), and \(N_{0}\in\mathbb{N}\) such that, for every \(s\in M\) with \(s>N_{0}\), at least one of the sets

\(M_{k}\setminus M((r,s),i_{k},\varepsilon)\)

is finite. Choose \(Q\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(Q\varepsilon>\|T\|\), and choose distinct \(s_{1},\dots,s_{KQ}\in M\) with \(s_{u}>N_{0}\). For at least one \(k_{0}\in\{1,\dots,K\}\), the set \(M_{k_{0}}\setminus M((r,s_{u}),i_{k_{0}},\varepsilon)\) is finite for at least \(Q\) of these indices; call them \(s_{u_{1}},\dots,s_{u_{Q}}\). Since \(M_{k_{0}}\) is infinite, choose

\(j_{0}\in M_{k_{0}}\cap\bigcap_{q=1}^{Q}M((r,s_{u_{q}}),i_{k_{0}},\varepsilon).\)

Pick unimodular scalars \(\lambda_{q}\) aligning the numbers \(e_{(i_{k_{0}},j_{0})}^{*}Te_{(r,s_{u_{q}})}\). The vector \(x=\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\lambda_{q}e_{(r,s_{u_{q}})}\) has norm one, and therefore

\(\|T\|\geqslant|e_{(i_{k_{0}},j_{0})}^{*}Tx|=\sum_{q=1}^{Q}|e_{(i_{k_{0}},j_{0})}^{*}Te_{(r,s_{u_{q}})}|>Q\varepsilon,\)

a contradiction.

Finally, if \(y=Te_{(r,s)}\), then the sequence of outer row norms \((\|Q_{i}y\|_{\ell_{\infty}})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\) belongs to \(X\). Since the basis of \(X\) is Schauder, its coordinate tails tend to zero. Therefore

\(\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}|e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)}|\leqslant\|Q_{i}y\|_{\ell_{\infty}}\longrightarrow 0,\)

proving (c). ∎

The next selection is the only place where the mixed \(X(\ell_{\infty})\) geometry requires more care than the ordinary symmetric-basis argument. Inside a fixed outer row, finite sums of coordinate vectors have uniformly bounded norm, so one cannot simply rely on coordinate-wise decay. The reservoir condition in Lemma 3.22(b) is designed precisely to preserve infinitely many admissible future coordinates in each row.

Let \(X\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis and symmetric norm whose basis is not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\), and let \(T\colon X(\ell_{\infty})\to X(\ell_{\infty})\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist a strictly increasing sequence \((n_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\) and infinite sets \(M_{i}=\{m_{i}^{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\), with \(m_{i}^{1}<m_{i}^{2}<\cdots\), such that for every \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\),

\(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\\ (r,s)\neq(i,j)\end{subarray}}|e_{(n_{i},m_{i}^{j})}^{*}Te_{(n_{r},m_{r}^{s})}|<\varepsilon 2^{-i}.\)
Proof.Fold proof

Fix an enumeration \((\rho_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\) of \(\mathbb{N}^{2}\) such that \((k,1)\) appears before \((k,2)\), \((k,2)\) before \((k,3)\), and the rows are opened in the order \(1,2,\dots\). Write \(\rho_{t}=(k_{t},\ell_{t})\), and put

\(\alpha(i,r,s)=\varepsilon 2^{-(i+r+s+2)}.\)

We construct the selected coordinates recursively. After stage \(n\) we have active rows \(A_{n}\), outer indices \(n_{i}\) for \(i\in A_{n}\), selected inner coordinates \(m_{i}^{j}\) for the pairs \(\rho_{t}=(i,j)\) with \(t\leqslant n\), and infinite reservoirs \(R_{i}^{(n)}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) for \(i\in A_{n}\). The induction requirements are:

  1. (i)

    if \(\rho_{a}=(i,j)\) and \(\rho_{b}=(r,s)\) are distinct selected pairs, then

    \(|e^{*}_{(n_{i},m_{i}^{j})}Te_{(n_{r},m_{r}^{s})}|\leqslant\alpha(i,r,s);\)
  2. (ii)

    if \(\rho_{b}=(r,s)\) is a selected source pair, \(i\in A_{n}\), and \(m\in R_{i}^{(n)}\), then

    \(|e^{*}_{(n_{i},m)}Te_{(n_{r},m_{r}^{s})}|\leqslant\alpha(i,r,s);\)
  3. (iii)

    every element of \(R_{i}^{(n)}\) is larger than all coordinates already selected in row \(i\).

These conditions are void at stage \(0\).

Suppose the construction has been carried out up to stage \(n\), and let \(\rho_{n+1}=(k,\ell)\). If \(\ell=1\), choose a new outer index \(n_{k}\) larger than all previously chosen outer indices and so large that, for every previously selected source pair \(\rho_{b}=(r,s)\),

(3.5) \(\sup_{m\in\mathbb{N}}|e^{*}_{(n_{k},m)}Te_{(n_{r},m_{r}^{s})}|\leqslant\alpha(k,r,s).\)

This is possible by Lemma 3.22(c). Set \(\widetilde{R}=\mathbb{N}\).

If \(\ell>1\), row \(k\) is already active. Set \(\widetilde{R}=R_{k}^{(n)}\). Then (ii) gives (3.5) with \(m\in\widetilde{R}\) in place of the supremum over \(\mathbb{N}\).

We now protect all old target coordinates from the new source coordinate. For every previously selected target pair \(\rho_{a}=(i,j)\) define

\(G_{i,j}=\{m\in\widetilde{R}:|e^{*}_{(n_{i},m_{i}^{j})}Te_{(n_{k},m)}|>\alpha(i,k,\ell)\}.\)

Lemma 3.22(a) shows that each \(G_{i,j}\) is finite. Hence

\(R=\widetilde{R}\setminus\bigcup_{\rho_{a}=(i,j),\,a\leqslant n}G_{i,j}\)

is infinite, and every \(m\in R\) satisfies

(3.6) \(|e^{*}_{(n_{i},m_{i}^{j})}Te_{(n_{k},m)}|\leqslant\alpha(i,k,\ell)\)

for every previously selected target pair \((i,j)\).

Let \(A_{n+1}=A_{n}\cup\{k\}\) and define

\(H_{i}=\begin{cases}R,&i=k,\\ R_{i}^{(n)},&i\in A_{n}\setminus\{k\}.\end{cases}\)

Put \(\eta=\min_{i\in A_{n+1}}\alpha(i,k,\ell)\). Apply Lemma 3.22(b) with source row \(n_{k}\), source reservoir \(R\), threshold \(\eta\), target rows \(\{n_{i}:i\in A_{n+1}\}\), target reservoirs \((H_{i})_{i\in A_{n+1}}\), and with \(N_{0}\) equal to the largest coordinate already selected in row \(k\) (or \(0\) if none has been selected). We obtain \(m_{k}^{\ell}\in R\) such that, for every \(i\in A_{n+1}\),

\(L_{i}=H_{i}\setminus M((n_{k},m_{k}^{\ell}),n_{i},\eta)\)

is infinite. Equivalently,

(3.7) \(|e^{*}_{(n_{i},m)}Te_{(n_{k},m_{k}^{\ell})}|\leqslant\eta\leqslant\alpha(i,k,\ell)\qquad(m\in L_{i}).\)

For each \(i\in A_{n+1}\), let \(p_{i}\) be the largest coordinate already selected in row \(i\) after adding \(m_{k}^{\ell}\), and set

\(R_{i}^{(n+1)}=\{m\in L_{i}:m>p_{i}\}.\)

These reservoirs are infinite. Conditions (i) and (ii) at stage \(n+1\) follow from the induction hypotheses, (3.5), (3.6), and (3.7).

This completes the recursion. Let \(M_{i}=\{m_{i}^{j}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}\). For every pair of distinct selected coordinates we have

\(|e^{*}_{(n_{i},m_{i}^{j})}Te_{(n_{r},m_{r}^{s})}|\leqslant\varepsilon 2^{-(i+r+s+2)}.\)

Therefore, for fixed \((i,j)\),

\(\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\\ (r,s)\neq(i,j)\end{subarray}}|e^{*}_{(n_{i},m_{i}^{j})}Te_{(n_{r},m_{r}^{s})}|\) \(\displaystyle\leqslant\varepsilon 2^{-i-2}\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}2^{-r}\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}2^{-s}\)
\(\displaystyle<\varepsilon 2^{-i}.\)

This proves the lemma. ∎

We argue that, after restricting to a suitable copy, the operator \(T\) can be represented as an infinite matrix.

Let \(T\colon X(\ell_{\infty})\to X(\ell_{\infty})\) be an operator. Then for any \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) and any \(x=(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in X(\ell_{\infty})\) we have

\(\sum_{(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}}|(e^{*}_{(r,s)}x)(e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)})|\leqslant\lVert T\rVert\lVert x\rVert.\)

In particular \(\sum_{(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}}(e^{*}_{(r,s)}x)(e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)})\) is absolutely summable.

Proof.Fold proof

Let \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) and \(x\in X(\ell_{\infty})\) be fixed. For each \((r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) choose an unimodular scalar \(\lambda_{(r,s)}\) such that

\(\lambda_{(r,s)}(e^{*}_{(r,s)}x)(e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)})=|(e^{*}_{(r,s)}x)(e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)})|.\)

For each \(N\in\mathbb{N}\), consider the vector \(x_{N}\in X(\ell_{\infty})\) defined coordinate-wise by \(e_{(r,s)}^{*}x_{N}=\lambda_{(r,s)}e_{(r,s)}^{*}x\) if \(r,s\leqslant N\) and \(e_{(r,s)}^{*}x_{N}=0\) otherwise. Since the basis of \(X\) is \(1\)-unconditional, it is clear that \(\lVert x_{N}\rVert\leqslant\lVert x\rVert\), so that

\(\displaystyle\lVert T\rVert\lVert x\rVert\) \(\displaystyle\geqslant\lVert T\rVert\lVert x_{N}\rVert\geqslant|e^{*}_{(i,j)}Tx_{N}|=\sum_{r,s\leqslant N}\lambda_{(r,s)}(e^{*}_{(r,s)}x)(e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)})\)
\(\displaystyle=\sum_{r,s\leqslant N}|(e^{*}_{(r,s)}x)(e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)})|,\)

and since this holds for all \(N\in\mathbb{N}\), the result follows. ∎

We now prove the matrix-representation step needed for \(X(\ell_{\infty})\). The proof is the almost-disjoint-family argument of Proposition 3.19, applied one outer row at a time and then extended by density from finite row support.

Let \(T\colon X(\ell_{\infty})\to X(\ell_{\infty})\) be an operator. Then there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that, for all \(x\in X(\ell_{\infty}(M))\) and every \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\),

\(e^{*}_{(i,j)}Tx=\sum_{(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}}(e^{*}_{(r,s)}x)(e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)}).\)
Proof.Fold proof

For each \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\), define a bounded linear functional \(\Lambda_{(i,j)}\colon X(\ell_{\infty})\to\mathbb{K}\) by

\(\Lambda_{(i,j)}(x)=e^{*}_{(i,j)}Tx-\sum_{(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}}(e^{*}_{(r,s)}x)(e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)}).\)

Lemma 3.24 shows that the series converges absolutely, and moreover

\(|\Lambda_{(i,j)}(x)|\leqslant 2\lVert T\rVert\,\lVert x\rVert\qquad(x\in X(\ell_{\infty})).\)

Also, by linearity, \(\Lambda_{(i,j)}\) vanishes on every finitely supported vector.

Let \((M_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\) be an uncountable family of infinite subsets of \(\mathbb{N}\) such that \(M_{\gamma}\cap M_{\beta}\) is finite whenever \(\gamma\neq\beta\). For \(l\in\mathbb{N}\), \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) and \(\eta>0\), define

\(\Gamma(l,(i,j),\eta)=\Bigl\{\gamma\in\Gamma:\ \exists x\in B_{X(\{l\})(\ell_{\infty}(M_{\gamma}))}\text{ with }|\Lambda_{(i,j)}(x)|>\eta\Bigr\}.\)

We claim that every set \(\Gamma(l,(i,j),\eta)\) is finite.

Indeed, assume that \(\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{k}\in\Gamma(l,(i,j),\eta)\) are distinct, and choose \(x_{t}\in B_{X(\{l\})(\ell_{\infty}(M_{\gamma_{t}}))}\) with \(|\Lambda_{(i,j)}(x_{t})|>\eta\) for \(t=1,\dots,k\). Since the sets \(M_{\gamma_{t}}\) have pairwise finite intersections, there exists a finite set \(F\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that the sets \(M_{\gamma_{t}}\setminus F\) are pairwise disjoint. Let \(y_{t}\) be obtained from \(x_{t}\) by deleting the coordinates in \(F\). Because \(x_{t}-y_{t}\) is finitely supported, we still have \(\Lambda_{(i,j)}(y_{t})=\Lambda_{(i,j)}(x_{t})\). Thus the vectors \(y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\) are supported in the same outer coordinate \(l\) and have pairwise disjoint inner supports. In particular,

\(\Bigl\|\sum_{t=1}^{k}\lambda_{t}y_{t}\Bigr\|\leqslant 1\)

for every choice of unimodular scalars \((\lambda_{t})_{t=1}^{k}\). Choose \(\lambda_{t}\) so that \(\lambda_{t}\Lambda_{(i,j)}(y_{t})=|\Lambda_{(i,j)}(y_{t})|\). Then, with \(y=\sum_{t=1}^{k}\lambda_{t}y_{t}\), we obtain

\(2\lVert T\rVert\geqslant|\Lambda_{(i,j)}(y)|=\sum_{t=1}^{k}|\Lambda_{(i,j)}(y_{t})|>k\eta.\)

Hence \(k<2\lVert T\rVert/\eta\), proving the claim.

Now set

\(\widetilde{\Gamma}=\bigcup_{l\in\mathbb{N}}\ \bigcup_{(i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}}\ \bigcup_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\Gamma\bigl(l,(i,j),1/m\bigr).\)

This is countable. Choose \(\gamma_{0}\in\Gamma\setminus\widetilde{\Gamma}\) and set \(M=M_{\gamma_{0}}\). Then \(\Lambda_{(i,j)}\) vanishes on each one-row subspace \(X(\{l\})(\ell_{\infty}(M))\), for every \(l\in\mathbb{N}\). Since \(\Lambda_{(i,j)}\) is linear, it vanishes on every finite sum of such subspaces, i.e. on every vector of \(X(\ell_{\infty}(M))\) supported in finitely many rows. Those vectors are dense in \(X(\ell_{\infty}(M))\) because the outer basis of \(X\) is a Schauder basis. Therefore \(\Lambda_{(i,j)}\) vanishes identically on \(X(\ell_{\infty}(M))\). This is exactly the desired matrix representation. ∎

Finally, we can prove the following result.

Let \(X\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis and symmetric norm, and assume that this basis is not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}\). Then \(X(\ell_{\infty})\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP.

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(T\colon X(\ell_{\infty})\to X(\ell_{\infty})\) and fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(\delta>0\) so small that

\(\frac{2}{1-\delta}<2+\varepsilon.\)

For each row \(i\), colour an index \(j\) red if \(|e_{(i,j)}^{*}Te_{(i,j)}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\) and blue otherwise. In the blue case we have \(|e_{(i,j)}^{*}(\mathrm{Id}-T)e_{(i,j)}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\). For every \(i\) at least one colour occurs infinitely often, and therefore one of the two colours occurs infinitely often in infinitely many rows. Passing to those rows, and to infinite subsets of the corresponding fibres, we obtain a \(1\)-complemented isometric copy of \(X(\ell_{\infty})\). Replacing \(T\) by \(\mathrm{Id}-T\) if necessary, and then reindexing, we may assume that

\(|e_{(i,j)}^{*}Te_{(i,j)}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\qquad((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}).\)

By Proposition 3.25, after passing to a further \(1\)-complemented isometric copy, we may also assume that

(3.8) \(e^{*}_{(i,j)}Tx=\sum_{(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}}(e^{*}_{(r,s)}x)(e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)})\)

for all \(x\in X(\ell_{\infty})\) and all \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\).

Finally, apply Lemma 3.23 with parameter \(\delta/2\), and pass to another \(1\)-complemented isometric copy so that

(3.9) \(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\\ (r,s)\neq(i,j)\end{subarray}}|e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)}|<\delta\,2^{-i-1}\qquad((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}).\)

Define the diagonal operator \(D\colon X(\ell_{\infty})\to X(\ell_{\infty})\) by

\(D\bigl(e_{(i,j)}\bigr)=\frac{1}{e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(i,j)}}e_{(i,j)}\qquad((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}).\)

Equivalently,

\(D\bigl((x_{i}(j))_{i,j\in\mathbb{N}}\bigr)=\Bigl(\frac{x_{i}(j)}{e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(i,j)}}\Bigr)_{i,j\in\mathbb{N}}.\)

Because \(|e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(i,j)}|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\), we have \(\lVert D\rVert\leqslant 2\).

Let \(x\in B_{X(\ell_{\infty})}\) and define

\(c_{i}=\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}|e^{*}_{(i,j)}(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{\infty})}-DT)x|,\qquad i\in\mathbb{N}.\)

Using (3.8), for each \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\) we get

\(e^{*}_{(i,j)}(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{\infty})}-DT)x=-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(r,s)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\\ (r,s)\neq(i,j)\end{subarray}}(e^{*}_{(r,s)}x)\,\frac{e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(r,s)}}{e^{*}_{(i,j)}Te_{(i,j)}}.\)

Hence, by (3.9) and the estimate \(|e^{*}_{(r,s)}x|\leqslant 1\), we get

\(c_{i}\leqslant\delta\,2^{-i}\qquad(i\in\mathbb{N}).\)

The \(i\)-th row of \((\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{\infty})}-DT)x\) has sup norm exactly \(c_{i}\), so

\(\lVert(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{\infty})}-DT)x\rVert=\Bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}c_{i}e_{i}\Bigr\|_{X}\leqslant\delta\Bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}2^{-i}e_{i}\Bigr\|_{X}\leqslant\delta.\)

Therefore

\(\lVert\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{\infty})}-DT\rVert\leqslant\delta.\)

Thus \(DT\) is invertible; writing \(R=(DT)^{-1}\), we have

\(\lVert R\rVert\leqslant\frac{1}{1-\delta}\qquad\text{and}\qquad RDT=\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{\infty})}.\)

Consequently, on the selected copy, \(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{\infty})}\) factors through either \(T\) or \(\mathrm{Id}_{X(\ell_{\infty})}-T\), and the factorisation constant is bounded by

\(\lVert RD\rVert\leqslant\frac{2}{1-\delta}<2+\varepsilon.\)

Composing with the canonical isometry onto the selected copy, its inclusion, and the norm-one coordinate projection gives the same bound for the original operator. This proves that \(X(\ell_{\infty})\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP. ∎

As an automatic consequence, we extend the results of Casazza, Kottman, and Lin to include the \(c_{0}\)-sum of \(\ell_{\infty}\).

The space \(c_{0}(\ell_{\infty})\) is primary.

Proof.Fold proof

Apply Theorem 3.26 with \(X=c_{0}\), whose canonical basis is symmetric. Thus \(c_{0}(\ell_{\infty})\) has the primary factorisation property. Since \(c_{0}(\ell_{\infty})\cong c_{0}(\mathbb{N},c_{0}(\ell_{\infty}))\), Pełczyński’s decomposition method 2.3 yields that \(c_{0}(\ell_{\infty})\) is primary. ∎

4.

Uncountable direct sums

−
4.1.

Overview and main results

−

In the previous section we studied spaces with symmetric bases in the separable setting. In the non-separable setting one has an additional tool: after reducing the action of an operator to countable coordinate supports, set-mapping theorems can be used to pass to a large subfamily on which all off-diagonal coordinate interactions vanish.

There are two different regimes, and it is important not to conflate them. If both the outgoing and incoming interaction sets of each coordinate are countable, a direct transfinite recursion gives the required free set in ZFC for every uncountable index set. This is the case for sums of separable coefficient spaces over scalar bases other than \(\ell_{1}\). If only one side is known to be countable, we use Hajnal’s set mapping theorem with values of size at most \(\omega\), and this requires the ambient cardinal to be strictly larger than \(\omega_{1}\). For continuum-indexed sums this latter assumption is exactly \(\neg\mathrm{CH}\).

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis \((e_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\). Then \(E\) can be realised as an \(E\)-sum of copies of the scalar field \(\mathbb{K}\), that is,

\(E=\bigl(\mathbb{K}\oplus\mathbb{K}\oplus\cdots\bigr)_{E}.\)

Since \(\mathbb{K}\) trivially has the UPFP, the results of Section 3 may be viewed as preservation results for countable sums. The purpose of this section is to give corresponding transfer principles for uncountable sums of Banach spaces.

Our first result concerns primariness. The \(\ell_{1}\)-part is deliberately stated with the cardinal restriction \(\left|\Gamma\right|>\omega_{1}\); when \(\left|\Gamma\right|=2^{\aleph_{0}}\), this is precisely the negation of the continuum hypothesis. The \(\ell_{p}\)- and \(c_{0}\)-parts for separable coefficient spaces are ZFC statements for arbitrary uncountable \(\Gamma\).

(Primariness of \(\ell_{p}\)- and \(c_{0}\)-sums).

Let \(\Gamma\) be an uncountable set with \(\kappa=\left|\Gamma\right|\).

  1. (i)

    Let \(Y\) be a WCG Banach space and suppose that \(\kappa>\omega_{1}\). Put

    \(X_{1}=\ell_{1}(\mathbb{N},Y).\)

    Assume that either

    1. (U)

      \(X_{1}\) is uniformly primary;

    2. (CF)

      \(X_{1}\) is primary and \(\mathrm{cf}(\kappa)>\omega\).

    Then \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma,Y)\) is primary, and uniformly primary in case (i).

  2. (iv)

    Let \(Y\) be separable. For \(1<p<\infty\), put

    \(X_{p}=\ell_{p}(\mathbb{N},Y),\)

    and put \(X_{0}=c_{0}(\mathbb{N},Y)\). If the corresponding countable model \(X_{p}\), respectively \(X_{0}\), is uniformly primary, then \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma,Y)\), respectively \(c_{0}(\Gamma,Y)\), is uniformly primary. If the corresponding countable model is primary and \(\mathrm{cf}(\kappa)>\omega\), then the corresponding uncountable sum is primary.

The cofinality assumption \(\mathrm{cf}(\kappa)>\omega\) in the non-uniform alternatives is used only to extract a full-size family of blocks with uniformly bounded Banach–Mazur constants. It is not a set-theoretic assumption such as CH; in particular, \(\mathrm{cf}(2^{\aleph_{0}})>\omega\) by König’s theorem. The separate hypothesis \(\kappa>\omega_{1}\) in the WCG \(\ell_{1}\)-case is different: it is the price paid for using a one-sided countable support reduction.

The results below distinguish two mechanisms. The two-sided countability mechanism applies to sums of separable spaces, over scalar bases not equivalent to \(\ell_{1}\), and works in ZFC for every uncountable \(\Gamma\). The one-sided mechanism applies to WCG \(\ell_{1}\)-sums and to certain non-separable coefficient spaces; it requires \(\left|\Gamma\right|>\omega_{1}\). Thus, for continuum-indexed WCG sums, the hypothesis becomes exactly \(\neg\mathrm{CH}\).

In the same spirit, we prove inheritance theorems for the PFP and UPFP.

(Primary factorisation property).

Let \(\Gamma\) be an uncountable set with \(\kappa=\left|\Gamma\right|\), and let \(X\) be a Banach space. Assume that one of the following holds:

  1. (UF)

    \(X\) has the uniform primary factorisation property;

  2. (CF)

    \(X\) has the primary factorisation property and \(\mathrm{cf}(\kappa)>\omega\).

Then the following assertions hold.

  1. (i)

    If \(\kappa>\omega_{1}\) and \(X\) is WCG, then \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma,X)\) has the primary factorisation property, uniformly in case (UF).

  2. (ii)

    Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis \((e_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\) not equivalent to the canonical basis of \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\). If \(X\) is separable, then \(E(\Gamma,X)\) has the primary factorisation property, uniformly in case (UF). This part has no cardinal assumption beyond the uncountability of \(\Gamma\).

  3. (iii)

    Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis \((e_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\) not equivalent to the canonical basis of \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\). If \(\kappa>\omega_{1}\) and \(X^{*}\) contains a countable total set, then \(E(\Gamma,X)\) has the primary factorisation property, uniformly in case (UF).

The space \(\ell_{\infty}(\Gamma,X)\) is not covered by the arguments below: its canonical unit vectors do not form a Schauder basis in the sense used here, and the countable-support lemmas fail in that setting. We therefore make no assertion about \(\ell_{\infty}\)-sums in this section.

In the parts of Theorem 4.3 where \(\kappa>\omega_{1}\), the WCG assumption in the \(\ell_{1}\)-case may be replaced by the requirement that every operator \(S\colon X\to\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\) has separable range. Likewise, in the non-\(\ell_{1}\) \(E\)-sum case one may replace the countable-total-set assumption by the requirement that every operator \(S\colon X\to E\) has separable range. In both replacements one uses the one-sided outgoing-coordinate alternative in Lemma 4.27, and therefore the assumption \(\kappa>\omega_{1}\) remains essential for this proof. The ZFC separable-coefficient part of Theorem 4.3(ii) uses a different, two-sided argument.

4.2.

Applications and consequences

−

We now record some immediate consequences of the transfer theorems.

(WCG \(\ell_{1}\)-sums at the continuum under \(\neg\mathrm{CH}\)).

Assume \(\neg\mathrm{CH}\), and let \(Y\) be a WCG Banach space. Put \(\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_{0}}\). If \(\ell_{1}(\mathbb{N},Y)\) is uniformly primary, then \(\ell_{1}(\mathfrak{c},Y)\) is uniformly primary. If \(\ell_{1}(\mathbb{N},Y)\) is primary, then \(\ell_{1}(\mathfrak{c},Y)\) is primary.

Proof.Fold proof

Under \(\neg\mathrm{CH}\) we have \(\mathfrak{c}>\omega_{1}\), while \(\mathrm{cf}(\mathfrak{c})>\omega\) by König’s theorem. The assertion is therefore Theorem 4.1(i) applied with \(\Gamma\) of cardinality \(\mathfrak{c}\). ∎

Assume \(\neg\mathrm{CH}\). Then the space \(\mathcal{M}[0,1]=C[0,1]^{*}\) is primary.

Proof.Fold proof

By a classical result (see ), the space \(C[0,1]^{*}\) is isomorphic to \(\ell_{1}(2^{\aleph_{0}},L_{1}[0,1])\). The space \(L_{1}[0,1]\) is separable, hence WCG, and

\(\ell_{1}(\mathbb{N},L_{1}[0,1])\simeq L_{1}[0,1]\)

is primary. Since \(\neg\mathrm{CH}\) is equivalent to \(2^{\aleph_{0}}>\omega_{1}\), the result follows from Corollary 4.6. This gives an interesting example of a positive structural result obtained under the mere negation of the continuum hypothesis. ∎

Corollary 4.7 is not a ZFC consequence of the present direct-sum argument. The representation

\(C[0,1]^{*}\simeq\ell_{1}(2^{\aleph_{0}},L_{1}[0,1])\)

writes \(C[0,1]^{*}\) as an \(\ell_{1}\)-sum of separable spaces, but separability of the coefficient space does not give the two-sided countability needed in Proposition 4.22. Indeed, if \(X\neq\{0\}\), choose \(x_{0}\in X\) and \(x_{0}^{*}\in X^{*}\) with \(x_{0}^{*}(x_{0})=1\). For a fixed \(\eta_{0}\in\Gamma\), the formula

\(R_{\eta_{0}}T((x_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma})=\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}x_{0}^{*}(x_{\gamma})x_{0},\qquad R_{\eta}T=0\quad(\eta\neq\eta_{0}),\)

defines a bounded operator on \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma,X)\), and

\(R_{\eta_{0}}TR_{\gamma}\neq 0\qquad(\gamma\in\Gamma).\)

Thus a single target coordinate may receive non-zero contributions from all source coordinates. This is precisely the one-sided phenomenon in the \(\ell_{1}\)-case, and at \(2^{\aleph_{0}}=\omega_{1}\) the Hajnal argument cannot be applied. A ZFC proof of the primariness of \(C[0,1]^{*}\), if one is available, would therefore have to use additional structure of \(C[0,1]^{*}\), not merely the above \(\ell_{1}(2^{\aleph_{0}},L_{1}[0,1])\) decomposition.

Let \(\Gamma\) be an uncountable set, let \(X\) be a separable Banach space with the UPFP, and let \(E\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis \((e_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\) not equivalent to the canonical basis of \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\). Then \(E(\Gamma,X)\) has the UPFP. In particular, \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma,X)\), \(1<p<\infty\), and \(c_{0}(\Gamma,X)\) have the UPFP.

Proof.Fold proof

This is Theorem 4.3(ii) in the uniform case. The scalar bases of \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma)\), \(1<p<\infty\), and \(c_{0}(\Gamma)\) are not equivalent to the canonical basis of \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\). ∎

Let \(\alpha\) be an ordinal.

  1. (i)

    If \(\left|\Gamma\right|>\omega_{1}\) and \(1\leqslant p<\infty\), then \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma,C(\alpha))\) has the uniform primary factorisation property. In particular, it is primary.

  2. (ii)

    If \(\alpha<\omega_{1}\), \(\Gamma\) is uncountable, and \(1<p<\infty\), then \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma,C(\alpha))\) has the uniform primary factorisation property. The same is true of \(c_{0}(\Gamma,C(\alpha))\).

Proof.Fold proof

We first reduce to a coefficient space known to have the UPFP. If \(C(\alpha)\) is not isomorphic to \(C(\xi\cdot n)\) for any uncountable regular ordinal \(\xi\) and any integer \(n\geqslant 2\), set \(\beta=\alpha\); then \(C(\beta)\) has the UPFP by . In the remaining case, \(C(\alpha)\simeq C(\xi\cdot n)\) for some such \(\xi\) and \(n\), and the standard finite-decomposition of ordinal \(C\)-spaces gives

\(\ell_{p}(\Gamma,C(\alpha))\simeq\ell_{p}(\Gamma,C(\xi\cdot n))\simeq\ell_{p}(\Gamma,C(\xi)).\)

For \(c_{0}\)-sums the same finite reindexing gives

\(c_{0}(\Gamma,C(\alpha))\simeq c_{0}(\Gamma,C(\xi\cdot n))\simeq c_{0}(\Gamma,C(\xi)).\)

Set \(\beta=\xi\) in this case. Thus it is enough, by Proposition 2.5, to prove the stated assertions with \(C(\beta)\) in place of \(C(\alpha)\), where \(C(\beta)\) has the UPFP.

Assume first that \(\left|\Gamma\right|>\omega_{1}\) and \(1\leqslant p<\infty\). We verify the separable-range hypothesis from Remark 4.5. Let

\(S\colon C(\beta)\to\ell_{p}(\Gamma)\)

be bounded. We claim that \(S\) is compact. By Pełczyński’s theorem , every operator from a \(C(K)\)-space either fixes a copy of \(c_{0}\) or is weakly compact. Since the compact ordinal interval \([0,\beta]\) is scattered, \(C(\beta)^{*}\cong\ell_{1}([0,\beta])\) has the Schur property. Hence the adjoint of every weakly compact operator from \(C(\beta)\) is compact, and Schauder’s theorem implies that every weakly compact operator from \(C(\beta)\) is compact.

The alternative that \(S\) fixes a copy of \(c_{0}\) cannot occur. Indeed, \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma)\) contains no subspace isomorphic to \(c_{0}\) for \(1\leqslant p<\infty\): every separable subspace of \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma)\) is contained in \(\ell_{p}(\Lambda)\) for some countable \(\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma\), and \(\ell_{p}(\Lambda)\) contains no copy of \(c_{0}\). Consequently \(S\) is compact, and in particular has separable range. By the separable-range formulation of Theorem 4.3, recorded in Remark 4.5, \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma,C(\beta))\) has the UPFP. Since \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma,C(\beta))\simeq\ell_{p}(\mathbb{N},\ell_{p}(\Gamma,C(\beta)))\), primariness follows from Pełczyński’s decomposition method. This proves (i).

Now assume that \(\alpha<\omega_{1}\), that \(\Gamma\) is uncountable, and that \(1<p<\infty\). Then the ordinal interval \([0,\alpha]\) is countable and compact, so \(C(\alpha)\) is separable. Part (ii) follows directly from Corollary 4.9. The preceding finite-decomposition reduction is unnecessary in this separable case, but it is compatible with it. ∎

The \(\ell_{1}\)-case for separable coefficient spaces is not included in the ZFC statement above. Even for scalar coefficients, a bounded functional on \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\) may depend on all coordinates, so the incoming interaction sets need not be countable. This is exactly why the WCG \(\ell_{1}\)-results are stated under the one-sided hypothesis \(\left|\Gamma\right|>\omega_{1}\), and why continuum-indexed WCG applications are stated under \(\neg\mathrm{CH}\).

4.3.

‘Small’ spaces and support lemmas

−
4.3.1.

Direct sums and coordinate projections

−

Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(E\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis \((e_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\). We denote by \(E(\Gamma,X)\) the Banach space of all families \(x=(x_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\) with \(x_{\gamma}\in X\) such that

\(\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\lVert x_{\gamma}\rVert_{X}e_{\gamma}\in E,\)

equipped with the norm

\(\lVert x\rVert=\lVert\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\lVert x_{\gamma}\rVert_{X}e_{\gamma}\rVert_{E}.\)

In contrast with Section 3, and to emphasise the role of \(\Gamma\), we write \(E(\Gamma,X)\) instead of \(E(X)\). In this spirit, we write \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma,X)\) and \(c_{0}(\Gamma,X)\) when \((e_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\) is the canonical basis of \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma)\) or \(c_{0}(\Gamma)\), respectively, for \(1\leqslant p<\infty\).

For \(x\in E(\Gamma,X)\), we define

\(\operatorname{supp}(x)=\{\gamma\in\Gamma:x_{\gamma}\neq 0\}.\)

For \(\Delta\subseteq\Gamma\), we denote by \(R_{\Delta}\) the canonical coordinate projection onto the subspace

\(E(\Delta,X)=\{x\in E(\Gamma,X):\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq\Delta\}.\)

By renormalising, we may always assume that \(E\) is equipped with a symmetric norm and thus that \(R_{\Delta}\) is a contractive projection, and in particular \(E(\Delta,X)\) is \(1\)-complemented in \(E(\Gamma,X)\).

In the case where \(\Delta\) is a singleton, say \(\Delta=\{\gamma\}\), we use the standard abuse of notation and write \(R_{\gamma}\) for \(R_{\{\gamma\}}\) and \(E(\gamma,X)\) for \(E(\{\gamma\},X)\).

4.3.2.

Support lemmas

−

For a bounded operator \(T\colon E(\Gamma,X)\to E(\Gamma,X)\), the idea is to separate the influence of a given coordinate in two ways: the influence that a single coordinate has on the others or the influence that the other coordinates have on a single coordinate. This will determine when a space \(X\) is “small”, and we shall formalise this through separation lemmas. We start by studying how a given coordinate may influence all the other coordinates. Before doing so, we will need some elementary results.

Let \(X\) be a Banach space. Then every \(x\in E(\Gamma,X)\) has countable support.

Proof.Fold proof

Fix \(x=(x_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\in E(\Gamma,X)\). Observe that by definition \((\lVert x_{\gamma}\rVert)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\in E\), in other words the net of finite partial sums

\(\sum_{\gamma\in\Delta}\lVert x_{\gamma}\rVert e_{\gamma}\to(\lVert x_{\gamma}\rVert)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\in E\quad(\Delta\subseteq\Gamma,\ \Delta\text{ finite}).\)

Equivalently, the tails go to zero, that is, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists a finite set \(\Delta_{\varepsilon}\subseteq\Gamma\) such that for every finite \(\Delta\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\Delta_{\varepsilon}\), then

\(\lVert\sum_{\gamma\in\Delta}\lVert x_{\gamma}\rVert e_{\gamma}\rVert<\varepsilon.\)

For \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), by the tail condition, there exists a finite set \(\Delta_{n}\subseteq\Gamma\) such that for every finite \(\Delta\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\Delta_{n}\), we have

\(\lVert\sum_{\gamma\in\Delta}\lVert x_{\gamma}\rVert e_{\gamma}\rVert<\frac{1}{n}.\)

In particular, since \(\lVert e_{\gamma}\rVert=1\), i.e the basis is normalised, the previous condition implies

\(\{\gamma\in\Gamma:\lVert x_{\gamma}\rVert\geqslant 1/n\}\subseteq\Delta_{n}.\)

It follows that

\(\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\Delta_{n},\)

which is countable, finishing the proof. ∎

(Separable sets have countable support).

If \(Y\subseteq E(\Gamma,X)\) is separable, then there exists a countable \(\Delta\subseteq\Gamma\) such that \(Y\subseteq E(\Delta,X)\).

Proof.Fold proof

Choose a dense sequence \((y_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) in \(Y\) and set \(\Delta=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\operatorname{supp}(y_{n})\), which is countable by Lemma 4.12. Then \(y_{n}\in E(\Delta,X)\) for all \(n\), and \(E(\Delta,X)\) is closed in \(E(\Gamma,X)\), hence \(Y\subseteq E(\Delta,X)\). ∎

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis \((e_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\), and let \(X\) be a Banach space. Assume that for every bounded operator \(S\colon X\to E\) there exists a countable set \(\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma\) such that \(S(X)\subseteq E(\Lambda)\). Then, for every bounded operator \(T\colon X\to E(\Gamma,X)\) there exists a countable set \(\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma\) such that \(T(X)\subseteq E(\Lambda,X)\).

Proof.Fold proof

Suppose, towards a contradiction, that \(T\colon X\to E(\Gamma,X)\) is bounded and that \(T(X)\) is not contained in \(E(\Lambda,X)\) for any countable \(\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma\). Set

\(\Delta=\{\alpha\in\Gamma:\ R_{\alpha}Tx\neq 0\text{ for some }x\in B_{X}\}.\)

Then \(\Delta\) is uncountable. For every \(\alpha\in\Delta\) choose \(x_{\alpha}\in B_{X}\) with \(R_{\alpha}Tx_{\alpha}\neq 0\). After passing to an uncountable subset of \(\Delta\), there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that

\(\lVert R_{\alpha}Tx_{\alpha}\rVert\geqslant\varepsilon\qquad(\alpha\in\Delta).\)

Choose \(x_{\alpha}^{*}\in B_{X^{*}}\) with

\(x_{\alpha}^{*}(R_{\alpha}Tx_{\alpha})=\lVert R_{\alpha}Tx_{\alpha}\rVert\)

in the real case, and with modulus equal to this norm in the complex case. Multiplying \(x_{\alpha}^{*}\) by a scalar of modulus one in the complex case, we may assume the displayed equality is literal.

Define \(\widehat{T}\colon X\to E(\Gamma)\) by

\(\widehat{T}x=\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}x_{\alpha}^{*}(R_{\alpha}Tx)e_{\alpha}.\)

For each \(x\in X\), the scalar family defining \(\widehat{T}x\) is coordinate-wise dominated by \((\lVert R_{\alpha}Tx\rVert)_{\alpha\in\Gamma}\). Since the norm of \(E\) is symmetric, this gives

\(\lVert\widehat{T}x\rVert_{E(\Gamma)}\leqslant\lVert Tx\rVert_{E(\Gamma,X)}\leqslant\lVert T\rVert\,\lVert x\rVert,\)

so \(\widehat{T}\) is bounded. On the other hand,

\(\widehat{T}x_{\alpha}(\alpha)\neq 0\qquad(\alpha\in\Delta),\)

and therefore \(\widehat{T}(X)\) is not contained in \(E(\Lambda)\) for any countable \(\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma\). This contradicts the hypothesis. ∎

We are finally ready to state our first support reduction lemma.

(Support reduction).

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis \((e_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\), let \(X\) be a Banach space, and let

\(T\colon E(\Gamma,X)\to E(\Gamma,X)\)

be a bounded operator. Assume that every bounded operator \(S\colon X\to E\) has separable range. Then, for every countable set \(\Delta\subseteq\Gamma\), there exists a countable set \(\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma\) such that

\(T(E(\Delta,X))\subseteq E(\Lambda,X).\)
Proof.Fold proof

For each \(\alpha\in\Delta\), let

\(J_{\alpha}\colon X\to E(\Gamma,X)\)

denote the canonical embedding into the \(\alpha\)-th coordinate. Then \(T\circ J_{\alpha}\) is a bounded operator from \(X\) into \(E(\Gamma,X)\), so by the assumption and Lemmas 4.13 and 4.14, there exists a countable set \(\Lambda_{\alpha}\subseteq\Gamma\) such that

\(T(J_{\alpha}(X))\subseteq E(\Lambda_{\alpha},X).\)

Set

\(\Lambda=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Delta}\Lambda_{\alpha}.\)

Since \(\Delta\) is countable and each \(\Lambda_{\alpha}\) is countable, the set \(\Lambda\) is countable.

Let \(x=(x_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in\Gamma}\in E(\Delta,X)\). Since \(\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq\Delta\), we may write

\(x=\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}J_{\alpha}x_{\alpha},\)

with convergence in \(E(\Gamma,X)\). Hence

\(Tx=\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}T(J_{\alpha}x_{\alpha}).\)

Each term belongs to \(E(\Lambda_{\alpha},X)\subseteq E(\Lambda,X)\), and since \(E(\Lambda,X)\) is a closed subspace of \(E(\Gamma,X)\), it follows that \(Tx\in E(\Lambda,X).\) Therefore, \(T(E(\Delta,X))\subseteq E(\Lambda,X),\) as required. ∎

As a consequence, we obtain the following.

(Support reduction).

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis \((e_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\), let \(X\) be a Banach space, and let

\(T\colon E(\Gamma,X)\to E(\Gamma,X)\)

be a bounded operator. Assume that one of the following holds:

  1. (1)

    \(X\) is separable;

  2. (2)

    \(E=\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\) and \(X\) is WCG.

Then, for every countable set \(\Delta\subseteq\Gamma\), there exists a countable set \(\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma\) such that

\(T(E(\Delta,X))\subseteq E(\Lambda,X).\)
Proof.Fold proof

The first assertion is immediate from Lemma 4.15, since every operator from a separable Banach space has separable range.

Assume now that \(E=\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\) and that \(X\) is WCG. Let \(S\colon X\to\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\) be bounded. Choose a weakly compact set \(K\subseteq X\) with \(X=\overline{\operatorname{span}}(K)\). Then \(S(K)\) is weakly compact in \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\), and hence norm compact because \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\) has the Schur property. Thus \(S(K)\) is separable, and

\(\overline{S(X)}=\overline{\operatorname{span}}(S(K))\)

is separable. In particular, \(S(X)\) is separable. Applying Lemma 4.15 completes the proof. ∎

So far, we have explored how one coordinate affects the others. For a space \(E\) with a symmetric basis not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\), we now establish a further separation result under the assumption that \(X^{*}\) admits a countable total set. Roughly speaking, this condition ensures that each coordinate can be influenced by at most countably many others. Recall that if \(X\) is a Banach space, a subset \(M\subseteq X^{*}\) is said to be total for \(X\) if \(x^{*}(x)=0\) for all \(x^{*}\in M\) implies that \(x=0\). Before stating the separation lemma, we will need the following preliminary result.

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis \((e_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\) not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\), and let \(X\) be a Banach space. Then for every \(x^{*}\in X^{*}\) and every bounded operator \(T\colon E(\Gamma,X)\to X\) there exists a countable set \(\Delta\subseteq\Gamma\) such that

\(x^{*}TR_{\gamma}=0\qquad(\gamma\in\Gamma\setminus\Delta).\)
Proof.Fold proof

The assertion is trivial if \(x^{*}=0\) or \(T=0\), so assume otherwise. Suppose that

\(A=\{\gamma\in\Gamma:\ x^{*}TR_{\gamma}\neq 0\}\)

is uncountable. Passing to an uncountable subset, choose \(\varepsilon>0\) and an uncountable \(J\subseteq A\) such that, for every \(\gamma\in J\), there is \(u_{\gamma}\in E(\gamma,X)\) with \(\lVert u_{\gamma}\rVert=1\) and

\(|x^{*}(Tu_{\gamma})|\geqslant\varepsilon.\)

Multiplying \(u_{\gamma}\) by a scalar of modulus one, we may assume that \(x^{*}(Tu_{\gamma})=|x^{*}(Tu_{\gamma})|\geqslant\varepsilon\) for all \(\gamma\in J\).

Let \((b_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in J}\) be a finitely supported family of non-negative scalars. Since the vectors \(u_{\gamma}\) are supported on pairwise distinct coordinates and have norm one in their respective fibres,

\(\Bigl\|\sum_{\gamma\in J}b_{\gamma}u_{\gamma}\Bigr\|_{E(\Gamma,X)}=\Bigl\|\sum_{\gamma\in J}b_{\gamma}e_{\gamma}\Bigr\|_{E}.\)

Consequently,

\(\|x^{*}\|\,\|T\|\,\Bigl\|\sum_{\gamma\in J}b_{\gamma}e_{\gamma}\Bigr\|_{E}\geqslant\Bigl|x^{*}T\Bigl(\sum_{\gamma\in J}b_{\gamma}u_{\gamma}\Bigr)\Bigr|\geqslant\varepsilon\sum_{\gamma\in J}b_{\gamma}.\)

By symmetry of the basis, this lower estimate is equivalent to

\(\Bigl\|\sum_{\gamma\in J}a_{\gamma}e_{\gamma}\Bigr\|_{E}\geqslant\frac{\varepsilon}{\|x^{*}\|\,\|T\|}\sum_{\gamma\in J}|a_{\gamma}|\)

for every finitely supported scalar family \((a_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in J}\). The reverse estimate follows from the normalisation and the triangle inequality. Hence \((e_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in J}\) is equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}(J)\). Since the basis is symmetric, the same two-sided estimates hold, with the same constants, on every finite subset of \(\Gamma\). Thus the full basis of \(E\) is equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\), a contradiction. ∎

Let \(E\) be a Banach space with a symmetric basis \((e_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\) not equivalent to the unit vector basis of \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma)\), and let \(X\) be a Banach space which admits a countable total set \(M\subseteq X^{*}\). Then for every bounded operator \(T\colon E(\Gamma,X)\to X\), there exists a countable set \(\Delta\subseteq\Gamma\) such that

\(TR_{\gamma}=0\qquad(\gamma\in\Gamma\setminus\Delta).\)
Proof.Fold proof

Let \(M=\{x_{n}^{*}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\) be an enumeration of a countable total set. By Lemma 4.17, for each \(n\) there is a countable set \(\Delta_{n}\subseteq\Gamma\) such that \(x_{n}^{*}TR_{\gamma}=0\) whenever \(\gamma\notin\Delta_{n}\). Put \(\Delta=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\Delta_{n}\). If \(\gamma\notin\Delta\), then \(x_{n}^{*}TR_{\gamma}=0\) for every \(n\). Since \(M\) is total, \(TR_{\gamma}=0\). ∎

4.4.

A combinatorial reduction to diagonal projections

−

We start with the following elementary observation.

(Countable blocks).

Let \(Y\) be a Banach space and \(\Delta\) a non-empty countable set.

  1. (a)

    If \(1\leqslant p<\infty\) and \(X=\ell_{p}(\mathbb{N},Y)\), then \(\ell_{p}(\Delta,X)\) is linearly isometric to \(X\).

  2. (b)

    If \(X=c_{0}(\mathbb{N},Y)\), then \(c_{0}(\Delta,X)\) is linearly isometric to \(X\).

Proof.Fold proof

Fix a bijection \(\phi\colon\Delta\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\). In case (a),

\(\ell_{p}(\Delta,X)=\ell_{p}(\Delta,\ell_{p}(\mathbb{N},Y))\cong\ell_{p}(\Delta\times\mathbb{N},Y)\cong\ell_{p}(\mathbb{N},Y)=X\)

via reindexing by \(\phi\), which preserves the \(\ell_{p}\)-norm. In case (b) the same reindexing argument applies with the \(c_{0}\)-norm, since \(\sup\) is preserved under bijections. ∎

We now present the standard free-set selection theorem. For a set \(S\) and a cardinal \(\mu\) we write \([S]^{<\mu}\) for the family of subsets of \(S\) of cardinality \(<\mu\). First, we record the following almost-trivial lemma with a proof for the sake of completeness.

(Cofinality pigeonhole).

Let \(\kappa\) be an infinite cardinal with \(\mathrm{cf}(\kappa)>\omega\), and let \(S\) be a set with \(\left|S\right|=\kappa\). If \(S=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}S_{n}\), then \(\left|S_{n}\right|=\kappa\) for some \(n\in\mathbb{N}\).

Proof.Fold proof

If \(\left|S_{n}\right|<\kappa\) for all \(n\), then \(\left|\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}S_{n}\right|<\kappa\) because \(\mathrm{cf}(\kappa)>\omega\). This contradicts \(\left|S\right|=\kappa\). ∎

A classical theorem of Hajnal provides the combinatorial ingredient needed in our one-sided arguments. The result, originally conjectured by Ruziewicz  and proved by Hajnal , is used below in the form where \(F:\kappa\to[\kappa]^{<\lambda}\) for some cardinal \(\lambda<\kappa\). For countable-valued mappings this means that the one-sided argument applies when \(\kappa>\omega_{1}\).

(Hajnal’s set mapping theorem).

Let \(\kappa\) be an infinite cardinal and let \(\lambda<\kappa\) be a cardinal. Let \(F\colon\kappa\to[\kappa]^{<\lambda}\) be a set mapping (i.e., \(\alpha\notin F(\alpha)\) for all \(\alpha\)). Then there exists \(H\subseteq\kappa\) with \(\left|H\right|=\kappa\) such that for all distinct \(\alpha,\beta\in H\) one has \(\alpha\notin F(\beta)\) and \(\beta\notin F(\alpha)\).

Proof.Fold proof

For background and further discussion see or . ∎

(Two-sided countable free set).

Let \(\kappa\) be an uncountable cardinal and let

\(F\colon\kappa\to[\kappa]^{\leqslant\omega}\)

be a set mapping. Assume, in addition, that every inverse fibre

\(F^{-1}(\{\alpha\})=\{\beta<\kappa:\alpha\in F(\beta)\}\)

is countable. Then there is \(H\subseteq\kappa\) with \(\left|H\right|=\kappa\) such that, for all distinct \(\alpha,\beta\in H\),

\(\alpha\notin F(\beta)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\beta\notin F(\alpha).\)
Proof.Fold proof

We construct \(H=\{\alpha_{\xi}:\xi<\kappa\}\) by recursion. Suppose that \(\alpha_{\eta}\) has been chosen for every \(\eta<\xi\). Put

\(B_{\xi}=\{\alpha_{\eta}:\eta<\xi\}\cup\bigcup_{\eta<\xi}F(\alpha_{\eta})\cup\bigcup_{\eta<\xi}F^{-1}(\{\alpha_{\eta}\}).\)

Each set appearing in the two unions is countable, and \(\xi<\kappa\). Hence

\(\left|B_{\xi}\right|\leqslant\left|\xi\right|\cdot\omega<\kappa.\)

Choose \(\alpha_{\xi}\in\kappa\setminus B_{\xi}\). This completes the recursion.

If \(\eta<\xi\), then \(\alpha_{\xi}\notin F(\alpha_{\eta})\) because \(\alpha_{\xi}\notin B_{\xi}\), and also \(\alpha_{\eta}\notin F(\alpha_{\xi})\) because \(\alpha_{\xi}\notin F^{-1}(\{\alpha_{\eta}\})\). Thus \(H\) is free. ∎

The one-sided countable-valued hypothesis is not enough at \(\kappa=\omega_{1}\). Indeed, the map \(F(\alpha)=\{\beta:\beta<\alpha\}\) on \(\omega_{1}\) is countable-valued and has no two-point free set. Thus every use below of Hajnal’s theorem with merely countable values is made under the explicit assumption \(\kappa>\omega_{1}\), unless a two-sided countability hypothesis is available.

Let \(X\) be a WCG Banach space, let \(P\colon\ell_{1}(\Gamma,X)\to\ell_{1}(\Gamma,X)\) be a bounded projection, and put \(\kappa=\left|\Gamma\right|\). Then there exist pairwise disjoint countable sets \((\Gamma_{\alpha})_{\alpha<\kappa}\) with

\(\Gamma=\bigsqcup_{\alpha<\kappa}\Gamma_{\alpha}\)

such that the following hold.

  1. (i)

    for each \(\alpha<\kappa\),

    \(P(\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X))\subseteq\ell_{1}\Bigl(\bigcup_{\beta\leqslant\alpha}\Gamma_{\beta},X\Bigr);\)
  2. (ii)

    for each \(\alpha<\kappa\), the operator

    \(Q_{\alpha}:=R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}P|_{\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)}\colon\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)\to\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)\)

    is a bounded projection;

  3. (iii)

    the set mapping

    \(F(\alpha)=\Bigl\{\beta<\alpha:\ R_{\Gamma_{\beta}}P|_{\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)}\neq 0\Bigr\}\)

    takes countable values.

Proof.Fold proof

Fix a well-ordering \((\theta_{\xi})_{\xi<\kappa}\) of \(\Gamma\). We construct the sets \(\Gamma_{\alpha}\) by transfinite recursion. Assume that disjoint countable sets \(\Gamma_{\beta}\) have been chosen for \(\beta<\alpha\), and put

\(\Delta_{\alpha}=\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}\Gamma_{\beta}.\)

Then \(\left|\Delta_{\alpha}\right|<\kappa\). Let \(\gamma_{\alpha}\) be the first element of the well-ordering which is not in \(\Delta_{\alpha}\).

Define increasing countable sets \(C_{n}\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\Delta_{\alpha}\) as follows. Put \(C_{0}=\{\gamma_{\alpha}\}\). Once \(C_{n}\) is known, Corollary 4.16 gives a countable \(\Lambda_{n}\subseteq\Gamma\) such that

\(P(\ell_{1}(C_{n},X))\subseteq\ell_{1}(\Lambda_{n},X).\)

Set

\(C_{n+1}=C_{n}\cup(\Lambda_{n}\setminus\Delta_{\alpha}).\)

Finally put \(\Gamma_{\alpha}=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}C_{n}\). Then \(\Gamma_{\alpha}\) is countable and disjoint from \(\Delta_{\alpha}\).

The use of the first unused point in the fixed well-ordering ensures that the construction exhausts \(\Gamma\). Indeed, if \(\theta_{\xi}\) were not in \(\bigcup_{\alpha<\kappa}\Gamma_{\alpha}\), then at every stage the first unused point would have index at most \(\xi\); this would give \(\kappa\) many distinct chosen points among the set \(\{\theta_{\eta}:\eta\leqslant\xi\}\), whose cardinality is strictly smaller than \(\kappa\), a contradiction.

We verify the three asserted properties. Since \(\Gamma_{\alpha}=\bigcup_{n}C_{n}\) and \((C_{n})\) is increasing,

\(\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)=\overline{\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\ell_{1}(C_{n},X)}.\)

For each \(n\),

\(P(\ell_{1}(C_{n},X))\subseteq\ell_{1}(\Lambda_{n},X)\subseteq\ell_{1}(\Delta_{\alpha}\cup C_{n+1},X)\subseteq\ell_{1}(\Delta_{\alpha}\cup\Gamma_{\alpha},X).\)

Taking closures gives

(4.1) \(P(\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X))\subseteq\ell_{1}(\Delta_{\alpha}\cup\Gamma_{\alpha},X)=\ell_{1}\Bigl(\bigcup_{\beta\leqslant\alpha}\Gamma_{\beta},X\Bigr),\)

which is (i).

Fix \(\alpha<\kappa\). From (4.1) applied to every \(\beta<\alpha\) and from density of finite block sums, we obtain

(4.2) \(P(\ell_{1}(\Delta_{\alpha},X))\subseteq\ell_{1}(\Delta_{\alpha},X).\)

Let \(x\in\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)\) and write, using (4.1),

\(Px=u+v,\qquad u\in\ell_{1}(\Delta_{\alpha},X),\quad v\in\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X).\)

Then \(v=R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}Px=Q_{\alpha}x\). Since \(P^{2}=P\), we have \(Pu+Pv=u+v\). Applying \(R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}\) and using (4.2) yields \(R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}Pv=v.\) Consequently,

\(Q_{\alpha}^{2}x=R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}P(R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}Px)=R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}Pv=v=Q_{\alpha}x,\)

so \(Q_{\alpha}\) is a projection.

Finally, for each \(\alpha\), another application of Corollary 4.16 gives a countable set \(\Lambda_{\alpha}\subseteq\Gamma\) such that

\(P(\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X))\subseteq\ell_{1}(\Lambda_{\alpha},X).\)

Since the blocks \((\Gamma_{\beta})_{\beta<\kappa}\) are disjoint, only countably many of them meet \(\Lambda_{\alpha}\). Hence \(F(\alpha)\) is countable. ∎

(A large diagonal family).

With notation as in Lemma 4.24, assume in addition that \(\kappa>\omega_{1}\). Then there exists \(H\subseteq\kappa\) with \(\left|H\right|=\kappa\) such that

\(R_{\Gamma_{\beta}}P(\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X))=\{0\}\qquad(\alpha,\beta\in H,\ \alpha\neq\beta).\)

In particular, on the subspace

\(W=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in H}\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)\Bigr)_{\ell_{1}(H)}\subseteq\ell_{1}(\Gamma,X),\)

the operator \(P\) is diagonal: if \(w=\sum_{\beta\in H}x_{\beta}\in W\), with \(x_{\beta}\in\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\beta},X)\), then

\(R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}Pw=Q_{\alpha}x_{\alpha}\qquad(\alpha\in H).\)
Proof.Fold proof

Apply Proposition 4.21, with \(\lambda=\omega_{1}\), to the countable-valued set mapping \(F\) from Lemma 4.24(iii). We obtain \(H\subseteq\kappa\), \(\left|H\right|=\kappa\), such that for distinct \(\alpha,\beta\in H\) one has \(\beta\notin F(\alpha)\) and \(\alpha\notin F(\beta)\). If \(\alpha<\beta\) are in \(H\), Lemma 4.24(i) already gives

\(R_{\Gamma_{\beta}}P|_{\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)}=0,\)

whereas \(\alpha\notin F(\beta)\) gives

\(R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}P|_{\ell_{1}(\Gamma_{\beta},X)}=0.\)

Thus all off-diagonal block entries vanish on the family \(H\).

For the final assertion, first check the displayed identity for finite block sums. The general case follows by approximating \(w\) by finite block sums and using continuity of \(P\) and of the coordinate projection \(R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}\). ∎

Let \(X\) be a separable Banach space, and let \(E_{0}(\Gamma,X)\) be either \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma,X)\), \(1<p<\infty\), or \(c_{0}(\Gamma,X)\). If \(P\colon E_{0}(\Gamma,X)\to E_{0}(\Gamma,X)\) is a bounded projection, then there are pairwise disjoint countable sets \((\Gamma_{\alpha})_{\alpha<\kappa}\) partitioning \(\Gamma\), block projections

\(Q_{\alpha}=R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}P|_{E_{0}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)},\)

and a set \(H\subseteq\kappa\) with \(\left|H\right|=\kappa\) such that

\(R_{\Gamma_{\beta}}P(E_{0}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X))=\{0\}\qquad(\alpha,\beta\in H,\ \alpha\neq\beta).\)

The construction of the countable blocks and the proof that the operators \(Q_{\alpha}\) are projections are identical to the proof of Lemma 4.24, using Corollary 4.16 in place of the WCG support reduction. Define

\(F(\alpha)=\{\beta<\alpha:R_{\Gamma_{\beta}}P|_{E_{0}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)}\neq 0\}.\)

As before, \(F(\alpha)\) is countable for every \(\alpha\).

We claim that the inverse fibres of \(F\) are also countable. Fix \(\beta<\kappa\). The range space \(E_{0}(\Gamma_{\beta},X)\) is separable, so choose a countable total set \(M_{\beta}\subseteq E_{0}(\Gamma_{\beta},X)^{*}\). For each \(y^{*}\in M_{\beta}\), the scalar functional

\(y^{*}R_{\Gamma_{\beta}}P\colon E_{0}(\Gamma,X)\to\mathbb{K}\)

can be non-zero on only countably many coordinate fibres. This follows from the same finite-disjoint-support estimate used in the proof of Lemma 4.17: if such a scalar functional were non-zero on uncountably many coordinate fibres, then on an uncountable subfamily it would be bounded below by a fixed positive constant, forcing the scalar basis of \(E_{0}\) to dominate the \(\ell_{1}\)-basis, which is impossible for \(\ell_{p}\), \(1<p<\infty\), and for \(c_{0}\). Hence the set of blocks \(\Gamma_{\alpha}\) on which \(y^{*}R_{\Gamma_{\beta}}P\) is non-zero is countable. Taking the union over the countable set \(M_{\beta}\) shows that

\(F^{-1}(\{\beta\})=\{\alpha<\kappa:\beta\in F(\alpha)\}\)

is countable.

Proposition 4.22 now gives a free set \(H\subseteq\kappa\) with \(\left|H\right|=\kappa\). If \(\alpha<\beta\) are in \(H\), then triangularity of the block construction gives \(R_{\Gamma_{\beta}}P|_{E_{0}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)}=0\), while \(\alpha\notin F(\beta)\) gives \(R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}P|_{E_{0}(\Gamma_{\beta},X)}=0\). Thus all off-diagonal block entries vanish on \(H\). ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.1: embedding a full copy into one of the halves

−

Using the previous results, we are ready for the proof of Theorem 4.1.

Proof of Theorem 4.1.Fold proof

We give one argument which covers all the asserted sums. Let \(\mathcal{E}\) denote one of the functors

\(\ell_{1},\qquad\ell_{p}\ (1<p<\infty),\qquad c_{0},\)

and put \(X=\mathcal{E}(\mathbb{N},Y)\) and \(Z=\mathcal{E}(\Gamma,X)\). Since \(\left|\Gamma\times\mathbb{N}\right|=\left|\Gamma\right|\), the space \(Z\) is isometric, by reindexing, to \(\mathcal{E}(\Gamma,Y)\). Let \(P\colon Z\to Z\) be a bounded projection. Choose countable blocks \((\Gamma_{\alpha})_{\alpha<\kappa}\), block projections

\(Q_{\alpha}=R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}P|_{\mathcal{E}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)}\)

and a set \(H\subseteq\kappa\) of cardinality \(\kappa\) as in the corresponding block-diagonalisation lemmas.

For each \(\alpha\in H\), the block \(\mathcal{E}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)\) is isomorphic, indeed isometric after reindexing, to \(X\) by Lemma 4.19. Put \(L=1+\lVert P\rVert.\) If the relevant countable model \(X\) is \(C\)-primary, where \(C\colon[1,\infty)\to[1,\infty)\) is increasing, choose, for each \(\alpha\in H\), one of the two projections \(Q_{\alpha},I-Q_{\alpha}\) whose range is \(C(L)\)-isomorphic to \(\mathcal{E}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)\). If instead \(X\) is merely primary, choose for each \(\alpha\in H\) one of the two projections \(Q_{\alpha}\) or \(I-Q_{\alpha}\) whose range is isomorphic to \(\mathcal{E}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)\). Passing to a subset of \(H\) of cardinality \(\kappa\), we may suppose that the same choice, \(Q_{\alpha}\) or \(I-Q_{\alpha}\), has been made for every remaining \(\alpha\).

In the first case set \(P_{0}=P\) and \(Q_{\alpha}^{0}=Q_{\alpha}\); in the second set \(P_{0}=I-P\) and \(Q_{\alpha}^{0}=I-Q_{\alpha}\). Then \(\lVert P_{0}\rVert\leqslant L\) and \(\lVert Q_{\alpha}^{0}\rVert\leqslant L\).

Let

\(Z_{\alpha}=Q_{\alpha}^{0}\mathcal{E}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X),\qquad c_{\alpha}=d_{BM}\bigl(Z_{\alpha},\mathcal{E}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)\bigr).\)

In the uniformly primary case the preceding choice gives \(c_{\alpha}\leqslant C(L)\) for all \(\alpha\) in the chosen family; fix \(M=C(L)+1.\) In the primary, non-uniform case, where \(\mathrm{cf}(\kappa)>\omega\), write the chosen family as

\(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\{\alpha:\ c_{\alpha}<n\}.\)

By Lemma 4.20, one of these sets has cardinality \(\kappa\); after passing to it, fix \(M>1\) such that \(c_{\alpha}<M\) for every remaining \(\alpha\). Thus in either case there are \(H^{\prime\prime}\subseteq H\) with \(\left|H^{\prime\prime}\right|=\kappa\) and \(M>1\) such that

(4.3) \(d_{BM}\bigl(Z_{\alpha},\mathcal{E}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)\bigr)<M\qquad(\alpha\in H^{\prime\prime}).\)

Set \(\mathscr{Y}=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in H^{\prime\prime}}Z_{\alpha}\Bigr)_{\mathcal{E}(H^{\prime\prime})}\subseteq Z.\) For each \(\alpha\in H^{\prime\prime}\), choose an isomorphism

\(\widetilde{J}_{\alpha}\colon\mathcal{E}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)\to Z_{\alpha}\)

with \(\lVert\widetilde{J}_{\alpha}\rVert\lVert\widetilde{J}_{\alpha}^{-1}\rVert<M\), and rescale it to \(J_{\alpha}\) so that \(\lVert J_{\alpha}\rVert=\lVert J_{\alpha}^{-1}\rVert<\sqrt{M}.\) The block-diagonal operator

\(J\colon\Bigl(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in H^{\prime\prime}}\mathcal{E}(\Gamma_{\alpha},X)\Bigr)_{\mathcal{E}(H^{\prime\prime})}\longrightarrow\mathscr{Y},\qquad J((x_{\alpha})_{\alpha})=(J_{\alpha}x_{\alpha})_{\alpha},\)

satisfies \(\lVert J\rVert\lVert J^{-1}\rVert<M\). Since \(\left|H^{\prime\prime}\right|=\kappa\) and all blocks are countable, the domain of \(J\) is isometric to \(Z\). Hence

(4.4) \(\mathscr{Y}\simeq_{M}Z.\)

We now embed this copy complementably into the range of \(P_{0}\). Define

\(T\colon\mathscr{Y}\to P_{0}Z,\qquad T\Bigl(\sum_{\alpha\in H^{\prime\prime}}z_{\alpha}\Bigr)=\sum_{\alpha\in H^{\prime\prime}}P_{0}z_{\alpha}.\)

The sum converges in the corresponding \(\mathcal{E}\)-sum and \(\lVert T\rVert\leqslant\lVert P_{0}\rVert\). The off-diagonal block entries of \(P_{0}\) vanish on \(H^{\prime\prime}\), and therefore

\(R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}T\Bigl(\sum_{\beta\in H^{\prime\prime}}z_{\beta}\Bigr)=z_{\alpha}\qquad(\alpha\in H^{\prime\prime}).\)

Define

\(S\colon P_{0}Z\to\mathscr{Y},\qquad Sx=\sum_{\alpha\in H^{\prime\prime}}Q_{\alpha}^{0}(R_{\Gamma_{\alpha}}x).\)

For \(\ell_{p}\)-sums this is bounded by the usual \(\ell_{p}\) estimate, and for \(c_{0}\) by the corresponding supremum estimate; in all cases

\(\lVert S\rVert\leqslant\sup_{\alpha\in H^{\prime\prime}}\lVert Q_{\alpha}^{0}\rVert\leqslant L.\)

Moreover \(ST=\mathrm{Id}_{\mathscr{Y}}\). Hence \(TS\) is a bounded projection on \(P_{0}Z\) onto \(T(\mathscr{Y})\), and \(T(\mathscr{Y})\simeq Z\) by (4.4). Thus either \(PZ\) or \((I-P)Z\) contains a complemented copy of \(Z\).

Since \(P_{0}Z\) is itself complemented in \(Z\), Pełczyński’s decomposition method, Theorem 2.3, and the stability \(Z\simeq\mathcal{E}(\mathbb{N},Z)\) imply that \(P_{0}Z\simeq Z\). This proves primariness.

In the uniformly primary case, the same proof gives uniform constants. Indeed, \(P_{0}Z\) is \(L\)-complemented in \(Z\); the subspace \(T(\mathscr{Y})\) is at most \(L^{2}\)-complemented in \(P_{0}Z\); and, by (4.4), it is \(ML^{2}\)-isomorphic to \(Z\), where \(M=C(L)+1\) depends only on \(\lVert P\rVert\). Applying the quantitative Pełczyński decomposition theorem, Theorem A.1, gives a bound for \(d_{BM}(P_{0}Z,Z)\) depending only on \(\lVert P\rVert\). Therefore the uncountable sum is uniformly primary whenever the countable model is uniformly primary. ∎

(Coordinate diagonalisation).

As in this section, Γ is uncountable.

\(R_{\beta}TR_{\alpha}=0\qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda,\ \alpha\neq\beta).\)

(4.5) \(R_{\beta}AR_{\alpha}=0\qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda,\ \alpha\neq\beta).\)

\(\widetilde{A}_{\alpha}=R_{\alpha}\widetilde{A}|_{X_{\alpha}}\qquad(\alpha\in\Lambda).\)

\(\lVert U_{\alpha}\rVert\lVert V_{\alpha}\rVert\leqslant C\qquad(\alpha\in\Lambda).\)

5.

PFP and UPFP in other Banach spaces

−

In this section, we collect several further examples that do not fit neatly into the symmetric-basis framework of the previous sections. Some of them are naturally handled by existing primariness arguments, while others require a separate factorisation argument. We have grouped them according to the underlying mechanism rather than historical chronology.

5.1.

\(\ell_{\infty}/c_{0}\cong C(\omega^{*})\)

−

The space \(\ell_{\infty}/c_{0}\cong C(\omega^{*})\) has the \(2\)-PFP.

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(C=C(\omega^{*})\) and let \(T\in\mathscr{B}(C)\). By (applied with \(A=\omega^{*}\)), there exist a non-empty clopen \(B\subseteq\omega^{*}\) and a scalar \(\gamma\) such that

\(\chi_{B}\,T(x)=\gamma x\qquad(x\in C(B)),\)

where we identify \(C(B)\) with the closed subspace \(\{x\in C(\omega^{*}):x=\chi_{B}x\}\) of functions supported on \(B\). Equivalently, writing \(I_{B}\colon C(B)\to C\) for the canonical inclusion (extension by \(0\) outside \(B\)) and \(R_{B}\colon C\to C(B)\) for restriction, we have

\(R_{B}TI_{B}=\gamma\,\mathrm{Id}_{C(B)}.\)

Since \(|\gamma|+|1-\gamma|\geqslant|\gamma+(1-\gamma)|=1\), we have \(\max\{|\gamma|,|1-\gamma|\}\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\).

As \(B\) is a non-empty clopen subset of \(\omega^{*}\), it is homeomorphic to \(\omega^{*}\) and hence there exists an isometric isomorphism \(J\colon C\to C(B)\). If \(|\gamma|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\), define \(V=I_{B}J\) and \(U=(1/\gamma)\,J^{-1}R_{B}\). Then

\(UTV=(1/\gamma)\,J^{-1}(R_{B}TI_{B})J=\mathrm{Id}_{C},\)

and \(\|U\|\,\|V\|\leqslant 2\).

If instead \(|1-\gamma|\geqslant\tfrac{1}{2}\), we apply the same construction to the operator \(\mathrm{Id}_{C}-T\): since \(R_{B}(\mathrm{Id}_{C}-T)I_{B}=(1-\gamma)\mathrm{Id}_{C(B)}\), we obtain bounded \(U,V\) with \(U(\mathrm{Id}_{C}-T)V=\mathrm{Id}_{C}\) and \(\|U\|\,\|V\|\leqslant 2\). ∎

Here X is assumed to be separable.

As noted in , if \(X\) has the PFP, then so does \(C(\omega^{*},X)\), and the same argument yields the corresponding statement for the UPFP.
