5.2.

The \(p\)-James tree space \(JT_{p}\)

−

We start by recalling the following well-known lemma.

Let \(E\) be a Banach space and let \(S\colon E\to E\) be bounded. Assume that there exist complemented subspaces \(Y,Z\subseteq E\) and an isomorphism \(V\colon E\to Y\) such that \(S|_{Y}\colon Y\to Z\) is an isomorphism. Then \(\mathrm{Id}_{E}\) factors through \(S\).

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(P_{Z}\colon E\to Z\) be a bounded projection. Define

\(U=V^{-1}\,(S|_{Y})^{-1}\,P_{Z}\in\mathscr{B}(E)\qquad\text{and}\qquad W=\iota_{Y}\circ V\in\mathscr{B}(E),\)

where \(\iota_{Y}\colon Y\hookrightarrow E\) is the inclusion map. Then, since \(S(Wx)=S(Vx)\in Z\) and \(P_{Z}\) acts as the identity on \(Z\),

\(USW=V^{-1}(S|_{Y})^{-1}P_{Z}\,S\,V=V^{-1}(S|_{Y})^{-1}S|_{Y}\,V=\mathrm{Id}_{E}.\)

∎

Fix \(1<p<\infty\) and write \(q\) for the conjugate exponent, \(1/p+1/q=1\). Let \(\mathcal{T}\) denote the dyadic tree

\(\mathcal{T}=\{(n,i):n\in\mathbb{N}_{0},\ 0\leqslant i<2^{n}\},\)

partially ordered by the predecessor relation: \((n,i)\prec(m,j)\) if \((m,j)\) is a strict descendant of \((n,i)\) in the usual dyadic splitting. A segment is a finite chain \(S=\{t_{1}\prec t_{2}\prec\cdots\prec t_{k}\}\) in \(\mathcal{T}\), and a branch is an infinite chain (starting at some level).

For each \(t\in\mathcal{T}\) let \(x_{t}\) denote the canonical unit vector in \(c_{00}(\mathcal{T})\). The \(p\)-James tree space \(JT_{p}\) is the completion of \(c_{00}(\mathcal{T})\) for the norm

(5.1) \(\Bigl\|\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}a_{t}x_{t}\Bigr\|_{JT_{p}}=\sup\Biggl\{\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Bigl|\sum_{t\in S_{j}}a_{t}\Bigr|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p}:S_{1},\dots,S_{m}\ \text{pairwise disjoint segments of }\mathcal{T}\Biggr\}.\)

For \(p=2\) this is James’ original tree space \(JT\); see Andrew  for this formulation and the associated segment functionals and projections.

For any segment \(S\subseteq\mathcal{T}\) we write \(f_{S}\in(JT_{p})^{*}\) for the segment functional

\(f_{S}\Bigl(\sum_{t}a_{t}x_{t}\Bigr)=\sum_{t\in S}a_{t},\)

so \(\|f_{S}\|=1\) (take the single segment \(S\) in (5.1)). If \(B\) is a branch, we similarly write \(f_{B}(\sum_{t}a_{t}x_{t})=\sum_{t\in B}a_{t}\); this is bounded because the branch subspace is (isometric to) the corresponding \(p\)-James space (compare Andrew, Proposition 1(b)).

We shall use the following standard structural facts (proved in Andrew for \(p=2\) and valid, with the same proofs, for \(1<p<\infty\) after replacing \(\ell_{2}\)-estimates by \(\ell_{p}\)-estimates):

  • (i)

    For every subtree \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\), the subspace \([x_{t}:t\in\mathcal{S}]\) is isometric to \(JT_{p}\) and is \(1\)-complemented in \(JT_{p}\) by a norm-one projection built from a tree-like family of disjoint segments (as in Andrew, Proposition 1(a)).

  • (ii)

    If \(t_{1},\dots,t_{m}\) are pairwise incomparable nodes, then

    \(\Bigl\|\sum_{k=1}^{m}a_{k}x_{t_{k}}\Bigr\|_{JT_{p}}=\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^{m}|a_{k}|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},\)

    since every segment intersects \(\{t_{1},\dots,t_{m}\}\) in at most one point. Thus, antichains span isometric copies of \(\ell_{p}\).

For every \(1<p<\infty\), the space \(JT_{p}\) has the uniform primary factorisation property. That is, there exists a constant \(C_{p}\geqslant 1\) such that for every bounded operator \(T\colon JT_{p}\to JT_{p}\) there are \(U,V\in\mathscr{B}(JT_{p})\) with either \(UTV=\mathrm{Id}_{JT_{p}}\) or \(U(\mathrm{Id}_{JT_{p}}-T)V=\mathrm{Id}_{JT_{p}}\) and \(\|U\|\,\|V\|\leqslant C_{p}\).

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(T\in\mathscr{B}(JT_{p})\) and set \(U=T\) and \(V=\mathrm{Id}-T\). Fix once and for all a scalar \(y\in(0,1/4)\).

Andrew proved for \(JT=JT_{2}\) that there exists a subtree \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\) such that, writing \(X=[x_{t}:t\in\mathcal{S}]\), one has:

  1. (a)

    \(X\) is isometric to \(JT\) and \(1\)-complemented in \(JT\);

  2. (b)

    either \(U|_{X}\) or \(V|_{X}\) is an isomorphism;

  3. (c)

    the corresponding range \(U(X)\) or \(V(X)\) is complemented in \(JT\).

Moreover, the proof is quantitative once \(y\) is fixed: it produces a uniform lower bound (depending on \(y\)) for the diagonal coefficients on the chosen subtree, and a uniform invertibility estimate obtained by a Neumann-series argument for the branch multipliers (see the construction around Theorem 6 in Andrew ).

We claim that the same conclusion holds for \(JT_{p}\), \(1<p<\infty\), with constants depending only on \(p\) (and the fixed \(y\)). Indeed, Andrew’s proof uses:

  • •

    a dichotomy on each basis vector using a branch functional:

    \(1=f_{B_{t}}(x_{t})=f_{B_{t}}(Ux_{t})+f_{B_{t}}(Vx_{t}),\)

    hence for each \(t\) either \(|f_{B_{t}}(Ux_{t})|\geqslant 1/2\) or \(|f_{B_{t}}(Vx_{t})|\geqslant 1/2\);

  • •

    a Ramsey-type subtree selection and a bounded-variation selection on branches ;

  • •

    two “gliding hump” propositions whose contradiction step exploits that large antichains behave like \(\ell_{2}\) inside \(JT\).

In \(JT_{p}\) the antichain estimate in the last bullet is exactly (ii) above with \(\ell_{2}\) replaced by \(\ell_{p}\), so the same contradiction goes through for \(p>1\) (since the lower bound grows like \(L\) while the upper bound grows like \(L^{1/p}\)). All other parts of the argument are combinatorial or use only the segment/branch norming mechanism, hence are unchanged. Therefore we obtain a subtree \(\mathcal{S}\) and a choice \(W\in\{T,\mathrm{Id}-T\}\) such that \(W|_{X}\) is an isomorphism and \(W(X)\) is complemented, where \(X=[x_{t}:t\in\mathcal{S}]\simeq JT_{p}\) is \(1\)-complemented.

Finally, apply Lemma 5.3 to \(E=JT_{p}\) and \(S=W\). We have complemented subspaces \(Y=X\) and \(Z=W(X)\), and \(W|_{X}\colon X\to W(X)\) is an isomorphism. The factorisation produced by Lemma 5.3 yields \(\mathrm{Id}_{JT_{p}}\) factoring through \(W\) with a constant controlled by the projection constants of \(X\) and \(W(X)\) and by \(\|(W|_{X})^{-1}\|\). All these bounds depend only on \(p\) (and the fixed \(y\)), hence one obtains a uniform constant \(C_{p}\) independent of \(T\). Thus \(\mathrm{Id}_{JT_{p}}\) factors through either \(T\) or \(\mathrm{Id}_{JT_{p}}-T\), with uniform control, i.e. \(JT_{p}\) has the UPFP. ∎

5.3.

\(\mathcal{B}(\ell_{p})\)

−

For context, Blower’s theorem that \(\mathcal{B}(\ell_{2})\) is primary and Wark’s primariness results for certain \(\ell_{\infty}\)-direct sums are formulated in terms of projections and decompositions. They therefore do not, at least not directly, yield the PFP or the UPFP. The argument below for \(\mathcal{B}(\ell_{p})\) is instead genuinely operator-theoretic.

Fix \(p\in(1,\infty)\) and write \(q=\frac{p}{p-1}\). For \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) let \(X_{n}=\mathcal{B}(\ell_{p}^{n})\) with the operator norm. Set

\(\mathcal{M}_{p}\;=\;\Big(\bigoplus_{n=1}^{\infty}X_{n}\Big)_{\ell_{\infty}},\qquad\lVert(x_{n})\rVert_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}=\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\lVert x_{n}\rVert.\)

We shall use the fact (proved using Pełczyński’s decomposition method in ) that \(\mathcal{B}(\ell_{p})\) is (linearly) isomorphic to \(\mathcal{M}_{p}\). Hence, it suffices to prove UPFP for \(\mathcal{M}_{p}\). Christensen and Sinclair acknowledge that Lindenstrauss and Haagerup were aware of the existence of such an isomorphism at least for \(p=2\).

5.3.1.

Block maps in \(\mathcal{B}(\ell_{p}^{N})\)

−

For \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) let \((e_{i})_{i=1}^{N}\) be the canonical basis of \(\ell_{p}^{N}\) and write \(e_{ij}\in X_{N}\) for the rank-one operator \(e_{ij}(e_{j})=e_{i}\) and \(e_{ij}(e_{k})=0\) for \(k\neq j\). Then \(\lVert e_{ij}\rVert=1\).

Given ordered subsets \(\alpha=\{\alpha_{1}<\cdots<\alpha_{n}\}\) and \(\tau=\{\tau_{1}<\cdots<\tau_{n}\}\) of \(\{1,\dots,N\}\), define the coordinate embedding \(I_{\alpha}\colon\ell_{p}^{n}\to\ell_{p}^{N}\) by \(I_{\alpha}(e_{k})=e_{\alpha_{k}}\) and the coordinate projection \(P_{\alpha}\colon\ell_{p}^{N}\to\ell_{p}^{n}\) by \(P_{\alpha}(e_{\alpha_{k}})=e_{k}\) and \(P_{\alpha}(e_{i})=0\) if \(i\notin\alpha\). Then \(\lVert I_{\alpha}\rVert=\lVert P_{\alpha}\rVert=1\).

Define operators

\(J_{\alpha,\tau}\colon X_{n}\to X_{N},\qquad J_{\alpha,\tau}(A)=I_{\alpha}\,A\,P_{\tau},\)
\(K_{\alpha,\tau}\colon X_{N}\to X_{n},\qquad K_{\alpha,\tau}(B)=P_{\alpha}\,B\,I_{\tau}.\)

They satisfy \(\lVert J_{\alpha,\tau}\rVert=\lVert K_{\alpha,\tau}\rVert=1\) and

\(K_{\alpha,\tau}J_{\alpha,\tau}=\mathrm{Id}_{X_{n}}.\)

Hence

\(Q_{\alpha,\tau}:=J_{\alpha,\tau}K_{\alpha,\tau}\in\mathcal{B}(X_{N})\quad\text{is a norm-one projection on the Banach space }X_{N},\)

because \(Q_{\alpha,\tau}^{2}=J_{\alpha,\tau}(K_{\alpha,\tau}J_{\alpha,\tau})K_{\alpha,\tau}=Q_{\alpha,\tau}\).

We also use entry functionals \(\varphi_{kl}\in X_{N}^{*}\) given by \(\varphi_{kl}(A)=e_{k}^{*}(Ae_{l})\); clearly \(\lVert\varphi_{kl}\rVert=1\).

Let \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(I,J\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}\) be finite non-empty sets. Then for unimodular scalars \((\varepsilon_{i})_{i\in I}\) and \((\delta_{j})_{j\in J}\):

\(\lVert\sum_{i\in I}\varepsilon_{i}e_{ij_{0}}\rVert=|I|^{1/p}\quad(\text{fixed }j_{0}),\qquad\lVert\sum_{j\in J}\delta_{j}e_{i_{0}j}\rVert=|J|^{1/q}\quad(\text{fixed }i_{0}).\)
Proof.Fold proof

The operator \(u=\sum_{i\in I}\varepsilon_{i}e_{ij_{0}}\) maps \(e_{j_{0}}\) to \(\sum_{i\in I}\varepsilon_{i}e_{i}\) and annihilates the other basis vectors, so \(\lVert u\rVert=\lVert\sum_{i\in I}\varepsilon_{i}e_{i}\rVert_{\ell_{p}^{N}}=|I|^{1/p}\). Similarly, \(v=\sum_{j\in J}\delta_{j}e_{i_{0}j}\) has rank one and is \(v(x)=\big(\sum_{j\in J}\delta_{j}x_{j}\big)e_{i_{0}}\), so \(\lVert v\rVert=\lVert(\delta_{j})_{j\in J}\rVert_{\ell_{q}}=|J|^{1/q}\). ∎

5.3.2.

Finite-dimensional scalarisation (Ramsey step)

−
(Finite-dimensional scalarisation).

Fix \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), \(K\geqslant 1\) and \(0<\varepsilon<\tfrac{1}{4}\). There exists \(N_{0}=N_{0}(n,K,\varepsilon,p)\in\mathbb{N}\) such that whenever \(N\geqslant N_{0}\) and \(T\in\mathcal{B}(X_{N})\) with \(\lVert T\rVert\leqslant K\), there exist disjoint subsets \(\alpha,\tau\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}\) with \(|\alpha|=|\tau|=n\) and a scalar \(c\in\mathbb{C}\) such that

\(\lVert K_{\alpha,\tau}\,T\,J_{\alpha,\tau}-c\,\mathrm{Id}_{X_{n}}\rVert<\varepsilon.\)

Consequently, one of \(K_{\alpha,\tau}TJ_{\alpha,\tau}\) and \(K_{\alpha,\tau}(\mathrm{Id}_{X_{N}}-T)J_{\alpha,\tau}\) is invertible on \(X_{n}\) and its inverse has norm at most \(4\).

Proof.Fold proof

The proof is a finite Ramsey selection, following Blower’s argument for \(p=2\) . The only analytic change is that the norms of row and column sums of matrix units are now those computed in Lemma 5.6.

Set \(\eta=\delta=\varepsilon/(8n^{3})\). Partition the disc \(\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|\leqslant K\}\) into finitely many sets of diameter at most \(\eta\).

Diagonal coefficients. Colour each two-element set \(\{i,j\}\), \(i<j\), by the part containing \(\varphi_{ij}(Te_{ij})\). Ramsey’s theorem gives, after choosing the initial Ramsey number sufficiently large, a set \(\Gamma_{1}\) of the required large size on which all these coefficients lie in one part. Choosing \(c\) in that part, we have

\(|\varphi_{ij}(Te_{ij})-c|\leqslant\eta\qquad(i<j,\\ i,j\in\Gamma_{1}).\)

Off-diagonal coefficients. We now perform finitely many further Ramsey thinnings. For each possible order pattern of four symbols corresponding to

\(\varphi_{kl}(Te_{ij}),\qquad(i,j)\neq(k,l),\)

with the row indices ultimately chosen from the first half of the final set and the column indices from the second half, colour the relevant finite subsets as bad when \(|\varphi_{kl}(Te_{ij})|\geqslant\delta\). A homogeneous bad set of arbitrarily large size is impossible. The reason is always one of the following two estimates.

If the source column is fixed and the source row varies, then for suitable unimodular scalars \(\varepsilon_{r}\),

\(K\Big\|\sum_{r=1}^{m}\varepsilon_{r}e_{rj}\Big\|\geqslant\Big|\varphi_{kl}\Big(T\sum_{r=1}^{m}\varepsilon_{r}e_{rj}\Big)\Big|\geqslant m\delta.\)

By Lemma 5.6, the norm on the left is \(m^{1/p}\), so \(K\geqslant\delta m^{1/q}\), impossible for large \(m\).

If the source row is fixed and the source column varies, the same argument gives

\(K\Big\|\sum_{s=1}^{m}\varepsilon_{s}e_{is}\Big\|\geqslant m\delta,\)

and now the norm is \(m^{1/q}\), so \(K\geqslant\delta m^{1/p}\), again impossible for large \(m\).

These two estimates cover the same-column and same-row off-diagonal cases directly. They also cover the four-distinct-index cases after fixing all but one of the varying source indices in the relevant order pattern. Since there are only finitely many order patterns, a finite iteration of Ramsey’s theorem yields a set \(\Gamma\) with \(|\Gamma|\geqslant 2n\) such that

\(|\varphi_{kl}(Te_{ij})|<\delta\)

whenever \((i,j)\neq(k,l)\), with \(i,k\) among the first \(n\) points of \(\Gamma\) and \(j,l\) among the last \(n\) points of \(\Gamma\).

Let \(\alpha\) be the first \(n\) elements of \(\Gamma\) and \(\tau\) the last \(n\) elements. For \(A=[a_{rs}]\in X_{n}\) and \(B=K_{\alpha,\tau}TJ_{\alpha,\tau}(A)\), we have

\(b_{kl}=\sum_{r,s=1}^{n}a_{rs}\,\varphi_{\alpha_{k},\tau_{l}}\bigl(Te_{\alpha_{r},\tau_{s}}\bigr).\)

Splitting off the term \((r,s)=(k,l)\) gives

\(|b_{kl}-ca_{kl}|\leqslant|a_{kl}|\eta+\sum_{(r,s)\neq(k,l)}|a_{rs}|\delta\leqslant(\eta+n^{2}\delta)\|A\|,\)

because \(|a_{rs}|\leqslant\|A\|\) for every entry. If \(U=B-cA\), then each entry of \(U\) is bounded by \((\eta+n^{2}\delta)\|A\|\), and hence

\(\|U\|\leqslant n\max_{k,l}|u_{kl}|\leqslant n(\eta+n^{2}\delta)\|A\|<\varepsilon\|A\|.\)

Thus

\(\|K_{\alpha,\tau}TJ_{\alpha,\tau}-c\mathrm{Id}_{X_{n}}\|<\varepsilon.\)

Finally, either \(|c|\geqslant 1/2\) or \(|1-c|\geqslant 1/2\). Since \(\varepsilon<1/4\), a Neumann-series argument shows that one of \(K_{\alpha,\tau}TJ_{\alpha,\tau}\) and \(K_{\alpha,\tau}(\mathrm{Id}_{X_{N}}-T)J_{\alpha,\tau}\) is invertible, with inverse norm at most \(4\). ∎

5.3.3.

A block projection lemma

−

For a matrix \(A=[a_{ij}]\in X_{N}\) define its Hilbert–Schmidt norm

\(\lVert A\rVert_{HS}=\Big(\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Big)^{1/2}.\)

(We use this auxiliary norm only for averaging; the operator norm remains the main norm.)

Let \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(A\in X_{N}\). Put \(a=\big|\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{2}\big|<\frac{1}{2}\). Then

\(\lVert A\rVert_{HS}\leqslant N^{\frac{1}{2}+a}\,\lVert A\rVert.\)

Moreover, if \(B\in X_{k}\) then \(\lVert B\rVert\leqslant k^{a}\lVert B\rVert_{HS}\).

Proof.Fold proof

Viewing \(A\) as an operator on \(\ell_{2}^{N}\), we have \(\lVert A\rVert_{HS}\leqslant\sqrt{N}\,\lVert A\rVert_{2\to 2}\). Also

\(\lVert A\rVert_{2\to 2}\leqslant\lVert\mathrm{Id}\colon\ell_{2}^{N}\to\ell_{p}^{N}\rVert\,\lVert A\rVert\,\lVert\mathrm{Id}\colon\ell_{p}^{N}\to\ell_{2}^{N}\rVert=N^{a}\,\lVert A\rVert,\)

by the standard \(\ell_{p}^{N}\)–\(\ell_{2}^{N}\) inequalities. Multiplying yields the first estimate.

For the second, similarly,

\(\lVert B\rVert\leqslant\lVert\mathrm{Id}:\ell_{2}^{k}\to\ell_{p}^{k}\rVert\,\lVert B\rVert_{2\to 2}\,\lVert\mathrm{Id}:\ell_{p}^{k}\to\ell_{2}^{k}\rVert\leqslant k^{a}\,\lVert B\rVert_{2\to 2}\leqslant k^{a}\lVert B\rVert_{HS}.\)

∎

(Block projection lemma).

Fix \(k,d\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\). There exists \(N_{0}=N_{0}(k,d,\varepsilon,p)\in\mathbb{N}\) such that for all \(N\geqslant N_{0}\) and every \(d\)-dimensional subspace \(E\subseteq X_{N}\) there exist subsets \(\alpha,\tau\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}\) with \(|\alpha|=|\tau|=k\) such that the block projection \(Q_{\alpha,\tau}=J_{\alpha,\tau}K_{\alpha,\tau}\) satisfies

\(\lVert Q_{\alpha,\tau}x\rVert\leqslant\varepsilon\lVert x\rVert\qquad(x\in E).\)
Proof.Fold proof

Let \(a=\big|\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{2}\big|\). Let \(m=\lfloor N/k\rfloor\) so \(m\to\infty\) with \(N\). Partition the first \(mk\) indices into consecutive blocks of size \(k\):

\(R_{s}=\{(s-1)k+1,\dots,sk\}\qquad(1\leqslant s\leqslant m).\)

For each \((s,t)\in\{1,\dots,m\}^{2}\) define \(\alpha_{s}=R_{s}\), \(\tau_{t}=R_{t}\) and

\(Q_{s,t}:=Q_{\alpha_{s},\tau_{t}}=J_{\alpha_{s},\tau_{t}}K_{\alpha_{s},\tau_{t}}\in\mathcal{B}(X_{N}).\)

Each \(Q_{s,t}\) is a norm-one projection on \(X_{N}\).

Moreover, the operators \(Q_{s,t}(A)\) have disjoint matrix-entry supports inside the \((mk)\times(mk)\) northwest corner. Hence, for every \(A\in X_{N}\),

(5.2) \(\sum_{s,t=1}^{m}\lVert Q_{s,t}A\rVert_{HS}^{2}\leqslant\lVert A\rVert_{HS}^{2}.\)

Let \(S_{E}=\{x\in E:\lVert x\rVert=1\}\). Choose an \((\varepsilon/2)\)-net \(\{x_{1},\dots,x_{L}\}\subseteq S_{E}\) in operator norm. A standard volume estimate, after viewing \(E\) as a real space if necessary, yields \(L\leqslant(1+4/\varepsilon)^{2d}\) in the complex case and \(L\leqslant(1+4/\varepsilon)^{d}\) in the real case. By Lemma 5.8, \(\lVert x_{r}\rVert_{HS}^{2}\leqslant N^{1+2a}\) for each \(r\). Summing and using (5.2),

\(\sum_{s,t=1}^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{L}\lVert Q_{s,t}x_{r}\rVert_{HS}^{2}\leqslant\sum_{r=1}^{L}\lVert x_{r}\rVert_{HS}^{2}\leqslant L\,N^{1+2a}.\)

Hence for some \((s_{0},t_{0})\),

\(\sum_{r=1}^{L}\lVert Q_{s_{0},t_{0}}x_{r}\rVert_{HS}^{2}\leqslant\frac{L\,N^{1+2a}}{m^{2}}.\)

Write \(Q=Q_{s_{0},t_{0}}=J_{\alpha,\tau}K_{\alpha,\tau}\) with \(|\alpha|=|\tau|=k\). Then for each \(r\),

\(\lVert Qx_{r}\rVert=\lVert J_{\alpha,\tau}K_{\alpha,\tau}x_{r}\rVert\leqslant\lVert K_{\alpha,\tau}x_{r}\rVert.\)

Now \(K_{\alpha,\tau}x_{r}\in X_{k}\), and \(K_{\alpha,\tau}\) simply extracts the \(k\times k\) block of entries, so \(\lVert K_{\alpha,\tau}x_{r}\rVert_{HS}=\lVert Qx_{r}\rVert_{HS}\). Lemma 5.8 gives

\(\lVert Qx_{r}\rVert\leqslant\lVert K_{\alpha,\tau}x_{r}\rVert\leqslant k^{a}\lVert K_{\alpha,\tau}x_{r}\rVert_{HS}=k^{a}\lVert Qx_{r}\rVert_{HS}.\)

Therefore,

\(\max_{1\leqslant r\leqslant L}\lVert Qx_{r}\rVert^{2}\leqslant\sum_{r=1}^{L}\lVert Qx_{r}\rVert^{2}\leqslant k^{2a}\sum_{r=1}^{L}\lVert Qx_{r}\rVert_{HS}^{2}\leqslant k^{2a}\frac{L\,N^{1+2a}}{m^{2}}.\)

Since \(m\asymp N/k\), the right-hand side is bounded by \(C(p)\,L\,k^{1+4a}\,m^{-(1-2a)}\), which tends to \(0\) as \(m\to\infty\) because \(1-2a>0\). Choose \(N_{0}\) so large that this bound is at most \((\varepsilon/2)^{2}\). Then \(\lVert Qx_{r}\rVert\leqslant\varepsilon/2\) for all \(r\).

Finally, given \(x\in S_{E}\) choose \(r\) with \(\lVert x-x_{r}\rVert\leqslant\varepsilon/2\). Since \(\lVert Q\rVert=1\),

\(\lVert Qx\rVert\leqslant\lVert Qx_{r}\rVert+\lVert Q(x-x_{r})\rVert\leqslant\varepsilon/2+\varepsilon/2=\varepsilon.\)

Thus \(Q_{\alpha,\tau}=Q\) works. ∎

Write \(\pi_{n}\colon\mathcal{M}_{p}\to X_{n}\) for the \(n\)th coordinate projection, and \(\iota_{n}\colon X_{n}\to\mathcal{M}_{p}\) for the coordinate embedding. For \(I\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) let \(P_{I}\colon\mathcal{M}_{p}\to\mathcal{M}_{p}\) be the coordinate projection

\(P_{I}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots)=(y_{1},y_{2},\dots),\qquad y_{n}=\begin{cases}x_{n},&n\in I,\\ 0,&n\notin I.\end{cases}\)

Then \(\lVert P_{I}\rVert=1\).

Let \(F\) be finite-dimensional, let \(S\colon\mathcal{M}_{p}\to F\) be bounded, and let \(J\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) be infinite. Then for every \(\eta>0\) there exists an infinite set \(I\subseteq J\) such that \(\|SP_{I}\|<\eta\).

Proof.Fold proof

First suppose that \(F=\mathbb{K}\). Partition \(J\) into \(m\) disjoint infinite sets \(J_{1},\ldots,J_{m}\). On the band \(P_{J}\mathcal{M}_{p}=P_{J_{1}}\mathcal{M}_{p}\oplus_{\infty}\cdots\oplus_{\infty}P_{J_{m}}\mathcal{M}_{p}\), the dual norm decomposes as an \(\ell_{1}\)-sum, hence

\(\|SP_{J}\|=\sum_{r=1}^{m}\|SP_{J_{r}}\|.\)

Thus some \(J_{r}\) satisfies \(\|SP_{J_{r}}\|\leqslant\|S\|/m\). Choosing \(m\) large proves the scalar case.

For finite-dimensional \(F\), choose \(f_{1},\ldots,f_{M}\in B_{F^{*}}\) such that

\(\|y\|\leqslant 2\max_{1\leqslant r\leqslant M}|f_{r}(y)|\qquad(y\in F).\)

Starting with \(I^{(0)}=J\), apply the scalar case successively to the functionals \((f_{r}\circ S)P_{I^{(r-1)}}\). This gives decreasing infinite sets \(I^{(0)}\supset I^{(1)}\supset\cdots\supset I^{(M)}\) such that

\(\|(f_{r}\circ S)P_{I^{(M)}}\|<\eta/2\qquad(r=1,\ldots,M).\)

For \(I=I^{(M)}\) we obtain \(\|SP_{I}\|<\eta\). ∎

5.3.4.

Almost diagonalisation on \(\mathcal{M}_{p}\)

−
(Almost diagonalisation).

Let \(T\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{M}_{p})\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). There exist contractions \(A,B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{M}_{p})\) with \(AB=\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}\) and an operator

\(T^{\prime}=ATB\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{M}_{p})\)

such that \(\lVert T^{\prime}-D\rVert<\varepsilon\) for a diagonal operator \(D=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{\infty}D_{k}\). Moreover, \(T^{\prime}\) factors through \(T\) and \(\mathrm{Id}-T^{\prime}\) factors through \(\mathrm{Id}-T\) (via the same \(A,B\)).

Set \(K=\lVert T\rVert\) and choose a summable control sequence

\(b_{k}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{k+3}(1+K)}\qquad(k\in\mathbb{N}).\)

For later use set

\(d_{k}=\max\Bigl\{1,\sum_{j<k}\dim X_{j}\Bigr\}=\max\Bigl\{1,\sum_{j<k}j^{2}\Bigr\}.\)

We build inductively:

  • •

    decreasing infinite sets \(I_{1}\supset I_{2}\supset\cdots\),

  • •

    a strictly increasing sequence \(m_{1}<m_{2}<\cdots\) with \(m_{k}\in I_{k}\) and \(m_{k}\geqslant k\),

  • •

    maps \(r_{k}\colon X_{k}\to X_{m_{k}}\) and \(s_{k}\colon X_{m_{k}}\to X_{k}\) with \(\lVert r_{k}\rVert=\lVert s_{k}\rVert=1\) and \(s_{k}r_{k}=\mathrm{Id}_{X_{k}}\),

  • •

    block projections \(q_{k}=r_{k}s_{k}\) on \(X_{m_{k}}\) of order \(k\),

such that

  1. (i)

    if

    \(E_{k}:=\pi_{m_{k}}T\Big(\sum_{j<k}\iota_{m_{j}}r_{j}(X_{j})\Big)\subseteq X_{m_{k}},\)

  2. (ii)

    \(\lVert\pi_{m_{k}}TP_{I_{k+1}}\rVert\leqslant b_{k}\).

Start with \(I_{1}=\mathbb{N}\). Assume \(I_{k}\) and the data up to \(k-1\) have been chosen. Pick \(m_{k}\in I_{k}\) so large that \(m_{k}>\max\{m_{k-1},k\}\) and Lemma 5.9 applies inside \(X_{m_{k}}\) to the \(d_{k}\)-dimensional subspace \(E_{k}\) with tolerance \(b_{k}\) and order \(k\). Thus there exist \(\alpha_{k},\tau_{k}\subseteq\{1,\dots,m_{k}\}\) with \(|\alpha_{k}|=|\tau_{k}|=k\) such that \(q_{k}=Q_{\alpha_{k},\tau_{k}}\) satisfies (i). \(\|\pi_{m_{k}}TP_{I_{k+1}}\|\leqslant b_{k}.\)

Define \(B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{M}_{p})\) by

\((Bx)_{m_{k}}=r_{k}(x_{k})\quad(k\in\mathbb{N}),\qquad(Bx)_{n}=0\ \text{if }n\notin\{m_{k}:k\in\mathbb{N}\}.\)

Then \(\lVert B\rVert=1\). Define \(A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{M}_{p})\) by

\((Ay)_{k}=s_{k}q_{k}(\pi_{m_{k}}y)\quad(k\in\mathbb{N}).\)

Then \(\lVert A\rVert\leqslant 1\) and \(AB=\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}\) since \(s_{k}q_{k}r_{k}=s_{k}r_{k}=\mathrm{Id}_{X_{k}}\).

\(\pi_{k}(T^{\prime}-D)x=\pi_{k}T^{\prime}(x-\iota_{k}\pi_{k}x)=s_{k}q_{k}\,\pi_{m_{k}}T\,B(x-\iota_{k}\pi_{k}x).\)

Write \(u=B(x-\iota_{k}\pi_{k}x)=u^{<k}+u^{>k}\) where \(u^{<k}\) is supported on \(\{m_{j}:j<k\}\) and \(u^{>k}\) on \(\{m_{j}:j>k\}\). Then \(\lVert u^{<k}\rVert\leqslant 1\) and \(\lVert u^{>k}\rVert\leqslant 1\) since \(\lVert B\rVert=1\).

\(\lVert q_{k}y^{<k}\rVert\leqslant b_{k}\lVert y^{<k}\rVert\leqslant b_{k}\lVert\pi_{m_{k}}T\rVert\,\lVert u^{<k}\rVert\leqslant b_{k}K.\)

\(\lVert\pi_{m_{k}}T(u^{>k})\rVert\leqslant b_{k}\lVert u^{>k}\rVert\leqslant b_{k}.\)

\(\lVert\pi_{k}(T^{\prime}-D)x\rVert\leqslant b_{k}K+b_{k}=b_{k}(1+K)=\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{k+3}}.\)

Let \((n_{j})_{j\geqslant 1}\) be strictly increasing with \(n_{j}\geqslant j\). Then the coordinate subspace of \(\mathcal{M}_{p}\) supported on \(\{n_{j}:j\geqslant 1\}\) contains a \(1\)-complemented copy of \(\mathcal{M}_{p}\).

\(\lVert K_{k}D_{m_{k}}J_{k}-c_{k}\mathrm{Id}_{X_{k}}\rVert<\tfrac{1}{8},\)

so either \(S_{k}:=K_{k}D_{m_{k}}J_{k}\) is invertible with \(\lVert S_{k}^{-1}\rVert\leqslant 4\) or \(S_{k}^{\prime}:=K_{k}(\mathrm{Id}-D_{m_{k}})J_{k}\) is invertible with \(\lVert(S_{k}^{\prime})^{-1}\rVert\leqslant 4\). Let \(\sigma_{k}\in\{0,1\}\) record which case holds.

By infinite pigeonhole there exist an infinite set \(L=\{k_{1}<k_{2}<\cdots\}\) and a fixed \(\sigma\in\{0,1\}\) such that \(\sigma_{k_{j}}=\sigma\) for all \(j\). Let

\(\mathcal{N}=P_{L}\mathcal{M}_{p}\)

be the full coordinate subspace supported on \(L\). By Lemma 5.12, there are contractions \(E_{0}\colon\mathcal{M}_{p}\to\mathcal{N}\) and \(P_{0}\colon\mathcal{N}\to\mathcal{M}_{p}\) such that \(P_{0}E_{0}=\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}\).

Define \(B\colon\mathcal{N}\to\mathcal{M}_{p}\) by

\((By)_{m_{k_{j}}}=J_{k_{j}}(y_{k_{j}}),\qquad(By)_{n}=0\quad(n\notin\{m_{k_{j}}:j\in\mathbb{N}\}).\)

Define \(A\colon\mathcal{M}_{p}\to\mathcal{N}\) by

\((Az)_{k_{j}}=\begin{cases}S_{k_{j}}^{-1}K_{k_{j}}(z_{m_{k_{j}}}),&\sigma=0,\\ (S_{k_{j}}^{\prime})^{-1}K_{k_{j}}(z_{m_{k_{j}}}),&\sigma=1,\end{cases}\qquad(Az)_{n}=0\quad(n\notin L).\)

Then \(\|B\|\leqslant 1\) and \(\|A\|\leqslant 4\).

If \(\sigma=0\), then for \(y\in\mathcal{N}\),

\((ADBy)_{k_{j}}=S_{k_{j}}^{-1}K_{k_{j}}\bigl(D_{m_{k_{j}}}J_{k_{j}}(y_{k_{j}})\bigr)=y_{k_{j}},\)

so \(ADB=\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{N}}\). If \(\sigma=1\), the same computation gives \(A(\mathrm{Id}-D)B=\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{N}}\).

Finally set \(V=BE_{0}\) and \(U=P_{0}A\). Then either \(UDV=\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}\) or \(U(\mathrm{Id}-D)V=\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{M}_{p}}\), and \(\|U\|\|V\|\leqslant\|P_{0}\|\|A\|\|B\|\|E_{0}\|\leqslant 4.\) ∎

For every \(p\in(1,\infty)\) the space \(\mathcal{M}_{p}\) has the \(8\)-primary factorisation property.

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(T\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{M}_{p})\). Apply Lemma 5.11 with \(\varepsilon=\tfrac{1}{16}\) to obtain contractions \(A_{0},B_{0}\) with \(A_{0}B_{0}=\mathrm{Id}\) and \(T^{\prime}=A_{0}TB_{0}\) satisfying \(\lVert T^{\prime}-D\rVert<\tfrac{1}{16}\) for a diagonal operator \(D\).

By Proposition 5.13, there exist \(U_{0},V_{0}\) with \(\|U_{0}\|\|V_{0}\|\leqslant 4\) such that either

\(U_{0}DV_{0}=\mathrm{Id}\qquad\text{or}\qquad U_{0}(\mathrm{Id}-D)V_{0}=\mathrm{Id}.\)

In the first case set \(E=U_{0}(T^{\prime}-D)V_{0}\). Then \(\|E\|\leqslant 1/4\), so \(\mathrm{Id}+E\) is invertible with inverse norm at most \(4/3<2\). With \(U_{1}=(\mathrm{Id}+E)^{-1}U_{0}\) and \(V_{1}=V_{0}\), we obtain

\(U_{1}T^{\prime}V_{1}=\mathrm{Id},\qquad\|U_{1}\|\|V_{1}\|\leqslant 8.\)

Since \(T^{\prime}=A_{0}TB_{0}\), we have

\((U_{1}A_{0})\,T\,(B_{0}V_{1})=\mathrm{Id},\)

so this is a factorisation through \(T\) with the same bound.

In the second case set

\(E=U_{0}\bigl((\mathrm{Id}-T^{\prime})-(\mathrm{Id}-D)\bigr)V_{0}=-U_{0}(T^{\prime}-D)V_{0}.\)

Again \(\|E\|\leqslant 1/4\), and the same Neumann-series argument gives operators \(U_{1},V_{1}\) with

\(U_{1}(\mathrm{Id}-T^{\prime})V_{1}=\mathrm{Id},\qquad\|U_{1}\|\|V_{1}\|\leqslant 8.\)

Since \(\mathrm{Id}-T^{\prime}=A_{0}(\mathrm{Id}-T)B_{0}\), we have

\((U_{1}A_{0})\,(\mathrm{Id}-T)\,(B_{0}V_{1})=\mathrm{Id},\)

so this is a factorisation through \(\mathrm{Id}-T\) with the same bound. ∎

For every \(p\in(1,\infty)\) the Banach space \(\mathcal{B}(\ell_{p})\) has the uniform primary factorisation property.

Proof.Fold proof

By , \(\mathcal{B}(\ell_{p})\) is linearly isomorphic to \(\mathcal{M}_{p}\). Let \(S\colon\mathcal{B}(\ell_{p})\to\mathcal{M}_{p}\) be an isomorphism. By Theorem 5.14, \(\mathcal{M}_{p}\) has the \(8\)-PFP. Proposition 2.5 transfers this to \(\mathcal{B}(\ell_{p})\) with constant \(8\,\lVert S\rVert^{2}\lVert S^{-1}\rVert^{2}<\infty\). Hence \(\mathcal{B}(\ell_{p})\) has UPFP. ∎

6.

Filter-convergence spaces

−

In this section, we give a filter-theoretic criterion for the primary factorisation property. The abstract criterion is deliberately separated from a more concrete, set-theoretic sufficient condition. The latter is often the condition one checks in examples; it implies the required operator diagonalisation by Rosenthal’s lemma.

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a proper filter on an infinite set \(\Gamma\), and put

\(X_{\mathcal{F}}=c_{\mathcal{F}}(\Gamma)=\{x\in\ell_{\infty}(\Gamma):x\to 0\text{ along }\mathcal{F}\}.\)

Thus \(x\in X_{\mathcal{F}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\{\gamma\in\Gamma:|x(\gamma)|<\varepsilon\}\in\mathcal{F}\quad(\varepsilon>0).\) For \(A\subseteq\Gamma\), let \(P_{A}\) be the coordinate projection and write \(X_{\mathcal{F}}(A)=P_{A}X_{\mathcal{F}}=\{x\in X_{\mathcal{F}}:\operatorname{supp}x\subseteq A\}.\) If \(a\in\ell_{\infty}(\Gamma)\), we denote by \(M_{a}\) the corresponding multiplication operator on \(X_{\mathcal{F}}\).

For \(A\subseteq\Gamma\), define the trace filter

\(\mathcal{F}_{A}=\{B\subseteq A:B\cup(\Gamma\setminus A)\in\mathcal{F}\}.\)

With the convention that \(c_{\mathcal{F}_{A}}(A)=\ell_{\infty}(A)\) if \(\mathcal{F}_{A}\) is improper, restriction to \(A\) identifies \(X_{\mathcal{F}}(A)\) isometrically with \(c_{\mathcal{F}_{A}}(A)\). Consequently, whenever \(\Gamma=A\sqcup B\), \(X_{\mathcal{F}}=X_{\mathcal{F}}(A)\oplus_{\infty}X_{\mathcal{F}}(B).\)

6.1.

The abstract criterion

−

Let \(K\geqslant 1\). A subset \(A\subseteq\Gamma\) is called a \(K\)-copying set for \(\mathcal{F}\) if

\(X_{\mathcal{F}}(A)\simeq_{K}X_{\mathcal{F}}.\)

Let \(K\geqslant 1\). We say that \(\mathcal{F}\) is \(K\)-primary under sums if, for every partition \(\Gamma=\Gamma_{0}\sqcup\Gamma_{1}\), at least one of \(\Gamma_{0}\) and \(\Gamma_{1}\) contains a \(K\)-copying set for \(\mathcal{F}\).

This is the filter analogue of a projection-level primariness condition. It only sees coordinate decompositions of \(X_{\mathcal{F}}\). To obtain a factorisation dichotomy for arbitrary operators, we use the following additional operator-level hypothesis.

Let \(D\geqslant 1\). We say that \(\mathcal{F}\) is \(D\)-diagonalisable if, for every \(T\in\mathcal{B}(X_{\mathcal{F}})\) and every \(\eta>0\), there are \(A\subseteq\Gamma\), an isomorphism

\(J\colon X_{\mathcal{F}}\longrightarrow X_{\mathcal{F}}(A),\qquad R=J^{-1}\colon X_{\mathcal{F}}(A)\longrightarrow X_{\mathcal{F}},\)

with \(\|J\|\,\|R\|\leqslant D,\) and a function \(a\in\ell_{\infty}(\Gamma)\) such that

\(\|RP_{A}TJ-M_{a}\|<\eta.\)

Let \(K,D\geqslant 1\). We say that \(\mathcal{F}\) is \((K,D)\)-primary for factorisation if it is \(K\)-primary under sums and \(D\)-diagonalisable.

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a \((K,D)\)-primary filter for factorisation on \(\Gamma\). Then

\(X_{\mathcal{F}}=c_{\mathcal{F}}(\Gamma)\)

has the \((2KD)^{+}\)-primary factorisation property. In particular, \(X_{\mathcal{F}}\) has the UPFP.

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(X=X_{\mathcal{F}}\), and let \(T\in\mathcal{B}(X)\). Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(\eta>0\) so small that

\(2K\eta<1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{2KD}{1-2K\eta}<2KD+\varepsilon.\)

By \(D\)-diagonalisability, there exist \(A\subseteq\Gamma\), an isomorphism

\(J\colon X\longrightarrow X_{\mathcal{F}}(A),\qquad R=J^{-1}\colon X_{\mathcal{F}}(A)\longrightarrow X,\)

with \(\|J\|\|R\|\leqslant D\), and \(a\in\ell_{\infty}(\Gamma)\), such that

\(S:=RP_{A}TJ\quad\text{satisfies}\quad\|S-M_{a}\|<\eta.\)

Partition \(\Gamma\) as

\(\Gamma_{0}=\{\gamma\in\Gamma:|a(\gamma)|\geqslant 1/2\},\qquad\Gamma_{1}=\Gamma\setminus\Gamma_{0}.\)

Then \(|1-a(\gamma)|\geqslant 1/2\) for every \(\gamma\in\Gamma_{1}\). Since \(\mathcal{F}\) is \(K\)-primary under sums, one of \(\Gamma_{0}\) and \(\Gamma_{1}\) contains a \(K\)-copying set. Choose such a set \(C\), and choose an isomorphism

\(L\colon X\longrightarrow X_{\mathcal{F}}(C),\qquad Q=L^{-1}\colon X_{\mathcal{F}}(C)\longrightarrow X,\)

with \(\|L\|\|Q\|\leqslant K\).

Assume first that \(C\subseteq\Gamma_{0}\). Consider

\(B=P_{C}SL=P_{C}RP_{A}TJL\colon X\longrightarrow X_{\mathcal{F}}(C).\)

The operator \(B_{0}=P_{C}M_{a}L\colon X\longrightarrow X_{\mathcal{F}}(C)\) is an isomorphism. Indeed, multiplication by \(a\) is invertible on \(X_{\mathcal{F}}(C)\), with inverse multiplication by \(1/a\) on \(C\), because \(|a|\geqslant 1/2\) on \(C\). Hence \(\|B_{0}^{-1}\|\leqslant 2\|Q\|.\) Moreover, \(\|B-B_{0}\|\leqslant\|S-M_{a}\|\,\|L\|<\eta\|L\|.\) Therefore

\(\|B_{0}^{-1}\|\,\|B-B_{0}\|<2\eta\|Q\|\|L\|\leqslant 2K\eta<1.\)

By the Neumann lemma, \(B\) is an isomorphism from \(X\) onto \(X_{\mathcal{F}}(C)\), and

\(\|B^{-1}\|\leqslant\frac{2\|Q\|}{1-2K\eta}.\)

Putting

\(U=B^{-1}P_{C}RP_{A},\qquad V=JL,\)

we get \(UTV=B^{-1}P_{C}RP_{A}TJL=B^{-1}B=\mathrm{Id}_{X},\) and

\(\|U\|\|V\|\leqslant\frac{2\|Q\|\|R\|\|J\|\|L\|}{1-2K\eta}\leqslant\frac{2KD}{1-2K\eta}<2KD+\varepsilon.\)

Thus \(\mathrm{Id}_{X}\) factors through \(T\) with constant less than \(2KD+\varepsilon\).

If instead \(C\subseteq\Gamma_{1}\), then

\(RP_{A}(\mathrm{Id}_{X}-T)J=\mathrm{Id}_{X}-S\)

and

\(\|(\mathrm{Id}_{X}-S)-M_{1-a}\|<\eta.\)

Since \(|1-a|\geqslant 1/2\) on \(C\), the preceding argument applied to \(\mathrm{Id}_{X}-T\) and to the multiplier \(M_{1-a}\) shows that \(\mathrm{Id}_{X}\) factors through \(\mathrm{Id}_{X}-T\) with constant less than \(2KD+\varepsilon\).

Since \(T\) and \(\varepsilon\) were arbitrary, \(X\) has the \((2KD)^{+}\)-PFP. ∎

6.2.

A set-theoretic sufficient condition

−

The preceding definition of diagonalisability is useful as an abstract criterion, but it is not a condition one can normally check directly. We now give a more concrete sufficient condition depending only on the existence of many coordinate copies of the filter.

Let \(B\subseteq\Gamma\). We say that \(B\) contains a coordinate copy of \(\mathcal{F}\) if there are \(C\subseteq B\) and a bijection \(\theta\colon\Gamma\to C\) such that, for every \(A\subseteq\Gamma\),

\(A\in\mathcal{F}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\theta(A)\cup(\Gamma\setminus C)\in\mathcal{F}.\)

Equivalently, the trace filter \(\mathcal{F}_{C}\) is isomorphic to \(\mathcal{F}\).

If \(C\) and \(\theta\) are as above, the formula

\((U_{\theta}x)(\theta(\gamma))=x(\gamma)\quad(\gamma\in\Gamma),\qquad(U_{\theta}x)(\alpha)=0\quad(\alpha\notin C),\)

defines a surjective linear isometry \(U_{\theta}\colon X_{\mathcal{F}}\longrightarrow X_{\mathcal{F}}(C).\)

Let \(\kappa=|\Gamma|\). We say that \(\mathcal{F}\) is large-set self-similar if every subset \(B\subseteq\Gamma\) with \(|B|=\kappa\) contains a coordinate copy of \(\mathcal{F}\).

Thus, large-set self-similarity is a purely set-theoretic strengthening of primariness under sums: in a partition of \(\Gamma\) into two pieces, one piece must have cardinality \(\kappa\), and therefore contains a copy of the original filter.

We shall use the following standard form of Rosenthal’s lemma from .

(Rosenthal’s lemma).

Let \(\Gamma\) be an infinite set, and let \((\mu_{\gamma})_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\) be a uniformly bounded family of finitely additive scalar measures on \(\Gamma\). Suppose that \(\mu_{\gamma}(\{\gamma\})=0\) for every \(\gamma\in\Gamma\). Then, for every \(\eta>0\), there is \(A\subseteq\Gamma\) with \(|A|=|\Gamma|\) such that

\(|\mu_{\gamma}|(A)<\eta\qquad(\gamma\in A).\)

If \(\mathcal{F}\) is large-set self-similar, then \(\mathcal{F}\) is \((1,1)\)-primary for factorisation. Consequently, \(X_{\mathcal{F}}\) has the \(2^{+}\)-primary factorisation property.

Proof.Fold proof

First let \(\Gamma=\Gamma_{0}\sqcup\Gamma_{1}\). Since \(\Gamma\) is infinite, one of \(\Gamma_{0}\) and \(\Gamma_{1}\) has cardinality \(|\Gamma|\). By large-set self-similarity, that piece contains a coordinate copy of \(\mathcal{F}\). Hence \(\mathcal{F}\) is \(1\)-primary under sums.

It remains to prove \(1\)-diagonalisability. Let \(T\in\mathcal{B}(X_{\mathcal{F}})\) and let \(\eta>0\). For each \(\alpha\in\Gamma\), the functional

\(x\mapsto(Tx)(\alpha)\qquad(x\in X_{\mathcal{F}})\)

has norm at most \(\|T\|\). By Hahn–Banach, choose a finitely additive measure \(\lambda_{\alpha}\in\operatorname{ba}(\Gamma)\) with \(\|\lambda_{\alpha}\|\leqslant\|T\|\) such that

\((Tx)(\alpha)=\int_{\Gamma}x\,d\lambda_{\alpha}\qquad(x\in X_{\mathcal{F}}).\)

Put

\(\mu_{\alpha}=\lambda_{\alpha}-\lambda_{\alpha}(\{\alpha\})\delta_{\alpha}\qquad(\alpha\in\Gamma).\)

Then \((\mu_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in\Gamma}\) is uniformly bounded and \(\mu_{\alpha}(\{\alpha\})=0\) for every \(\alpha\). By Lemma 6.8, there is \(A\subseteq\Gamma\) with \(|A|=|\Gamma|\) such that

\(|\mu_{\alpha}|(A)<\eta\qquad(\alpha\in A).\)

By large-set self-similarity, choose a coordinate copy \(C\subseteq A\) of \(\mathcal{F}\), and let \(\theta\colon\Gamma\to C\) witness this. Put

\(J=U_{\theta}\colon X_{\mathcal{F}}\to X_{\mathcal{F}}(C),\qquad R=U_{\theta}^{-1}\colon X_{\mathcal{F}}(C)\to X_{\mathcal{F}}.\)

Then \(\|J\|\|R\|=1\). Define \(a\in\ell_{\infty}(\Gamma)\) by

\(a(\gamma)=\lambda_{\theta(\gamma)}(\{\theta(\gamma)\})\qquad(\gamma\in\Gamma).\)

For \(x\in X_{\mathcal{F}}\) with \(\|x\|\leqslant 1\) and \(\gamma\in\Gamma\), we have

\(\displaystyle\bigl((RP_{C}TJ-M_{a})x\bigr)(\gamma)\) \(\displaystyle=(TJx)(\theta(\gamma))-a(\gamma)x(\gamma)\)
\(\displaystyle=\int_{\Gamma}Jx\,d\lambda_{\theta(\gamma)}-\lambda_{\theta(\gamma)}(\{\theta(\gamma)\})Jx(\theta(\gamma))\)
\(\displaystyle=\int_{C}Jx\,d\mu_{\theta(\gamma)}.\)

Since \(C\subseteq A\), it follows that \(\left|\bigl((RP_{C}TJ-M_{a})x\bigr)(\gamma)\right|\leqslant|\mu_{\theta(\gamma)}|(C)\leqslant|\mu_{\theta(\gamma)}|(A)<\eta.\) Taking the supremum over \(\gamma\in\Gamma\) gives \(\|RP_{C}TJ-M_{a}\|<\eta.\) Thus \(\mathcal{F}\) is \(1\)-diagonalisable. The final assertion follows from Theorem 6.5 with \(K=D=1\). ∎

Let \(\kappa=|\Gamma|\), and let \(\mu\leqslant\kappa\) be an infinite cardinal. Define

\(\mathcal{F}_{\mu}=\{A\subseteq\Gamma:|\Gamma\setminus A|<\mu\}.\)

Then \(\mathcal{F}_{\mu}\) is large-set self-similar. Indeed, if \(B\subseteq\Gamma\) has cardinality \(\kappa\), then the trace filter on \(B\) is

\((\mathcal{F}_{\mu})_{B}=\{C\subseteq B:|B\setminus C|<\mu\},\)

which is isomorphic to \(\mathcal{F}_{\mu}\) through any bijection \(\Gamma\to B\). Hence \(c_{\mathcal{F}_{\mu}}(\Gamma)\) has the \(2^{+}\)-PFP.

For \(\mu=\omega\), this recovers the usual cofinite-filter case \(c_{\mathcal{F}_{\omega}}(\Gamma)=c_{0}(\Gamma)\). For \(\mu=\omega_{1}\), it gives the co-countable-filter case \(c_{\mathcal{F}_{\omega_{1}}}(\Gamma)=\ell_{\infty}^{c}(\Gamma)\), whenever \(|\Gamma|\geqslant\omega_{1}\), which recovers .

Definition 6.3 should therefore be read as an abstract operator criterion, not as the primary source of examples. The set-theoretic condition in Definition 6.7 is stronger but much easier to verify: Rosenthal’s lemma turns large-set self-similarity into diagonalisation, and large set self-similarity also gives the required primariness under sums. Thus one obtains the concrete implication

\(\text{large-set self-similar filter}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c_{\mathcal{F}}(\Gamma)\text{ has the }2^{+}\text{-PFP}.\)
7.

Open Problems

−

The results of this paper suggest a number of natural questions. Some concern the relation between primariness and factorisation, while others arise from the limitations of the present methods in mixed and non-separable settings.

Primariness versus factorisation. A natural first question is whether the primary factorisation property is genuinely stronger than primariness. The following example shows that, in some sense, this is indeed the case. The authors are grateful to Niels Jakob Laustsen (Lancaster) for bringing this example to their attention.

(Primariness does not imply PFP).

Let \(X_{\mathrm{GM}}\) denote the prime Gowers–Maurey space, see . Then \(X_{\mathrm{GM}}\) is prime, hence primary. On the other hand, for this space the quotient of \(\mathcal{B}(X_{\mathrm{GM}})\) by the ideal of strictly singular operators is isomorphic, as a Banach algebra, to \(\ell_{1}(\mathbb{Z})\) equipped with the convolution product. Let

\(q\colon\mathcal{B}(X_{\mathrm{GM}})\to\mathcal{B}(X_{\mathrm{GM}})/\mathcal{SS}(X_{\mathrm{GM}})\cong\ell_{1}(\mathbb{Z})\)

denote the quotient map. For every maximal ideal \(M\) of \(\ell_{1}(\mathbb{Z})\), the preimage \(q^{-1}(M)\) is a maximal ideal of \(\mathcal{B}(X_{\mathrm{GM}})\); in fact, these are all the maximal ideals of \(\mathcal{B}(X_{\mathrm{GM}})\), since every maximal ideal of \(\mathcal{B}(X_{\mathrm{GM}})\) contains the ideal of strictly singular operators. Since the maximal ideal space of \(\ell_{1}(\mathbb{Z})\) is naturally identified with the unit circle \(\mathbb{T}\), the algebra \(\ell_{1}(\mathbb{Z})\) has continuum many maximal ideals. Hence \(\mathcal{B}(X_{\mathrm{GM}})\) has continuum many maximal ideals. By Proposition 2.6, it follows that \(X_{\mathrm{GM}}\) cannot have the PFP. Thus, primariness does not imply the PFP.

By Pełczyński’s decomposition method, the PFP implies primariness on spaces that are stable under the relevant direct-sum operation, but outside that framework, it is unclear if PFP implies primarity.

Does every Banach space with the PFP have to be primary?

A classical special case is still open.

Is every Banach space with a symmetric basis primary?

The results of Casazza, Kottman and Lin show that a large class of such spaces satisfy a strong range dichotomy, but this still falls short of a complete answer. We note, however, that Lin resolved the problem in the reflexive case.

PFP versus UPFP. In all examples presently known to us, the PFP is obtained together with quantitative control, so that one actually gets the UPFP. It is therefore natural to ask whether the uniform version is strictly stronger.

Does there exist a Banach space with the PFP but without the UPFP?

A positive answer would show that the uniform quantitative content of the classical arguments is a genuine extra feature rather than an artefact of the proofs.

Duality. Many classical primary spaces arise in dual pairs, but the known arguments are often highly asymmetric. The dual problem, therefore, remains largely open.

Let \(X\) be a primary Banach space. Must \(X^{*}\) be primary? What if \(X\) has the PFP or the UPFP? Do either of these properties pass to the dual space?

Even formulating a satisfactory converse is delicate, since non-isomorphic spaces may have isomorphic duals.

Countable versus uncountable sums. One of the main phenomena of this paper is that uncountability makes some problems easier rather than harder: free-selection arguments and support-reduction lemmas allow one to force exact coordinate separation. This leads to a natural meta-question.

To what extent can the arguments for uncountable sums be pushed back to the countable setting? For example, can the uncountable methods be adapted to recover the PFP or UPFP for difficult countable mixed sums, spaces such as \(C(\alpha,\ell_{p})\) or related bi-parameter spaces?

Quantitative decomposition. Several of the results proved here are genuinely quantitative, and Appendix A records a quantitative form of Pełczyński’s decomposition method tailored to the present paper. We do not claim originality for that appendix: it is included only to make the constant bookkeeping explicit in one convenient place. Closely related explicit bounds in the normalised square case were obtained by Korpalski and Plebanek and improved by the Lewicki and the second-named author ; see also Galego’s qualitative extensions of the decomposition method .

Can the constants in Appendix A be improved substantially, especially in the square case or in the \(c_{0}\)/\(\ell_{p}\)-stable case?

A.

A quantitative form of Pełczyński’s decomposition method

−

We record here, for convenience, a quantitative version of Pełczyński’s decomposition method in a form suited to the present paper. We do not claim originality for the result below: it should be viewed as a constant-tracking variant of the classical argument of Pełczyński . The bookkeeping involved seems to be part of the folklore, but it is not especially easy to locate in exactly the form needed here.

The closest explicit quantitative results we are aware of are due to Korpalski and Plebanek and, with an improved constant, the second-named author and Lewicki . In the normalised setting where each space is isometric to a \(1\)-complemented subspace of the other and both spaces are isometrically square, Korpalski and Plebanek obtain the estimate \(d_{BM}(X,Y)\leqslant(3+\sqrt{2})^{2}\), while the second-named author and Lewicki improve this to \(d_{BM}(X,Y)\leqslant 9+6\sqrt{3}\). For qualitative extensions of Pełczyński’s method in the direction of supplemented subspaces and finite-sum arithmetic, see Galego .

The formulation below is slightly more flexible than the normalised square case treated in those references: we allow arbitrary complementability and isomorphism constants, and we also include the familiar \(c_{0}\)- and \(\ell_{p}\)-stable alternative.

Before turning to the statement and proof, we record a few elementary facts that will be used repeatedly. If \(A\simeq_{C}B\) and \(B\simeq_{K}D\), then \(A\simeq_{CK}D\). Moreover, for every \(1\leqslant p\leqslant\infty\) and every Banach space \(Z\), one has \(A\oplus_{p}Z\simeq_{C}B\oplus_{p}Z.\) Also, for every \(1\leqslant p\leqslant\infty\), \(\ell_{p}(A)\simeq_{C}\ell_{p}(B),\) where the isomorphism is obtained by applying a fixed isomorphism \(A\to B\) coordinatewise. Likewise, \(c_{0}(A)\simeq_{C}c_{0}(B).\)

(A quantitative form of Pełczyński’s decomposition method).

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces such that

  1. (i)

    \(X\) has a \(C_{1}\)-complemented subspace \(E\) which is \(C_{2}\)-isomorphic to \(Y\);

  2. (ii)

    \(Y\) has a \(C_{3}\)-complemented subspace \(G\) which is \(C_{4}\)-isomorphic to \(X\).

Suppose further that either

  1. (a)

    there exists \(1\leqslant r\leqslant\infty\) such that

    \(X\simeq_{C_{5}}X\oplus_{r}X\qquad\text{and}\qquad Y\simeq_{C_{6}}Y\oplus_{r}Y,\)

    or

  2. (b)
    \(X\simeq_{C_{5}}c_{0}(X)\qquad\text{or}\qquad X\simeq_{C_{5}}\ell_{p}(X)\)

    for some \(1\leqslant p\leqslant\infty\).

Then there exists a constant \(C\geqslant 1\), depending only on \(C_{1},\dots,C_{6}\) in case (a), and only on \(C_{1},\dots,C_{5}\) in case (b), such that \(X\simeq_{C}Y\). Moreover, the proof below gives an explicit admissible choice of \(C\).

Proof.Fold proof

Choose a projection \(P\colon X\to E\) with \(\lVert P\rVert\leqslant C_{1}\), a projection \(Q\colon Y\to G\) with \(\lVert Q\rVert\leqslant C_{3}\), an isomorphism \(S\colon Y\to E\) with \(\lVert S\rVert\lVert S^{-1}\rVert\leqslant C_{2}\), and an isomorphism \(T\colon X\to G\) with \(\lVert T\rVert\lVert T^{-1}\rVert\leqslant C_{4}\). After rescaling \(S\) and \(T\), we may assume that

\(\lVert S\rVert=\lVert S^{-1}\rVert\leqslant\sqrt{C_{2}},\qquad\lVert T\rVert=\lVert T^{-1}\rVert\leqslant\sqrt{C_{4}}.\)

Set

\(F=\ker P,\qquad H=\ker Q.\)

We first show that, for each fixed \(1\leqslant r\leqslant\infty\), there exist constants \(a=a(C_{1},C_{2})\) and \(b=b(C_{3},C_{4})\) such that \(X\simeq_{a}Y\oplus_{r}F,\) and \(Y\simeq_{b}X\oplus_{r}H.\) To this end, define

\(\Phi_{X}\colon X\to Y\oplus_{r}F,\qquad\Phi_{X}x=\bigl(S^{-1}Px,(I_{X}-P)x\bigr),\)

and

\(\Psi_{X}\colon Y\oplus_{r}F\to X,\qquad\Psi_{X}(y,f)=Sy+f.\)

Since \(f\in F=\ker P\), we have \(Pf=0\), and hence

\(\Psi_{X}\Phi_{X}x=S(S^{-1}Px)+(I_{X}-P)x=Px+(I_{X}-P)x=x.\)

Also, if \(y\in Y\) and \(f\in F\), then

\(\Phi_{X}\Psi_{X}(y,f)=\bigl(S^{-1}P(Sy+f),(I_{X}-P)(Sy+f)\bigr)=(y,f),\)

because \(P(Sy)=Sy\) and \(Pf=0\). Thus \(\Phi_{X}\) and \(\Psi_{X}\) are inverse isomorphisms. Moreover,

\(\lVert\Phi_{X}x\rVert_{r}\leqslant\lVert S^{-1}Px\rVert+\lVert(I_{X}-P)x\rVert\leqslant\bigl(\sqrt{C_{2}}\,C_{1}+1+C_{1}\bigr)\lVert x\rVert.\)

Likewise,

\(\lVert\Psi_{X}(y,f)\rVert\leqslant\lVert Sy\rVert+\lVert f\rVert\leqslant(\sqrt{C_{2}}+1)(\lVert y\rVert+\lVert f\rVert)\leqslant 2(\sqrt{C_{2}}+1)\lVert(y,f)\rVert_{r}.\)

Hence \(X\simeq_{a}Y\oplus_{r}F,\) where \(a:=2(\sqrt{C_{2}}+1)\bigl(\sqrt{C_{2}}\,C_{1}+1+C_{1}\bigr).\)

Similarly, defining the operators \(\Phi_{Y}\colon Y\to X\oplus_{r}H,\Phi_{Y}y=\bigl(T^{-1}Qy,(I_{Y}-Q)y\bigr),\) and \(\Psi_{Y}\colon X\oplus_{r}H\to Y,\Psi_{Y}(x,h)=Tx+h,\) one obtains \(Y\simeq_{b}X\oplus_{r}H,\) where \(b:=2(\sqrt{C_{4}}+1)\bigl(\sqrt{C_{4}}\,C_{3}+1+C_{3}\bigr).\)

We now treat the two cases separately.

Case (a). Fix \(r\) as in the hypothesis. Since \(X\simeq_{a}Y\oplus_{r}F\), we obtain

\(X\simeq_{a}Y\oplus_{r}F\simeq_{C_{6}}(Y\oplus_{r}Y)\oplus_{r}F\simeq_{1}Y\oplus_{r}(Y\oplus_{r}F)\simeq_{a}Y\oplus_{r}X,\)

and therefore \(X\simeq_{a^{2}C_{6}}Y\oplus_{r}X.\) Likewise,

\(Y\simeq_{b}X\oplus_{r}H\simeq_{C_{5}}(X\oplus_{r}X)\oplus_{r}H\simeq_{1}X\oplus_{r}(X\oplus_{r}H)\simeq_{b}X\oplus_{r}Y,\)

so \(Y\simeq_{b^{2}C_{5}}X\oplus_{r}Y.\) Combining the last two displays, and using the canonical isometry \(Y\oplus_{r}X\simeq_{1}X\oplus_{r}Y\), we get

\(X\simeq_{a^{2}C_{6}}Y\oplus_{r}X\simeq_{1}X\oplus_{r}Y\simeq_{b^{2}C_{5}}Y.\)

Thus \(X\simeq_{a^{2}b^{2}C_{5}C_{6}}Y.\)

Case (b). We treat the case

\(X\simeq_{C_{5}}\ell_{p}(X),\qquad 1\leqslant p\leqslant\infty;\)

the case \(X\simeq_{C_{5}}c_{0}(X)\) is identical, replacing \(\ell_{p}\) by \(c_{0}\) and \(\oplus_{p}\) by \(\oplus_{\infty}\) throughout.

Since \(\ell_{p}(X)\) is canonically isometric to \(X\oplus_{p}\ell_{p}(X)\), we have

\(X\simeq_{C_{5}}\ell_{p}(X)\simeq_{1}X\oplus_{p}\ell_{p}(X)\simeq_{C_{5}}X\oplus_{p}X,\)

and so \(X\simeq_{C_{5}^{2}}X\oplus_{p}X.\)

Now take \(r=p\) in the first part of the proof. Then

\(X\simeq_{a}Y\oplus_{p}F,\qquad Y\simeq_{b}X\oplus_{p}H.\)

We next show that \(Y\simeq_{(abC_{5})^{2}}Y\oplus_{p}Y.\) Starting from \(Y\simeq_{b}X\oplus_{p}H\), we obtain

\(Y\simeq_{b}X\oplus_{p}H\simeq_{C_{5}}\ell_{p}(X)\oplus_{p}H\simeq_{a}\ell_{p}(Y\oplus_{p}F)\oplus_{p}H\simeq_{1}\ell_{p}(Y)\oplus_{p}\ell_{p}(F)\oplus_{p}H.\)

Since \(\ell_{p}(Y)\) is canonically isometric to \(Y\oplus_{p}\ell_{p}(Y)\), it follows that

\(Y\simeq_{abC_{5}}Y\oplus_{p}\bigl(\ell_{p}(Y)\oplus_{p}\ell_{p}(F)\oplus_{p}H\bigr).\)

On the other hand,

\(\ell_{p}(Y)\oplus_{p}\ell_{p}(F)\oplus_{p}H\simeq_{1}\ell_{p}(Y\oplus_{p}F)\oplus_{p}H\simeq_{a}\ell_{p}(X)\oplus_{p}H\simeq_{C_{5}}X\oplus_{p}H\simeq_{b}Y.\)

Therefore \(Y\simeq_{(abC_{5})^{2}}Y\oplus_{p}Y.\)

We now repeat the same decomposition argument with \(\oplus_{p}\) in place of \(\oplus_{r}\). Using \(X\simeq_{a}Y\oplus_{p}F\), we get

\(X\simeq_{a}Y\oplus_{p}F\simeq_{(abC_{5})^{2}}(Y\oplus_{p}Y)\oplus_{p}F\simeq_{1}Y\oplus_{p}(Y\oplus_{p}F)\simeq_{a}Y\oplus_{p}X,\)

whence \(X\simeq_{a^{2}(abC_{5})^{2}}Y\oplus_{p}X.\) Similarly, since \(X\simeq_{C_{5}^{2}}X\oplus_{p}X\), we have

\(Y\simeq_{b}X\oplus_{p}H\simeq_{C_{5}^{2}}(X\oplus_{p}X)\oplus_{p}H\simeq_{1}X\oplus_{p}(X\oplus_{p}H)\simeq_{b}X\oplus_{p}Y,\)

and therefore \(Y\simeq_{b^{2}C_{5}^{2}}X\oplus_{p}Y.\) Combining the last two displays, and using the canonical isometry \(Y\oplus_{p}X\simeq_{1}X\oplus_{p}Y\), we obtain \(X\simeq_{a^{2}(abC_{5})^{2}}Y\oplus_{p}X\simeq_{1}X\oplus_{p}Y\simeq_{b^{2}C_{5}^{2}}Y.\) Thus \(X\simeq_{a^{4}b^{4}C_{5}^{4}}Y\). This completes the proof. ∎

In case (a), the choice of the norm on the two-fold direct sums is only a normalisation. One may equally work with the max-norm, as in , or with any other standard norm on a finite direct sum; the resulting formulation is equivalent, with constants changing by a factor depending only on that choice.

B.

Duals of the \(p\)th James spaces

−

We record a short permanence argument for the duals of the \(p\)th James spaces. Throughout this appendix \(1<p<\infty\), and \(q\) denotes the conjugate exponent, so that \(1/p+1/q=1\). We use the standard facts that \(J_{p}\) is quasi-reflexive of order one and that every closed infinite-dimensional subspace of \(J_{p}\) contains a complemented subspace isomorphic to \(\ell_{p}\); see, for example, . For \(p=2\), the primarity input below is Casazza’s theorem ; for general \(p\) we state the result conditionally on primarity of \(J_{p}\).

Let \(X\) be an infinite-dimensional Banach space. Suppose that \(X\) contains a complemented subspace \(E\) such that

\(E\simeq E\oplus\mathbb{K}.\)

Then \(X\simeq X\oplus\mathbb{K}\). In particular, \(X\) is isomorphic to each of its hyperplanes.

Proof.Fold proof

Write \(X=E\oplus F\) for some closed subspace \(F\) of \(X\). Then

\(X\oplus\mathbb{K}\simeq E\oplus F\oplus\mathbb{K}\simeq(E\oplus\mathbb{K})\oplus F\simeq E\oplus F=X.\)

Hence \(X\) is isomorphic to one of its hyperplanes.

It remains only to recall the standard fact that any two hyperplanes of an infinite-dimensional Banach space are isomorphic. Indeed, let

\(H=\ker f,\qquad K=\ker g,\)

where \(f,g\in X^{*}\) are non-zero. If \(H=K\), there is nothing to prove. Otherwise \(f\) and \(g\) are linearly independent, and hence there exists \(u\in X\) such that

\(f(u)=g(u)=1.\)

Define

\(T\colon H\to K,\qquad Th=h-g(h)u.\)

Then \(g(Th)=0\), so \(T(H)\subseteq K\). Similarly,

\(S\colon K\to H,\qquad Sk=k-f(k)u\)

is well-defined. A direct calculation gives \(ST=\mathrm{Id}_{H}\) and \(TS=\mathrm{Id}_{K}\). Thus \(T\) is an isomorphism from \(H\) onto \(K\). Since \(X\) is isomorphic to one of its hyperplanes, every hyperplane of \(X\) is therefore isomorphic to \(X\). ∎

Let us record the following well-known fact.

Let \(X\) be quasi-reflexive of order one. Then \(X^{*}\) is quasi-reflexive of order one. Moreover, if \(X=Y\oplus Z\), then

\(X^{**}/\kappa_{X}(X)\simeq\bigl(Y^{**}/\kappa_{Y}(Y)\bigr)\oplus\bigl(Z^{**}/\kappa_{Z}(Z)\bigr),\)

where \(\kappa_{X}\), \(\kappa_{Y}\), and \(\kappa_{Z}\) denote the canonical embeddings.

Proof.Fold proof

Since \(X\) is quasi-reflexive of order one, \(\dim\bigl(X^{**}/\kappa_{X}(X)\bigr)=1.\) The annihilator \(\kappa_{X}(X)^{\perp}\) in \(X^{***}\) is therefore one-dimensional. For each \(\Phi\in X^{***}\), set \(x^{*}=\Phi\circ\kappa_{X}\in X^{*}\). Then \(\Phi-\kappa_{X^{*}}(x^{*})\) vanishes on \(\kappa_{X}(X)\). Hence

\(X^{***}=\kappa_{X^{*}}(X^{*})\oplus\kappa_{X}(X)^{\perp}.\)

Thus \(\kappa_{X^{*}}(X^{*})\) has codimension one in \(X^{***}\), so \(X^{*}\) is quasi-reflexive of order one.

Now suppose that \(X=Y\oplus Z\). The canonical identification

\(X^{**}\simeq Y^{**}\oplus Z^{**}\)

sends \(\kappa_{X}(y+z)\) to \(\kappa_{Y}(y)\oplus\kappa_{Z}(z)\). Hence

\(\kappa_{X}(X)\simeq\kappa_{Y}(Y)\oplus\kappa_{Z}(Z),\)

and the displayed quotient decomposition follows. ∎

Let \(X\) be a quasi-reflexive Banach space of order one. Suppose that

  1. (i)

    \(X\) is primary;

  2. (ii)

    \(X\) is isomorphic to each of its hyperplanes;

  3. (iii)

    \(X^{*}\) is isomorphic to each of its hyperplanes.

Then \(X^{*}\) is primary.

Proof.Fold proof

Since \(X\) is quasi-reflexive of order one, \(X^{**}\) is isomorphic to \(X\oplus\mathbb{K}\). By hypothesis, \(X\oplus\mathbb{K}\simeq X\), and therefore \(X^{**}\simeq X.\)

Let \(X^{*}=Y\oplus Z\) be a direct-sum decomposition. Passing to duals gives

\(X^{**}\simeq Y^{*}\oplus Z^{*}.\)

Since \(X^{**}\simeq X\) and \(X\) is primary, either \(Y^{*}\simeq X\) or \(Z^{*}\simeq X\). We may assume, without loss of generality, that \(Y^{*}\simeq X.\) Then \(Y\) is not reflexive, because \(X\) is not reflexive.

By Lemma B.2, \(X^{*}\) is quasi-reflexive of order one and

\((X^{*})^{**}/\kappa_{X^{*}}(X^{*})\simeq\bigl(Y^{**}/\kappa_{Y}(Y)\bigr)\oplus\bigl(Z^{**}/\kappa_{Z}(Z)\bigr).\)

The left-hand side is one-dimensional. Since \(Y\) is not reflexive, the quotient \(Y^{**}/\kappa_{Y}(Y)\) is non-zero. Consequently \(\dim\bigl(Y^{**}/\kappa_{Y}(Y)\bigr)=1.\) Thus \(Y\) is a hyperplane in \(Y^{**}\).

Dualising \(Y^{*}\simeq X\) gives \(Y^{**}\simeq X^{*}.\) Therefore \(Y\) is isomorphic to a hyperplane of \(X^{*}\). By hypothesis, every hyperplane of \(X^{*}\) is isomorphic to \(X^{*}\). Hence \(Y\simeq X^{*}\). Thus, in every decomposition of \(X^{*}\) into two complemented summands, at least one summand is isomorphic to \(X^{*}\), and so \(X^{*}\) is primary. ∎

Let \(1<p<\infty\). If \(J_{p}\) is primary, then \(J_{p}^{*}\) is primary. In particular, the dual of the classical James space \(J_{2}\) is primary.

Proof.Fold proof

By the standard complemented-subspace theorem for \(J_{p}\), the space \(J_{p}\) contains a complemented subspace \(E\) isomorphic to \(\ell_{p}\). Since \(\ell_{p}\simeq\ell_{p}\oplus\mathbb{K},\) Lemma B.1 shows that \(J_{p}\) is isomorphic to each of its hyperplanes.

Let \(P\colon J_{p}\to E\) be a bounded projection. Then \(P^{*}\colon J_{p}^{*}\to J_{p}^{*}\) is a bounded projection, and its range is naturally isomorphic to \(E^{*}\). Since \(E\simeq\ell_{p}\), we have \(E^{*}\simeq\ell_{q},\) where \(q\) is conjugate to \(p\). Thus \(J_{p}^{*}\) contains a complemented copy of \(\ell_{q}\). Since \(\ell_{q}\simeq\ell_{q}\oplus\mathbb{K},\) Lemma B.1 shows that \(J_{p}^{*}\) is also isomorphic to each of its hyperplanes.

The space \(J_{p}\) is quasi-reflexive of order one. If, in addition, \(J_{p}\) is primary, then Proposition B.3, applied with \(X=J_{p}\), gives that \(J_{p}^{*}\) is primary. For \(p=2\), the required primarity of \(J_{2}\) is precisely Casazza’s theorem . ∎

The proof above uses primarity of \(J_{p}\) only as an input. For \(p=2\), this input is classical by . The remaining structural ingredients used here are the quasi-reflexivity of \(J_{p}\) of order one and the complemented \(\ell_{p}\)-subspace theorem for \(J_{p}\); both are recorded in . Notice that the dual hyperplane reduction uses the complemented copy of \(\ell_{q}\) obtained by dualising a projection onto a complemented copy of \(\ell_{p}\) in \(J_{p}\); the exact exponent is immaterial for the argument, since every \(\ell_{r}\) with \(1<r<\infty\) is isomorphic to its hyperplanes.
